## Source 6
Slice read: notes 3750-4499 (750 notes, 50 videos; 365 opening / 265 middlegame / 120 endgame). Every computer citation below was checked by grep in /home/user/wt-work/src/services.

The reference coach teaches through about 26 repeating acts, and nearly all of them hang on one habit. He names the TEMPTING or NATURAL choice, says the concrete reason it fails, then gives the move that works. Examples: "not Bf5, which runs into Nh4"; "not the queen recapture, that loses a tempo"; "not e5, it drops a pawn". He almost never says a move without its point. In the opening he says WHY the line is theory: what the move prepares, what it stops, and what it allows. A small or quiet move gets its hidden job named, for example c6 exists so d4 can come with gain of time later, and a5 stops b4. He states consequences as a chain: "if X then Y, and that is why". He also gives the condition under which the idea works ("only because the bishop on c4 already covers the escape square"; "f6 is safe here because they have no light-squared bishop").

Golden nuggets in this slice:
- a pin is fatal when no pawn defends the pinned piece;
- defend with the least valuable piece;
- bad bishops defend good pawns;
- how far a long-range piece retreats says nothing about whether the move is good;
- whenever a pawn moves, look for the weaknesses it leaves;
- two pieces a knight's distance apart means a fork should light up;
- queen and king on one line means look for a pin;
- a piece defended only once is a target;
- telling temporary from permanent;
- the best-case-scenario test before a pawn storm;
- give the material back when unsure in a gambit.

Most acts already have a computer in src/services. The strongest matches are speedRunReads.ts (keepTension :49, provokes :125, overprotect :209, bestCasePlan :435, rejectedMoveLater :486, forceConcession :512, flexibleFirst :549), refutedAlternative.ts:81, deliberation.ts:144, moveInsight.ts (weakenedBy :523, doubleAttack :83, mechanismContrast :459), latentFork/forkTrick, pinGeometry/pinPressure, outpost, recaptureChoice, positionTransformation, ruleException, kingSafety and endgamePawnReads.

MISSING:
1. A "condition-it-depends-on" computer: why the same move is bad in one position and good in another.
2. A "trapped piece by pawn advance" live detector. The tag exists only in the classifiers and the puzzle tools; there is no live board computer.
3. "Induce a move you want": a check or attack whose real point is the forced reply that ruins the opponent's structure.
4. "Temporary vs permanent" weighing.
5. "Uncastled / stranded king as a standing target, with the plan built round it". detectCentralKingDanger (kingSafety.ts:142) covers part of this.
6. "Defended once = target" (overload by count). Partly covered in speedRunReads, but there is no named computer.
7. "Retreat is not passive" (long-range piece keeps its line).
8. "Least valuable defender" as a teaching fact. It exists only in the capture-order lines of thinkingExchangeChain.ts:191.
9. "Give the material back" in gambits.

Negative examples worth logging as anti-patterns for F01 (description, not teaching):
- Two stretches are pure play-by-play. Notes 4137-4188 (a whole game) and 4404-4454 read like "You develop the knight to c3."
- Some notes carry clock, ego and "I" chatter: 3915, 3925, 4068.
Neither must ever be copied.
RHYTHM: OPENING (book moves): one short clause per move that names the move and its single point ("You put the question to the bishop with a6"; "the knight to d2, not c3 — so the c-pawn can come to c3"). The opening is named the moment it appears, and alternatives are named in passing ("the Møller is …Bc5, the main move is the modest …Be7"). A run of book moves is still about one line each, never silent, and the long explanation is saved for the move where the opponent departs or the trap appears. That move gets 2-4 sentences: what the slip is, why it looks natural, the punishing move, and the line in words. EARLY MIDDLEGAME: the longest notes (3-5 sentences). The plan is stated once ("pile on d4: double rooks, knight to f5"), then each later move is one clause tied back to it. At a decision there is a short weighing of the tempting choice, why it fails and what works, plus a principle line. CRITICAL TACTICAL MOMENT: the full line in words, the forced reply named, and the condition that makes it work. CONVERSION / ENDGAME: drops to one clause or none per move: "simplify", "just push the g-pawn", "bring every piece in". The one exception is a single principle note on conversion order: king to the centre, rooks to open files, find the wing for the passed pawn. The density follows decision weight, not move number. Quiet-but-meaningful moves (a5, c6, h6, b3) always get their purpose, even mid-sequence.
- Names the tempting/natural alternative, says the concrete reason it fails, then gives the move that works (Any decision point where a natural-looking move loses something concrete; most dense in opening and early middlegame) e.g. Not the bishop to f5, which runs into a knight hitting it and toppling the structure; instead a pawn to f5 anchors the knight. -> refutedAlternative.ts:81 refutedAlternative + deliberation.ts:144 buildDeliberation / :289 deliberationWeighing; speedRunReads.ts:486 rejectedMoveLater
- States the hidden purpose of a quiet or prep move: what it prepares or what it stops (Small pawn moves and quiet developing moves in the opening and early middlegame) e.g. The c6 pawn exists so that d4 can later gain space while harassing the knight; a5 is there so the opponent can never push b4. -> speedRunReads.ts:549 flexibleFirst, :307 usefulWaiting; opponentIntent.ts:55 buildOpponentIntent (what it stops); preparation in speedRunReads.ts:463 preparationOf
- Explains why the theory is theory: the opening's idea, named, with the principle behind each main-line move (Opening book moves, especially the first time a system appears) e.g. The knight goes to d2 rather than c3 so the c-pawn stays free to come to c3 and reinforce the centre; there is the payoff now, c3 propping d4. -> openingIdentity.ts:51 identityFor + openingAnnouncement.ts; theory meaning partly in reviewOpeningTheory.ts; no computer derives 'the reason for this book move' from the board (partial)
- Names the opponent's slip as a known, common mistake at this level, then the punishment as a line (The ply the opponent leaves good play in the opening) e.g. This pawn push is a famous mistake: it opens the very diagonal your queen wants; the knight sacrifice then distracts and the queen arrives. -> openingTrapDetector.ts:79 detectTrapInPosition, gemFinder.ts:286, positionTrapScan.ts:126 scanPositionForTrap, theoryDeparture.ts:73 findTheoryDeparture
- Gives the CONDITION that makes a tactic or idea work (or not), naming the one piece or square that decides it (Before or at a tactical shot; when explaining why a familiar sac is premature) e.g. The queen trap works only because your bishop on c4 already covers the queen's one escape square; the sacrifice doesn't work yet because their queen still guards g4. -> partial: pinGeometry.ts:135 isRealPin / :178 pinBites, causalChain.ts:639; no general 'condition' computer — MISSING as a named fact
- Teaches that the same move changes value when the position changes, and says what changed (When a previously rejected idea becomes good) e.g. The bishop sortie you rejected earlier is now excellent: their h-pawn push weakened g4 and their queen has left the square that made the knight trick work. -> speedRunReads.ts:486 rejectedMoveLater (partial); the explicit 'what changed' diff is MISSING
- Names a golden-nugget principle in one line, stated as a reusable rule (Right after the move that shows it, as a takeaway) e.g. A pin is fatal when no pawn defends the pinned piece — pile on and collect it; do a defensive job with your cheapest adequate piece; bad bishops defend good pawns. -> pinPressure.ts:49 PIN_PRESSURE_PRINCIPLE (pin nugget); principleVoice.ts / principleAttribution.ts; least-valuable-defender and bad-bishop nuggets MISSING as facts
- Points out a drawback the move created and what it now means (weakened diagonal, hole, loose king) (After a weakening pawn move by either side) e.g. That f-pawn push weakens the king's diagonal; with the bishop already staring down it, castling becomes a nightmare. -> moveInsight.ts:523 weakenedBy; kingSafety.ts:56 detectKingExposure; latentDanger.ts:87
- Whenever a pawn advances, it scans for the weaknesses that move left behind (Opponent pawn moves in middlegame) e.g. A pawn just moved, so run the check: two pawns are now loose, and when you see a good capture, look for a better one that also hits the rook. -> moveInsight.ts:523 weakenedBy + loosePieces.ts:35 findLoosePieces; habit phrasing via methodBeat.ts:116
- Geometry cue: two pieces a knight's distance apart, or queen and king on one line, should set off the fork or pin alarm (When the shape appears, before the tactic is played) e.g. Their bishop and queen stand a knight's jump apart — that shape should light up the fork every time; queen and king on the same diagonal means look for the pin. -> latentFork.ts:161 detectLatentFork; forkTrick.ts:81; pinGeometry.ts:135; the 'alarm shape' phrased as a habit is partly in methodBeat.ts
- Weighs a pawn-storm/plan with the best-case-scenario test before committing (Before launching a pawn storm or a long plan) e.g. Even if a4-a5-a6 all landed, they just answer b5 and you've spent three moves for nothing — so attack with pieces instead. -> speedRunReads.ts:435 bestCasePlan
- Keep the tension: lets the opponent decide the central capture, explains why that burdens them (Pawn or piece tension in the centre) e.g. When unsure, keep the tension — carrying the decision is more of a headache for them than for you; a standoff of queens: don't be the one to release it. -> speedRunReads.ts:49 keepTension
- Which recapture: picks the recapture by what it does for development or structure, says why the other is worse (Any recapture choice) e.g. Recapture with the d-pawn: it opens the file and frees your light bishop, whereas the f-pawn would box that bishop in. -> recaptureChoice.ts:56 readRecapture / :103 recaptureChoice
- Transform an advantage: give up one edge (material, pawn mass, a piece back) to cash a lasting one (When up material or holding a static edge, especially vs gambits) e.g. You hand the extra pawn back for lasting positional pluses; when unsure in a gambit you can always give the piece back and cash development. -> positionTransformation.ts:83 detectPositionTransformation (partial); 'give the material back' as a teaching fact MISSING
- Temporary vs permanent: a short-term blemish is accepted for a permanent gain (Middlegame plan decisions) e.g. The knight clogs the file for a moment, but piece placement is temporary while prying that file open is permanent — don't confuse the two. -> MISSING
- Induce a move you want: a check or attack whose real point is the forced reply that damages the opponent (Opening/middlegame structural moments) e.g. The queen check doesn't win the bishop; its point is to induce the knight to c3, which permanently denies the c-pawn its job of supporting d4. -> speedRunReads.ts:125 provokes and :512 forceConcession (partial); the structural consequence of the induced reply is MISSING
- Outpost + support: plant a piece where no pawn can kick it, anchored by a pawn (Middlegame piece placement) e.g. The knight lands on e6 and paralyses them — propped up by the pawn chain, it can never be undermined; anchor an advanced knight with a pawn. -> outpost.ts:39 isOutpost / :22 noPawnCanChallenge; speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole, :316 keepSquareForKnight
- Target the weak piece or structural target: name the weakest piece, then the plan to pile on it (After structure settles) e.g. Their bishop on c3 is a bad piece, so you start a campaign: double the rooks on the d-file and reroute the knight, and the d4 pawn becomes a sitting duck. -> pieceQuality.ts:209 explainEvalByPieceQuality; boardStructure.ts:269 describeStructure; nextPlans.ts:81 findWorstPlacedPiece; reviewPieceItinerary.ts:47
- Piece defended only once / loose piece is a target (Middlegame scan) e.g. That bishop is defended only once and the diagonal is weakened — once the knight steps aside the queen swings in and the bishop falls. -> loosePieces.ts:35 findLoosePieces; speedRunReads.ts:209 overprotect (own side); 'defended exactly once' as an opponent target partly MISSING
- Trapped piece: shows how a pawn advance traps a piece with no retreat (When a piece strays to the edge or deep) e.g. The knight going to the rim looks natural but is a classic blunder — the b-pawn simply traps it. -> tag only in tacticClassifierService.ts:25 (trapped_piece); no live board computer — MISSING
- Stranded/uncastled king as the standing target; plan built around keeping it there (Opening-to-middlegame transition) e.g. They still haven't castled; a queen move stops castling, and every tempo they spend chasing the queen is one you spend expanding in the centre. -> kingSafety.ts:142 detectCentralKingDanger; reviewSacrifice.ts:113 enemyKingStuckInCenter (partial)
- A move that does two jobs is named as such; prefers the dual-purpose move (Choosing between candidate moves) e.g. The queen to d5 centralises, hits the rook and adds a second defender to d4 in one stroke; a pawn to c6 attacks the queen and defends the knight at once. -> moveInsight.ts:83 doubleAttack (attacking half); speedRunReads.ts:383 goodInEveryBranch; defending+attacking dual purpose partly MISSING
- Retreats aren't passive: a long-range piece keeps its line from further back (Retreat moves by long-range pieces) e.g. Don't fear dropping the bishop back — from d8 it eyes h4 just as it did from f6 and clears the file for the rook. -> speedRunReads.ts:421 retreatKeepsBreak (partial); MISSING as a general fact
- Order of operations: an in-between capture or move first turns a good position into a won one (Tactical sequences with move-order choice) e.g. Resist the tempting immediate check, which just meets a pawn block — capture first, then check. -> speedRunReads.ts:178 secureFirst, :294 skipMiddleman; causalChain.ts:639
- Defensive discipline habit before an aggressive move: check the opponent's checks and tricks first (Before committing moves in sharp positions) e.g. Before kicking the knight, do the discipline: look at their checks and rule out a mating trick; only then proceed. -> methodBeat.ts:116 methodBeatFor; safetyHabits.ts:25 blunderCheck
- Conversion technique: names the order for converting a material lead (simplify, centralise king, open files, make a passed pawn, activate every piece) (Winning middlegame into endgame) e.g. Up material, the skill is the conversion: offer the queen trade, centralise the king, bring rooks to open files, find the wing for a passed pawn. -> endgamePawnReads.ts:52 passerKinds / :77 outsidePasserDecoy; endgameTechnique.ts; planRace.ts:180; the 'conversion order' as one taught sequence is partly MISSING

## Source 7
Read all 1,500 notes (#4500-#5999; 100 videos; 760 opening / 592 middlegame / 148 endgame; 840 on the student's own move, 660 on the opponent's) end to end, and catalogued 97 distinct teaching acts, each mapped to verified code (file:line): 37 already computed, 48 partial, 11 missing, 1 not a computer by design.

The surprise is how much already exists. speedRunReads.ts holds about 27 of the reference coach's habits, and moveIntent, moveOrder, theirMoveCost, recaptureChoice, falseAlarm, bluffDetector, deliberation, buildRejectedTempting, tradeJudgement, conversionMethod, forkTrick, latentFork and the gem/trap-ahead computers cover most of the rest. The gap is mostly CONDITIONS and COMPARISONS, not whole computers.

OPENING GAPS (F02), highest value first:
1. The defining-move clause. openingIdentity.ts:20 computes `defining` offline, and nothing in src reads it. That is computed and then dropped (G8.5).
2. The opening's bargain in one sentence.
3. A contrast with the sibling opening.
4. On a book departure, the job the book move did that the played move doesn't.
5. Choosing, among close moves, the one that sets a trap, and setting bait.
6. Accepting vs declining a gambit.
7. Move-order safety at the repertoire level.

PATTERN-CONDITION GAPS (F04/S12):
- greekGift (moveInsight.ts:668) recognises the shape but checks none of its conditions.
- findOverloadedPieces skips duties to anything worth under 3 and duties to mating squares (tacticsDetector.ts:699).
- findTrappedPieces only counts a piece that is already attacked (tacticsDetector.ts:459-468), so nets built in advance are invisible (a rook in the corner, a queen after a pawn grab).

MISSING METHOD HABITS:
- don't move the attacked piece on reflex
- the two-pieces-attacked checklist
- which rook, decided by the other rook's job
- picture the board after castling
- which pawn gives real luft
- close the centre to attack on a wing
- whose attack lands first
- wait until they castle before storming
- credit the opponent's good defence
- create an imbalance to win an equal position
- give material back at the right moment
- pawns as anchors for pieces
- bad bishops defend good pawns

CORPUS HAZARDS if notes are voiced verbatim in 'teach me X opening' (S7):
- 169/1500 notes speak in the first person (V1).
- Teaching is credited to named people: #4693, #5555 (F0d).
- #5176 cites the coach's own game (V1).
- 10 notes carry digits or percentages: #4501, #4509, #4832, #5742 (V8).

TWO CODE FLAGS TO CHECK:
- theoryDeparture.ts:62 picks the 'what players at your level play' explorer band by rating (F10?).
- openingIdentity.ts:144 caps famous games at two with .slice(0, 2) (G4.5/V14).

On method: frequencies are regex counts over the slice (precision mixed, ±30%), anchored by the note ids given in each entry.
RHYTHM: These figures are measured over all 1,500 notes; they are not estimates.

WORDS PER NOTE: median 23, mean 27.6, p10 6, p90 51. By phase the median is 23 in the opening, 25 in the middlegame and 18 in the endgame.
- 1-9 words: 21%
- 10-24 words: 32%
- 25-49 words: 35%
- 50-99 words: 9%
- 100+ words: 1.5%

HE SPEAKS ON ALMOST EVERY PLY (V11). Of 1,400 consecutive note pairs in the same video, 1,089 skip no ply, 194 skip one, and 117 skip two or more. Only 148 notes (10%) are bare move-narration (9 words or fewer, no reason), and two videos account for most of those.

BOTH SIDES GET EQUAL AIRTIME: median 21 words on the opponent's move vs 22 on the student's own.

THE LONG MONOLOGUES (90+ words, 25 notes) never fall in the endgame: 17 are middlegame, 7 opening, 0 endgame. They sit at decision points, often on the OPPONENT's move, where he works through the student's coming choice in advance.
- Deliberation language appears in 13% of opponent-move notes vs 10% of own-move notes.
- Notes on the student's own move open by naming the move 35% of the time, vs 24% on the opponent's move.
- So he thinks while their move is on the board, then names his move with its reason.

BY PHASE:
- Opening: 86% of opening notes (655/760) carry an explicit reason. One opening ply typically stacks the name or theory status, the idea, and what the move prepares or stops (V19 holds).
- Middlegame: the longest thoughts.
- Endgame and conversion: shorter, technique-led, often 'several moves win'.

LINKING (F0b): 48% of notes over 9 words carry an explicit link (because / so / but / instead / the point). About 7% of thoughts (104) run across two plies: a sentence starts on one move and finishes on the next.

ORDER INSIDE A LONG NOTE (matches F18; e.g. #4517, #4841, #4935-4937, #5051):
1. What their move did or threatens.
2. The candidates, with the tempting one named and refuted by a short line.
3. Not yet: first this.
4. The choice, with its one deciding reason.
5. Close on a general habit or rule.
- Names the opening or structure on the move that defines it, and again when a transposition changes the family (The defining opening ply; a later transposition ply) e.g. After the early swap on d5 and the e-pawn recapture, this is the Carlsbad structure: their c-pawn against your e-pawn, everything else symmetric. That one imbalance is what the middlegame is about. -> PARTIAL. Name and transposition: openingAnnouncement.ts:54 (transposition clause :60-80). Structure: positionReadingService.ts:1060 namedPawnStructure and boardStructure.ts:269 describeStructure. MISSING: the 'this move is what makes it X' clause. openingIdentity.ts:20 computes `defining` and nothing in src reads it.
- States the opening's bargain or central question in one sentence (Early opening, once per game, right after the first characteristic move) e.g. Black lets White build the big pawn centre on purpose, planning to hit it later from the side with ...e5 or ...c5. The whole game is whether that centre cracks before White can use it. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine says what the opening provokes (:103-120), how long a gambit stays a pawn down (:121-125), what it aims for: locked centre, isolated pawn, fianchetto (:126-137), and whether it is sharp or quiet (:138-142). mastersPlanRead.ts:181 names each side's break. MISSING: the trade-off sentence (cede X to get Y; the question the opening poses).
- Names the system's key square or goal, then justifies later moves by it (When the opponent first challenges the key square; it recurs move after move) e.g. This whole setup lives on e5: lose it and their pawns start rolling. So you don't take on f6, you recapture with the knight, and even the modest Bf4 and Nd2-f3 are chosen because each adds a guard to e5. -> PARTIAL. mastersPlanRead.ts:83 (the break masters choose), keySquares.ts:97 keyTargetSquares, planArc.ts:236 stepArc (follows a plan's aims across moves). MISSING: a persistent 'square this system lives on' that later moves are measured against.
- Contrasts the line with its sibling opening: the one difference that changes the plan (When a familiar setup arises by an unusual order, or the opponent applies the sibling opening's standard plan) e.g. It looks like a Grünfeld setup, but your c-pawn isn't on c4, and that makes it far sharper. In the ordinary London you'd meet ...c5 with c3; here your knight on c3 already hits d5, so taking on c5 is the move. -> MISSING. structureSignature.ts:65 computeStructureSignature and :165 signatureMatchScore match structures, but only to pick notes; nothing speaks a sibling contrast.
- Move-order and transposition safety at the repertoire level (Moves 2-6 of anti-lines; whenever a reply could transpose) e.g. Answer with the knight first so your Dragon setup stays available. Pick the other reply and they can play Nf3 and d4 and drop you into a Sicilian you don't play. -> PARTIAL. openingAnnouncement.ts:54-80 notices a transposition after it happens; moveOrder.ts:65 covers the tactical 'X first because Y'. MISSING: choosing an order to avoid a transposition.
- Theory status of each opening move: main road, second-tier, rare, respectable (Each opening ply, especially at deviations) e.g. The usual move here is c3; the knight to f3 instead looks odd but is perfectly sound. Their reply is a second-tier option, not a mistake. -> COMPUTED. explorerTranslate.ts:15 translatePopularity (words, never digits), theoryDeparture.ts:73 findTheoryDeparture, bookDeparture.ts:49.
- Out of book: says what the book move would have done that the played move doesn't, then cashes it in (The departure ply, and the ply where the missing job becomes playable) e.g. They put the bishop on d3 instead of c4. That's out of book: it develops, but it doesn't do c4's job. A few moves later: the usual c4 is there to stop ...d5, so now ...d5 frees your game. -> PARTIAL. bookDeparture.ts:49 and theoryDeparture.ts:73 find the ply; moveIntent.ts:124 can compute any move's job. MISSING: comparing the book move's job with the opponent's actual move (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63 droppedJob is student-side only).
- The popular club reply, and what it hands you (The opponent's popular-but-inferior opening move) e.g. Plenty of players answer ...d6 here without knowing the theory. Your centre stays intact and your knight gets c3: a pleasant edge for free. -> PARTIAL. For the STUDENT's move: refutedAlternative.ts:81 with refutedAlternativeCore.ts:159 candidatesFromAmateur, and safetyHabits.ts:42 autopilotGuard. For the OPPONENT's popular move, only trap-tier gems fire (gemCrushLines.ts:572 gemMoveSignal) plus structural costs (theirMoveCost.ts:60). MISSING: the modest concession of their popular move. The amateur band is picked by rating (theoryDeparture.ts:62); check against F10.
- The only move, or only route to a playable position, in the opening (Forced moments in theory) e.g. Here they basically have to play ...d5; anything else hands you the whole centre. Against this attack there is exactly one defence. -> COMPUTED. criticalMoment.ts:164 readCriticalMoment (how many moves hold), criticalityScan.ts:103.
- Opening trap: the natural slip, the forced punishment, and the picture that makes it work (At the setup ply (invite or warn), and when the opponent walks in) e.g. Your queen on e7 looks down the e-file. If the e5-pawn disappeared and a knight landed on d3, it would be mate. So the knight takes e5, and if they grab the bishop instead, the knight to d3 is smothered mate. -> COMPUTED for the library. gemCrushLines.ts:554 trapAheadAt, :572 gemMoveSignal, :305 computeGemCrush; positionTrapScan.ts:126; trapLearning.ts:48 trapDecision; matePatterns.ts:341 classifyMatePattern. MISSING: the 'if X were gone, Y would be mate' visualisation line.
- Avoiding their trap: the tempting move is exactly what they want (When the student's natural move walks into a known trap) e.g. Hitting their queen with the bishop to c3 feels natural, but their bishop to b4 pins it to your king. Put the knight on c3 instead: same square, no pin, and their queen is still in trouble. -> PARTIAL. gemCrushLines.ts:554 trapAheadAt (trapAhead lane, computerRoles.ts:90), playCommentary.ts:497 buildRejectedTempting. MISSING: the 'same square, different piece' contrast.
- Chooses, among close moves, the one that sets a trap, or sets bait (When several moves are close and one hands the opponent a natural losing reply) e.g. The bishop to c5 is natural, but e3 blunts it. The check on b4 is the real try, because after the usual block the smothered-mate trick is live. Pushing h3 seems to drop the d4-pawn, but if the queen grabs it, Be3 shuts her in. -> MISSING. Every trap computer scans the CURRENT position for the opponent's slip (positionTrapScan.ts:9-15, openingTrapDetector.ts:79). None ranks the student's candidates by the trap each one sets.
- Develop with tempo; when they're behind, every developing move should threaten (Early queen sorties; gambit positions) e.g. The knight to c3 develops and hits their exposed queen. Then the bishop comes out to d6 already attacking the weak pawn. -> COMPUTED. moveFundamentals.ts:507 (develops with tempo, naming the piece hit), tempoCount.ts:32, moveInsight.ts:411-421 (don't hand them a tempo).
- Gambit decisions: accept or decline, and the compensation listed in one breath (On the gambit offer; when weighing a pawn-down position) e.g. Decline it: develop the knight and hit e4, because the gambit player wants you to grab. Later, a pawn down, your compensation is the d4 square, their stranded pawn, their bishop staring at its own pawns, and a king with nowhere safe to go. -> PARTIAL. reviewSacrifice.ts:44 sacrificeCompensation (what the material buys), openingIdentity.ts:121-125 (how long the gambit stays a pawn down). MISSING: the decline-vs-accept choice.
- A formula for punishing offbeat openings, with honest expectations (The first moves against an offbeat system) e.g. Against a strange setup: develop, open the centre, then go for the king. No early queen checks, because they just run into ...g6. And expect a healthy edge, not a quick mate. -> PARTIAL. thinkAloud.ts:180 opponentHabits (their minors at home, wasted tempi), development.ts:63 homeMinorCount, ruleException.ts:70 (early queen). MISSING: the formula itself and the expectation-setting.
- Two or more reasons for one move, ranked (The student's constructive quiet move) e.g. f3 does two jobs. Mainly it prepares g4 and h4-h5; second, it takes e4 away from both their knights. -> COMPUTED. moveIntent.ts:124 (prevents plus prepares = two jobs; stopReason :383, whatItDoes :423), deliberation.ts:144 (multi-job move-why). PARTIAL: ranking which job matters most.
- The drawback of your own good move, stated and weighed (Committal pawn moves; defensive moves with a side effect) e.g. d5 shuts out their light bishop and piles onto the knight. It does hand over a square and loosen your centre, but that's a price worth paying; every central pawn push gives up a square somewhere. -> PARTIAL. concessionBeat.ts:360 findStudentDrawback and backwardLook.ts:470 lookConcession (drawback lane, computerRoles.ts:54) speak only when the engine preferred another move; moveInsight.ts:523 weakenedBy. MISSING: weighing a drawback on the BEST move ('it costs X, worth it because Y').
- After every pawn push, the habit: what did it stop guarding? (Every opponent pawn move, and the student's own) e.g. They prop up the knight with a4. Any time a pawn moves, ask which squares it no longer covers: here b4 becomes a home for your knight. -> COMPUTED. theirMoveCost.ts:60 (hole, bishop shut in, castling lost, structure), moveInsight.ts:573 theirMoveChanged and :523 weakenedBy. The own-pawn version of the habit exists as a principle line, principleVoice.ts:68.
- What their move cost them, or which of their own pieces it blocked (The opponent's natural-looking opening moves) e.g. Their bishop to d3 shuts in their own dark bishop. Their c3 takes the c3-square from their own knight. Their queen check from e6 blocks their bishop and walks into the crossfire. -> COMPUTED. theirMoveCost.ts:60 (the 'bishop shut in' kind at theirMoveCost.ts:109); theirMoveCost lane, computerRoles.ts:82.
- What the move prevents (prophylaxis), including taking away a tempo; restrain first, act second (Quiet moves before the opponent's plan lands) e.g. h3, so their bishop can never pin from g4. The king to h7 guards h6 in advance, so Be3 won't come with tempo. Stop their pawn break before you start your own play. -> COMPUTED. moveIntent.ts:124 PREVENTS (null-move read, moveIntent.ts:4-12), stopReason :383.
- Take the sting out, rather than physically stopping the attacker (A looming fork or attack where the direct defence is passive) e.g. Don't try to stop the knight jump to b5. Move one of the two pieces it would fork, preferably to a better square (c5 rather than e7), and the jump becomes harmless. -> COMPUTED. speedRunReads.ts:400 takeTheSting.
- Move order: this first, because... (Whenever two good moves conflict in order) e.g. Take on d4 first, then deal with the knight. Bring the queen's knight out before the king's knight, or the bishop to g4 pins it. -> COMPUTED. moveOrder.ts:65 (moveOrder lane, computerRoles.ts:67).
- Skip the middleman: is the preparatory move needed at all? (Before preparing a pawn break) e.g. Everyone reaches for the rook move first. But do you need it? e5 works right now: if they take twice, the rook to e1 skewers their queen. -> COMPUTED for pawn breaks: speedRunReads.ts:294 skipMiddleman.
- Flexible move first; play the moves you'll need anyway; let them commit (Early opening or middlegame, while the plan is undecided) e.g. Start with ...d6, which every setup needs. Castling is the most flexible move and makes them commit first. Keep your bishop home until you see where theirs goes. -> COMPUTED. speedRunReads.ts:549 flexibleFirst, :307 usefulWaiting.
- Recapture choice, with its reason (Every recapture with more than one option) e.g. Take back with the bishop, not the queen, because a rook would hit the queen along the open file with tempo. Recapture with the c-pawn to keep the a-file shut in front of your king. -> COMPUTED. recaptureChoice.ts:103 (readRecapture :56); recapture lane, computerRoles.ts:66.
- Which piece to keep: the one that can use the weakness (Trades near a hole or outpost) e.g. Give up the bishop and keep the knight. d6 is the hole and only a knight can live there; a bishop would just stare at its own pawns. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole (a bishop on an outpost that a knight could reach). MISSING: the trade-decision framing.
- In-between moves; never recapture or trade on reflex (Inside exchanges; whenever a recapture looks automatic) e.g. Before taking their queen back, give the knight check on e7 first: you come out two pawns up. They took on e4, correctly, but you don't recapture by reflex: the pawn to d6 forks first. -> PARTIAL. thinkAloud.ts:145 notYet, moveInsight.ts:642 autopilotRecapture (Tactics), safetyHabits.ts:42 autopilotGuard, kneeJerk.ts:15 (the reflex recapture), speedRunReads.ts:178 secureFirst.
- Choose the capture that leaves them no in-between move; take the attacked piece first (Several captures are available) e.g. Win the pawn with the knight, not the pawn, because the pawn capture lets them slip in a knight capture of their own first. Take the hanging rook before collecting anything else. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:178 secureFirst. MISSING: ruling out the capture that permits THEIR in-between move.
- First question, what's their threat? Stated as their plan, with the clock it puts on yours (Every opponent move, especially quiet ones) e.g. They can't castle yet; their idea is to bring the knight back to f7 and then castle. So your window is short. -> COMPUTED. groundedAnswer.ts:6890 detectNewThreat (threat lane, computerRoles.ts:49), threatOut.ts:71 computeMustDefend, moveIntent.ts:124 on their seat (theirIntent lane, computerRoles.ts:84), opponentIntent.ts:55 buildOpponentIntent, methodBeat.ts:60 'opponent-threat' habit. MISSING: the time this gives you.
- Reads intent from a move, and deters it (The opponent's committal quiet move) e.g. Their queen to e2 hints at long castling. The pawn to a5 tells them: castle there and your king gets torn apart. -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124 on their seat (what the move prepares). MISSING: deterrence, making their plan unattractive before it happens.
- Don't panic: the threat isn't real, or the activity is fake, with the reason (After aggressive-looking opponent moves) e.g. The pawn to b4 is no threat; your knight just drops back to e2. What is that knight on e5 actually attacking? Nothing. A piece that looks menacing with no threat behind it is empty. -> COMPUTED. falseAlarm.ts:37 (lane computerRoles.ts:51), bluffDetector.ts:37 detectBluff, kneeJerk.ts:15, moveInsight.ts:909 emptyThreat.
- No trick without development: the lone-piece bluff (Early aggressive sorties) e.g. Their knight charges into d4 to scare you, but nothing is behind it. With one piece out there can't be a trick, so simply take on e5. -> COMPUTED. bluffDetector.ts:37 (its header describes this exact lesson, bluffDetector.ts:1-15). PARTIAL: the 'they have only one piece out' reason is not cited, though development.ts:63 homeMinorCount exists.
- Worst-case test: even if they got every move they wanted, could they win it? (Deciding whether to spend a move defending) e.g. Is that pawn really in danger? Give them all the moves they want and they still can't bring enough pieces to it, so don't waste a move. -> PARTIAL. kingSafety.ts:297 countKingAttack works for the king only. MISSING for any other target (countMethod.ts:17 counts current attackers only).
- Counts attackers against defenders on a square or a break (Before a capture or a pawn break) e.g. Their e4 break isn't coming: three of your pieces guard e4 and only two of theirs hit it. After the check, the bishop is attacked twice and defended once. -> COMPUTED. countMethod.ts:17 (lane computerRoles.ts:74), moveIntent.ts:383 stopReason (counts), exchangeLedger.ts:136.
- Names the opponent's slip as it happens: the refutation, and what they should have played (The opponent's mistake ply) e.g. That's the slip: the wrong knight went back. Now the bishop takes on g7 and the b-pawn rounds up the loose knight on c5. Had the other knight retreated, none of this was there. -> PARTIAL. backwardLook.ts:98 (coachMistake lane, computerRoles.ts:81), inaccuracyCall.ts:194 betterMoveReason, gemCrushLines.ts:572. MISSING: the 'right idea, wrong piece' contrast (the same plan with the other knight).
- Narrates the missed kill (a Miss) (When a side fails to punish) e.g. b4 was the knockout: the knight on c5 had nowhere to go. Instead the rook moved, and the win was gone. -> COMPUTED for the student: missedTacticService.ts:964 detectMissedTactics. PARTIAL for the opponent's miss on a live board (backwardLook, coach side).
- Credits the opponent's good move or defensive resource (The opponent finds an only move or a strong resource) e.g. Good defence. That knight jump was the one resource that kept them in the game. -> MISSING. criticalMoment.ts:164 knows when a move was the only one, but nothing says so for the opponent.
- What the opponent keeps doing wrong (After repeated tempo losses) e.g. They keep moving the same piece. Punish it by simply developing. All those pawn moves cost them time, so push d5 now. -> COMPUTED. thinkAloud.ts:180 opponentHabits, tempoCount.ts:32 (tempo lane, computerRoles.ts:86).
- Lists the loose pieces, then looks for one move that hits two (When a double attack exists) e.g. What's undefended? d6 is covered by their bishop, but f6 isn't, so the queen to d4 hits f6 and more. -> COMPUTED. loosePieces.ts:35 findLoosePieces, tacticsDetector.ts:119 findForks (every piece but the king, :126), moveInsight.ts:83 doubleAttack, looseTrigger.ts:14.
- End-of-line check: is anything loose when the line stops? (At the end of every calculated line) e.g. At the end of that line their knight on b5 is simply hanging. Missing a loose piece at the end of a calculation is one of the most common errors. The rook you took was guarded and your knight isn't attacked, so you're safe. -> PARTIAL. exchangeLedger.ts:241 settledNetForLine, lineCalc.ts:24 lineWins, safetyHabits.ts:25 blunderCheck (after the slip). MISSING: the spoken habit.
- Alignment geometry: a discovery or skewer in waiting, for either side, plus the mental note (The moment an alignment appears) e.g. The queens face each other on a diagonal with your knight in between: think discovery. Two loose bishops staring at each other are the seed of one. Their rook sees your queen through two bishops; they can't move both at once, so make a note and move the queen the moment one goes. -> PARTIAL. latentDanger.ts:87 detectLatentDanger (your king or queen behind a lesser piece, at most one shield); tacticsDetector.ts:571 findDiscoveredAttacks and :732 findBatteries for live ones. MISSING: the student's own discovery in waiting, and two-shield alignments.
- Forkable squares (Piece placement in the opening) e.g. Their queen sits on d5, a forkable square: the knight to b5 eyes c7. After ...a6 takes b5 away, b6 becomes the forkable square, so the knight heads for c4. -> COMPUTED. latentFork.ts:161 detectLatentFork.
- The centre-fork trick: name it and react automatically, or note it's premature (Open games, moves 3-8) e.g. Their bishop to c5 walks into the centre-fork trick: take on e5, and the d4 fork wins the piece back. Here the trick is available but premature, so keep it in reserve. -> COMPUTED. forkTrick.ts:81 forkTrickFor, :126 trickSidestepped.
- Pins: judge them, exploit them, and know what a pinned piece cannot do (Whenever a pin appears) e.g. Their pin doesn't actually threaten anything, so no need to react. When you have a pin, think about attacking the pinned piece. Your bishop is untouchable because the knight that could take it is pinned. -> PARTIAL. pinGeometry.ts:135 isRealPin, pinPressure.ts:85 findPinPressure, whyItFailed.ts:134 pinnedToMore. MISSING: 'untouchable because the capturer is pinned' as a defensive inventory, and the pin broken WITH TEMPO (questions.md item 7).
- Overloaded defender, including pawns and mate duties (When one defender has two jobs) e.g. Their f-pawn guards both g3 and the bishop, so it's overloaded and the rook takes on e3. They can't recapture on e7, because the queen also has to cover the back-rank mate. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:690 findOverloadedPieces skips targets worth under 3 (tacticsDetector.ts:699) and duties to mating squares, so both examples are invisible to it.
- Trapped pieces, including the net built before the attack (Pieces wandering to the rim or deep into your camp) e.g. d3 traps the knight on e4: their own e5-pawn covers both retreat squares. A rook in the corner looks safe, but the bishop to f4 and h6 plus a king walk cages it. It took five pieces working together to trap their queen. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:451 findTrappedPieces needs the piece already attacked (:459-468); moveInsight.ts:957 noRetreat. MISSING: a piece with no squares that isn't attacked yet (build the net, then attack).
- Mating mechanism found by the missing square: deflect its guard (Attacking near the enemy king) e.g. Your queen on a1 would be mate if d2 were covered. Your own bishop on d3 blocks the rook, so the rook to e2 forces their bishop to take it, and then the queen mates. Their knight is all that stops mate on h2, so plant a piece on d4 purely to lure it away. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:701 escapeSquareFirst (cover the flight square first), tacticsDetector.ts:630 findRemovableGuards (guards of pieces worth 3+, not of mating squares), reviewForcedSequence.ts:75 explainMatingSacMechanism (Review). MISSING: deflecting the guard of a MATING square.
- A pattern taught with its conditions (the Greek gift) (When the sacrifice is in the air) e.g. The bishop sacrifice on h7 needs g5 covered first; h4 does that, and if the king takes your knight, the h-pawn recaptures and opens the h-file. Here there's no Greek gift, because g4 is covered. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:668 greekGift recognises the shape: the bishop takes on h7 or h2 with check, a knight can reach g5 or g4, and a queen is on the board (moveInsight.ts:671-686). MISSING: every condition (is g5 covered, does the king capture lose to the pawn recapture).
- Moves ruled out by a check on a newly opened diagonal (Open games once the e8-h5 or e1-h4 diagonal opens) e.g. ...f6 isn't possible: the queen checks from h5. In these open positions never push the f-pawn, because the queen check is followed by Qxe5 forking king and rook. Don't take on e5 yet; the queen check on h4 is coming. -> PARTIAL. refutedAlternative.ts:81 refutes a natural alternative with its line. MISSING: the named 'diagonal check' nugget.
- Pawns attack too: pawn forks, a pawn winning a piece (Middlegame tactics) e.g. Don't forget the pawns: the d-pawn crashes in and wins the bishop. Pushing c5 and d5 loses to d6, forking queen and bishop. -> COMPUTED. tacticsDetector.ts:119 findForks (all non-king pieces, :126).
- Picture the board after castling: the rook changes lines (Before castling, or a queen move next to the castled rook) e.g. After you castle and bring the queen to f3, your rook and queen sit on one diagonal, and their bishop to g4 skewers them. People forget the rook moved. -> MISSING. latentDanger.ts:87 reads only the current board.
- Which pawn makes real luft (Making luft against a battery) e.g. With their bishop on d3 covering h7, pushing the h-pawn gives your king no square. The g-pawn does, and it shuts the bishop out; the weakened dark squares don't matter because they have no dark bishop. -> PARTIAL. moveFundamentals.ts:766-784 (luft as a fundamental). MISSING: choosing the pawn by which flight square it actually frees.
- Back rank: a mate threat needs pieces to deliver it; don't create one yourself (After trades, and in endgames) e.g. No need to make luft: they have no piece left that can mate on the back rank. Don't push the f-pawn, because it allows a sideways back-rank mate. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:384 findBackRankWeakness, endgameTechnique.ts:337 detectBackRankDefence.
- Pawn breaks: name the break, aim at the base of the chain, say why now (Structure-defining moments) e.g. ...c6 chips at the base of their chain to open the queenside. ...d5 now: get a good version of that break in and your opening problems are over. -> COMPUTED. positionReadingService.ts:400 findPawnBreaks, mastersPlanRead.ts:83, movePlan.ts:76 missedPlanClause.
- Hooks: their advanced pawn is your lever (The opponent pushes pawns near their king) e.g. Their g4 push handed you a hook: take on g4 and pry their shelter open. After ...h6, that pawn becomes a hook for your f4 later. -> COMPUTED. moveInsight.ts:782 pawnHook, :826 hookCreated.
- Wing-attack principles: castle opposite, don't storm where your own king lives, close the centre to attack on a wing, open it when their king is stuck (Before launching a storm; when their king can't castle) e.g. Castle long so the kingside pawns can go; you can't storm the wing your own king lives on. Then d5 shuts the centre so nothing distracts from h4-h5. Their king is stranded in the middle: open the centre fast and find the file that leads to it. -> PARTIAL. kingAttack.ts:71, splitPosition.ts:14 (opposite-side castling), kingSafety.ts:142 detectCentralKingDanger, reviewTeachingPoints.ts:557 describeNotableMove (Review only: 'the wing your own king lives on', :618). MISSING: close the centre to attack on a wing.
- Meet a flank storm with a central strike (The opponent advances wing pawns) e.g. They keep shoving pawns at your king and are only overextending. Hit back in the centre. -> PARTIAL. movePlan.ts:76 missedPlanClause (a centre break as the missed plan), principleAttribution.ts:49 'overextended-pawn' (diagnosis).
- Race assessment: whose attack lands first, so ignore the slower one (Opposite-side castling races) e.g. Ignore their queenside play; it simply isn't fast enough. Keep pushing your h-pawn. -> MISSING for attack races. planRace.ts:180 detectPlanRace only races passed pawns and files (same-kind races).
- Timing: not yet, or now is the moment (Before committal pawn or attacking moves) e.g. Not h4 yet: you don't know which side they'll castle. The pressure has peaked, so now ...f6. This is the moment to press. -> PARTIAL. moveTiming.ts:47 readTiming (looking back: a move earlier it lost material), thinkAloud.ts:145 notYet (the capture will still be there), speedRunReads.ts:224 positionOpened. MISSING: wait until the target commits (castles).
- Outposts: name it, route to it, say why it's permanent (Holes in the enemy camp) e.g. d6 is a dream square. The knight gets there via g5 or d2, and with no dark-squared bishop they can never challenge it. -> COMPUTED. outpost.ts:39 isOutpost (:22 noPawnCanChallenge), forwardTeaching.ts:186 computePieceRoute, moveInsight.ts:1102 holeAccess, speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole.
- Can it be kicked? A central piece needs an anchor (An enemy piece centralises) e.g. When their knight lands on a big central square, first ask whether you can kick it; here ...e5 does. Their knight on e5 has no pawn behind it, so it will have to move again. -> PARTIAL. outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge (the inverse test). MISSING: proposing the kick against an unanchored central piece.
- Pawns as anchors for pieces (Pieces developed without pawn support) e.g. f4 gives your position a spine. Pieces developed with no pawn behind them just float, and the push kicks their knight as well. -> MISSING.
- Use the least valuable piece for the job; the queen is the worst defender (Defensive choices) e.g. Hold the centre with c3, not with the bishop: let the cheapest piece do it. Don't guard a pawn with the queen, because she's the easiest piece to chase. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:889 pawnCanGuard (spoken as 'the cheapest defender', moveInsight.ts:220), reviewTeachingPoints.ts:142 (Review: king and queen are the worst defenders, about THEIR guards).
- Trade judgement: which trade, and who benefits (Every voluntary trade) e.g. Trade off their fianchettoed bishop, because it guards their whole king. Ask who gains from this bishop trade: you, since both of yours are passive. Leave them their bad light-squared bishop. -> COMPUTED. tradeJudgement.ts:40 (reasons at :26), tradeQuality.ts:124 readTrade, :273 findTradeTarget (trade lane, computerRoles.ts:64).
- Trade on your terms: who recaptures decides the structure (Equal trades where the recapture shapes the position) e.g. Don't swap queens on b6: they'd recapture with a pawn and own the half-open file. Push c4 and make them trade on your terms. Trade bishops so their knight has to recapture, and d5 is yours. -> PARTIAL. tradeQuality.ts:71 recaptureDamage (what a recapture does to their structure), recaptureChoice.ts:103 (the student's own recapture). MISSING: steering THEIR recapture.
- Keep pieces on, or trade down, according to the situation (Choosing whether to trade while ahead) e.g. Take the bishop but keep the queens on, because their king is stuck in the middle. When you're a piece up, trade. -> COMPUTED. conversionMethod.ts:44 readConversion (attack the king vs trade pieces, conversionMethod.ts:28), safetyHabits.ts:54 keepPressing.
- Keep the tension; let them be the one to release it (Central pawn tension) e.g. Leave the central tension. Castle and develop, and let them be the ones to capture. -> COMPUTED. speedRunReads.ts:49 keepTension.
- The threat is stronger than the execution (When grabbing material would relieve the opponent) e.g. Don't cash in on f3 and e5. Keeping them tied to that weak pawn hurts them more than winning it would. -> COMPUTED. speedRunReads.ts:144 threatStronger.
- A rule and its exception, stated with the condition (When the student's correct move breaks a beginner rule) e.g. Moving the bishop twice and giving up the pair breaks the opening rules, but it's fine here because the centre is closed and there's a bigger priority. Playing ...e6 and ...g6 together is only a sin when the centre is open and d6 is reachable. A bad bishop can be doing a good job defending good pawns. -> PARTIAL. ruleException.ts:70 covers only three rules: the same minor twice, an f/g-pawn in front of a castled king, the early queen (ruleException.ts:9-17). MISSING: the same pawn twice in a closed centre, the ...e6/...g6 holes, 'a square usually avoided', a knight going via the rim, a bad bishop guarding good pawns, not clinging to an extra pawn.
- Accumulation: small edges add up (Quiet manoeuvring positions) e.g. You can't do everything at once. Add pressure a little at a time until small problems become big ones. -> MISSING. reviewPositionalAssessment.ts:81 assesses the edge at one point; there is no trend across moves.
- Re-evaluates when the position transforms (After a structural change or a new offer) e.g. Earlier you wanted to keep that bishop. Now they're offering a better deal: wreck their structure, weaken their king and remove their dark bishop. Take it. -> PARTIAL. positionTransformation.ts:83 (favourable or unfavourable trades only), speedRunReads.ts:224 positionOpened.
- Plays for a win in an equal position: create an imbalance, avoid drawish lines (Equal positions) e.g. It's level, so make chances. Taking on c3 creates the imbalance. Keeping the isolated pawn avoids the queen trade that just draws. -> MISSING.
- Material imbalance rules (When an imbalance is created) e.g. Two minor pieces against a rook usually favour the rook, unless the minors are this active. - Accept a structural cost for activity (When a concession buys something) e.g. Yes, taking back with the g-pawn doubles your pawns, but it opens the g-file straight at their king. MISSING: 'accept a cost for a permanent gain' (marked not built in the docs insight catalogue, type 19).
- Callback: ties the current move to an earlier move's purpose (When an earlier preparatory move pays off) e.g. This is why the rook-pawn went to a3 earlier: now b4 cements the extra pawn. - When winning: simple, healthy moves; material before mate; many good roads (A decisive advantage) e.g. Close to winning? Don't only hunt for mate; take what wins material outright. - Endgame rules: active king, pawns off your bishop's colour, rook behind the passer, don't walk the king back, fortress, stalemate check, a passed pawn as a decoy (Entering and playing endgames) e.g. The queens are off, so march your king to the centre. - King hunt: cut off the retreat, and check from a distance (Attacking an exposed king) e.g. Their king wants to run back to e8, so cut that off and drive it toward the c-file where the rook mates. - Traps a queen methodically by covering its escape squares (A queen deep in your camp after a pawn grab) e.g. Their queen on a2 needs b2 to get out. Cover it and she's caged; it takes several pieces working together. -> MISSING. tacticsDetector.ts:451 only sees a piece once it is attacked.

## Source 8
TEACHING TRACK, notes 6000-7476 (1,477 notes, 85 videos), read end to end. 70 distinct teaching acts are catalogued above, each with a paraphrased example, the note id, the kind of moment, a measured or approximate frequency (regex counts, roughly ±15%), and the computer that produces it today with file:line, or MISSING.

COVERAGE. About half of the acts have a working computer, but the computers mostly reach Learn only. Examples: moveIntent, moveOrder and positionCharacter are called only from CoachTeachPage. falseAlarm, ruleException, recaptureChoice, kingAttack, splitPosition, countMethod, checkMethod and safetyHabits are imported only by learnBoardTeaching.ts. The 27 speed-run reads run through thinkAloud.ts:257, and only on the student's turn. Review runs a parallel set (reviewTeachingPoints, reviewFullData, reviewSacrifice). This matches census F18/S1: one coach does not run everywhere.

MISSING, ranked by how often he does it in this slice:
1. Opening knowledge facts: a live 'main line / move to know' on the student's own move; the reason half of the opponent's opening verdict (theirOpeningVerdict at openingAnnouncement.ts:166 gives only a cost in words and is never joined with theirMoveCost.ts:60); transposition and gateway moves; closing timing windows; comparative tempo counts.
2. Pattern trigger rules ('whenever X, look for Y') with their conditions, and sacrifice patterns' when-it-fails half (F04, Q7).
3. Pin judgement rules: proximity, comparing pin strength, the kickable counter-pin, 'a pin removes a defender'.
4. Calculation and safety habits beyond methodBeat's four: start with the simplest move, look one step further, refresh after exchanges, the queen-escape check before grabbing, the in-between-check check before cashing in.
5. Golden-nugget knowledge: material imbalance rules, castling long activates the rook, bad bishops defend good pawns, doubled pawns are not as bad as feared (recaptureChoice.ts:68 always counts doubling as a drawback), the queen exploits a colour complex, self-blocking checks.
6. Attack method: fix the king, clear your own blocker (F0c OBSTACLE / REMOVE IT), choose the hunting piece.
7. Gambit-handling strategy, transfer between openings, and a choice as a statement of intent.
Practical and psychological reads (panic, bluffing, the clock) have no board fact behind them and are not computers.

RHYTHM: Measured over the slice (1,477 distilled notes from 85 videos; these are paraphrases, so word counts run below his raw speech, which thinkAloud.ts:1-8 measured at about 50 words a move). Median words per note: opening 19 (p90 41), middlegame 20 (p90 45), endgame 13 (p90 28). He speaks on almost every ply: in the 35 videos with 15+ notes there are about 0.79 notes per ply of the covered span. Most plies get a short clause; 8 words or fewer on 19% of opening notes, 21% of middlegame, 32% of endgame. The long notes (40 of them at 60+ words) are all opening or middlegame (19 and 21), none endgame, and every one sits at a decision: a theory fork with several named branches (6304-6309, 6604, 6617-6618, 7004), a choice between candidates (6279, 6537, 6743, 7218, 7224), a branching tactical calculation (6181, 6525-6526, 6611, 6749, 6777), or the plan after material changes (6221, 6802, 7096). Long explanations are earned by the moment, not spread evenly. About 44% of opening notes and 43% of middlegame notes are about the OPPONENT's move: he diagnoses their choice (what it wants, whether it's good, what it gave up, how to punish it) almost as often as he guides the student's. Order inside one note: (1) what the move is, or its name; (2) its job or reason; (3) what it stops, allows or gives up; (4) the tempting alternative and why it fails, or the line with their reply; (5) the habit or principle, last (e.g. 6279: the queen defends; not the bishop, which would give up the pair; if Bf4, unpin with Bd6; habit: before moving an attacked queen, look for an intermezzo). By phase: the opening carries naming, purpose, theory status, verdicts on opponent moves, traps and move order. Quiet middlegames carry plans, prophylaxis, tension and piece improvement. Critical moments carry candidates, the failing tempting move, the line, and a safety check. After winning material comes the conversion method. Endgames get terse technique labels. The weighting order when choosing a move: concrete safety (is it hanging, does it lose to a check), then the line with their replies, then structural or tempo cost, then practical factors. Flashy tries are deferred until the king is safe and the pieces are out (6517: no premature trap-setting moves unless you are losing).

## Source 9
Sources read end to end: RULEBOOK.md, swarm-inputs/questions.md, the duplicate census, the speed-run study (2026-09-24), the 430-game teaching census (2026-09-27-…-teaching-census.md), and the one raw transcript (-4hTQEnwa7s). The transcript is a ~10-minute commented 15+10 game, playing Black against an 1800. Its real moves come from the voiced-corpus notes vc--4hTQEnwa7s-*: 1.b3 e5 2.Bb2 Nc6 3.Nf3 e4 4.Ne5 Qf6 5.Nc4 Qg6 6.Ne3 Nf6 7.g3 d5 8.Bg2 Be6 9.O-O h5 10.h4 O-O-O 11.a4 Bd6 12.Kh2 Ng4+ 13.Nxg4 hxg4 14.Ba3 Be5 15.Ra2 Rxh4+ 16.Kg1, resigns. Every file:line below is under /home/user/wt-work/src/services/.

HOW THE REFERENCE COACH TEACHES: one thread across moves, never isolated facts. The opponent breaks opening principles, so he keeps them. They neglect the queenside, so he attacks before he is fully developed. He pushes the h-pawn at the g3 hook. Their king walks into his bishop's pin, so g3 stops guarding h4. The knight check opens the h-file. He refuses to rush the capture. He takes with check, then explains why they resigned and what the moral is. Every link is joined by a 'so' or a 'but' (F0b).

WHAT OUR CODE DOES WITH HIS GAME. Most single facts already exist; thinkAloud.ts:1-7 says it was measured on this very transcript. I ran a read-only probe of the pure computers on his actual positions: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-chess-academy-pro/61fdf752-44c7-57cb-be1e-44a85a8d5754/scratchpad/probe/probe.mts, output in probe.log.

HITS:
- 7...d5: the principle with its reason (moveFundamentals.ts:1373).
- 12...Ng4+: 'the h-file opens toward their king' (thinkAloud.ts:114/:71).
- 14...Be5: 'not yet, first the bishop to e5' (thinkAloud.ts:145).
- 9...h5: the g3 hook (moveInsight.ts:782).
- 10.h4: leaves g3 with one guard (moveInsight.ts:573).
- 12.Kh2: the pin on g3 is named (tacticsDetector.ts:803).

MISSES:
- 6.Ne3, the same-piece-again habit: gated silent (tempoCount.ts:69, thinkAloud.ts:187).
- 9...h5: the hook is computed and then dropped for 'finish developing before anything else' (computed at moveInsight.ts:246, dropped by :250-264). That is the opposite of his decision, and h5's reason comes out as 'grabs space'.
- 12.Kh2: the pinned g3 pawn no longer guarding h4 is never said, because the guard count ignores pins (moveInsight.ts:494).
- 13...hxg4: the threat to win the h4 pawn with check is not detected, because a capture threat must win at least 3 points (groundedAnswer.ts:6955).
- 4...Qf6: his apparent self-pin is WARNED as a discovered attack instead of explained as harmless.
- 11.a4: gets no verdict.
- 16.Kg1, the finish: the rook-sacrifice line would be voiced as 'you come out 4 points down' (thinkAloud.ts:93), and the line is suppressed anyway (thinkAloud.ts:281).

MISSING COMPUTERS (new per B6, so they go to David):
- the pinned defender doesn't defend
- the line cuts both ways (dismissing an apparent drawback)
- the plan-level exception: attack early because they are further behind
- naming the opponent's only reply, and pawn-sized forcing threats
- the opponent's two-branch dilemma

- the last chance
- why they resigned: the finishing line with its mating compensation
- a recap of the opponent's violations when the student wins

The deeper gap is F0c. The links exist as about 40 separate lanes (speedRunReads alone has 25 reads, aggregated at speedRunReads.ts:585), and no composer carries one idea across moves the way he does. Two gates (tempoCount.ts:69 and moveInsight.ts:250-264) silence or contradict his key teaching moments in this game.
RHYTHM: Measured on the raw transcript. The live commentary is 692 words over his 15 moves, about 46 words a move. The opening block (moves 1-5) runs about 150 words, roughly 30 a move. Routine developing or castling moves take 38-47 words. Decision moments take 2-3 times that: about 76 for d5 with the punish-the-principle-breaker method, 92 for the move-9 strategic fork (h5), and 133 for 12...Ng4+, where he calculates out loud as candidate, objection, then answer. Opponent moves get 2-5 words ('they play g3') unless something changed; then he adds a one-clause verdict ('creative, not sound', 'walked right into it'). The post-game review runs about 870 words, longer than the whole live commentary. In it he replays the opponent's errors with the better move and its reason, plays out the finish behind the resignation, refutes the alternative defences, and closes on the moral plus repertoire advice. The intro is about 210 words.

The order inside one move (moves 7, 9, 12 and 14), with his self-questions recurring at step 3:
1. Name their move, with a short verdict if any.
2. Say what it changed or neglected.
3. Ask himself a question: what's left to do, do I want to rush this, what am I thinking about.
4. Weigh: on one hand / on the other, or candidate, objection, answer.
5. Play the move with its purpose ('to pry open the h-file').
6. Say what it now threatens and the opponent's one reply.
7. Sometimes add a foreshadow ('keep an eye on g3') or the method line ('don't panic, finish developing, attack when ready').

The speed-run study of two other games measured about 25-30 words a move: lead with the question or the threat, then the reason, then a 2-4-ply proof. He talks about what the opponent WANTS more than what a piece eyes. The census adds that he explains EVERY move, book moves included; nothing goes quiet for being routine.

By phase:
- Opening: principle plus purpose on every move, and the opening's identity and purpose at the start.
- Middlegame: plans, weighing and calculated lines, at 2-3 times the words.
- Endgame: not reached in this game. Census: endgame technique is about 1.2% of his lines, push-or-hold about 0.4%; conversion advice appears whenever he is winning.
- Low-rated opponents (700): safety, principle and the principle's exception, asked as questions.
- High-rated opponents (2300): plan and method.
- Name the opening and the kind of game it is (First move the opening is identifiable; refinements held until the game leaves book) e.g. This is a b3 opening — respectable, well-trodden theory, and a complicated one. -> BUILT — openingAnnouncement.ts:54 openingAnnouncement (names once, settles at book exit); openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine (sharp/quiet from theory depth + forcing rate; real famous games at :143). A respectable-vs-dubious verdict exists only for the opponent's book-exit move (openingAnnouncement.ts:166).
- The opening's purpose: what the setup provokes, and why (Right after the opponent's defining move) e.g. Their knight comes forward to tempt your pawns up the board — you get space now, and they intend to attack those advanced pawns later. -> PARTIAL — openingIdentity.ts:110 'provokes' renders only the usual reply and the pawn it hits; mastersPlanRead.ts:83/:181 names the master pawn break (Learn only, via learnBoardTeaching.ts:617); speedRunReads.ts:125 provokes covers only the student's own engine move. MISSING: the reason behind a provocation (lure, then attack the over-extended pawns); 'hypermodern' exists only as a tile style (openingDetectionService.ts:1586).

## Source 10
TEACHING TRACK: how the reference coach teaches, each act mapped to the code. Read end to end: RULEBOOK.md, questions.md, the duplicate census, 2026-09-29 full review + all of danya-review-2026-09-29/ (parts 0-7, sources, both tapes, the five brainstorm-r1 reports), the 2026-09-16 behaviour audit, every file in data/sources/danielnaroditsky-voice/, plus the 09-17 structures study, 09-24 speedrun target, 09-27 census, 08-23 coverage matrix, docs/naroditsky-insight-catalogue.md, the swarm-input transcript, and the two tape games in public/data/voiced-teachings.json. Every computer named was opened, not recalled.

HOW HE TEACHES, IN ONE PARAGRAPH. A game is one story. He names the opening and says where it stands. He turns the opponent's first concession into the game's single thesis (a target square, a weak pawn, a break) and points later beats back at it. On every move he asks what the opponent's move changed or gave up. He states a principle and then its exception, because the circumstances changed. At the few moments that matter he thinks out loud: the candidates, each rejected with a short line played to where it lands, then the move with its reason. His habits are concrete triggers: count before you take, list the loose pieces, the three answers to a check, take the escape square first, check for an in-between move before recapturing. He converts by a named method chosen by the size of the edge. Afterwards he rewinds to the 2-5 decision points ("if they X, you Y"), prunes the side branches and closes on takeaways. He rarely waits for an answer; his questions are rhetorical and answered in the same breath. He names the move with its reason (supports S3/F05).

CATALOGUE COUNT (73 acts). About 44 built, 16 partial, 13 missing. The breadth is mostly built: the WO-TEACH-GAPS beats, the census computers (moveIntent, moveOrder, theirMoveCost, kingAttack, recaptureChoice, ruleException, falseAlarm, pushOrHold), about 26 reads in speedRunReads.ts, about 20 in moveInsight.ts, and the endgame and concept engines.

What is missing is the chain and the selection, not the facts:
1. No decider has a thesis or relevance term. grep for 'thesis' in coachDecider.ts, factSelector.ts, learnTurnDoor.ts and voicePackage.ts finds nothing. teachingSelector.ts:192/:347 builds a thesis only for Review, phase narration and openings.
2. The think-aloud producer (thinkAloud.ts:226 depthClauses) has one caller, positionFacts.ts:1009. It ranks clauses with a fixed table (positionFacts.ts:1009-1018: not-yet 90, stop-flaw 70, line 60, hole-access 50, speedrun-read 45), not by computed stakes.

DATA CONFIRMS F02. 48% of his beats are in the opening, and the densest, longest stretch is moves 7-12, where the thesis and the break are declared.

CAVEAT. The voiced corpus is our LLM rewrite of his structure, so the rhythm numbers measure his structure, not his words.
RHYTHM: Measured on public/data/voiced-teachings.json (7,477 beats; 360 games with at least 5 in-game beats, cut at the first ply reset where the rewind starts).

LENGTH. A spoken beat is short: median 20 words (p25 10, p75 31, p90 46, p99 110).

DENSITY. 65% of in-game plies carry a beat. The per-game median is 74% (IQR 42-88%). The rest are bare or silent routine plies: book moves, recaptures, the opponent's filler.

BY PHASE.
- Opening: 3,617 beats (48% of all), median 20 words.
- Middlegame: 2,901 beats (39%), median 21 words, p90 50. The longest.
- Endgame: 959 beats (13%), median 15 words. Technique is said tersely.

BY PLY BAND.
- Moves 1-6: 61% of plies spoken, median 18 words. He names the opening, places it, and gives the principle of each move.
- Moves 7-12: 71% spoken, median 23 words. The densest and longest stretch: the opponent's concession is named, the thesis is declared, the break is chosen.
- Plies 25-50: 66% spoken, median 19 words.
- Plies 51 and later: 58% spoken, median 14 words. Conversion is clipped to the method plus the tactic.

LIVE COMMENTARY IS ABOUT 2.5 TIMES LONGER than the distilled beats. thinkAloud.ts:2-3 measured the swarm-input transcript at about 50 words a move: 20-47 on a routine move, 90-133 at a decision.

THE SHAPE IS BIMODAL. Most beats carry ONE idea plus its reason. Monologues of 5-15 ideas cluster only at the critical moment and in the post-game rewind. In 60-70% of videos the rewind is a second pass longer than the game itself.

## Source 11
Read notes[0..186] of public/data/voiced-teachings.json: 8 games, 187 notes (87 opening, 86 middlegame, 14 endgame; 102 on the student's move, 85 on the opponent's). Below, n# means the index into notes[]. I catalogued 70 teaching acts and mapped each one to src/services with file:line. Seven things the coarse census missed:

1) Computers that exist but are gated so the reference coach's own examples don't fire. tempoCount needs the student to have a development lead (tempoCount.ts:69); at n7 they had 1 minor out against 2, so it stays silent. opponentHabits needs at least 2 minors at home (thinkAloud.ts:187). ruleException's pawn-in-front-of-the-king exception needs a castled king, and its early-queen exception needs the queen to hit something (ruleException.ts:115, :124), which misses n47 and n121. moveTiming ignores costs under 2 points (moveTiming.ts:33). trappedOnBoard looks at rooks and queens only (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:812). bluffDetector skips pawn lunges (bluffDetector.ts:43). findXrays needs a friendly blocker and a more valuable target (positionReadingService.ts:851, :860). isRealPin rejects a piece shielding an equal piece (pinGeometry.ts:146). retreatKeepsBreak misses a pawn double-step through the vacated square (speedRunReads.ts:429). deliberation only weighs alternatives proven by a material or line loss (deliberation.ts:260, :278), and most of the reference coach's alternatives fail for positional reasons.

2) Computers that only work for one seat or one tense. noRetreat and heavyTiedDown can read either side but are called only on the student's own pieces (moveInsight.ts:287, :288). findConcession runs only on moves already played (backwardLook.ts:180, :305), never on the tempting candidate. refutedAlternative only covers the student's popular alternative (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:87). payoffFor closes a promise only on the student's own move, within 16 plies (learnBoardTeaching.ts:897, :917). The reference coach's callbacks fire on the opponent's move, and one comes 20 plies later (n38 to n55).

3) One computer gives a provably wrong plan. The closed-centre template (positionReadingService.ts:1087-1094) tells the student "you break on the queenside with c5". In game 4 after 11.Be3, both b6 and d6 attack c5 (checked with chess.js), and the reference coach teaches the opposite wing (n84-85).

4) Two facts are computed and then thrown away. walkForcedSequence (onlyMoveSequence.ts:57) has no production importer. structureSignature.lockedCenter (boardStructure.ts:303) has no reader. These are exactly the facts behind his "it holds to a perpetual" (n95) and "in a locked centre the move order stops mattering" (n79).

5) Teaching families with no computer at all in this slice:
- a flag for strategic decisions, plus weighing candidates by positional reasons;
- forward chains of consequences for a plan move;
- choosing the pawn structure, and choosing the wing;
- a teaser now with the reveal on the opponent's move;
- the common small slip at a position (between F04's trap bar and silence);
- king-hunt technique;
- "prefer the simpler win";
- "this is only safe because of that earlier move".

6) Defects in the corpus itself (D10/V1).
- 10 notes (n95, 100, 103, 106, 107, 109, 110, 111, 115, 139) speak in the first person or say "let's". They pass src/data/perspectiveVoice.test.ts: it bans only we/our/us (:28), exempts "let's" (:26-27), and still allows "I/my" (:10-12), which contradicts RULEBOOK V1/V2.
- vc--PSQS88VdZU-9 credits White's 5.Nxd4 to Black.
- vc--FRuDd_oXz4-2 and -8 recast the reference coach's own repertoire history as the student's.
- vc--9fPYlSEkJ0-30 says the f4 bishop cannot retreat, but Be3 is legal (chess.js).
- vc--rqPeGKVPbA-8 says "Ng2" for a bishop fianchetto.

7) Other sessions were editing the working tree during this read (learnBoardTeaching.ts, gemCrushLines.ts and reviewFullData.ts were modified). I re-checked the cited lines in those files at the end.
RHYTHM: He comments on every move.
- 31 of the 187 notes cover two or more plies as one unit, usually a capture with its recapture or a move with the obvious reply.
- In one fast game, 13 quiet plies become a single sentence (n102).

Length per note (distilled corpus):
- Overall: mean 26 words, median 21.
- Opening: 87 notes, median 23.
- Middlegame: 86 notes, median 21.
- Endgame: 14 notes, median 13.5.

Bare narration of 8 words or fewer:
- Opening 4 of 87, middlegame 9 of 86, endgame 5 of 14.
- Speech shrinks as the result becomes a matter of technique.

Long notes happen only at a decision with a tempting wrong option. Eight notes run over 60 words:
- n66 (190 words): the whole middlegame plan, given at the knight-development decision.
- n91 (131), n88 (126), n92 (122) and n100 (100): the f4-break deliberation.
- n132 (74), n72 (65) and n124 (64).

Their moves get as much breath as the student's: 85 notes averaging 25 words, against 102 averaging 27. Explanatory games run 30 to 42 words a note. Fast attacking or converting games run 17 to 18.

Order inside a decision note:
1. What their move did, cost or wants.
2. Flag the moment.
3. The natural or tempting candidates.
4. Each candidate's flaw, as a short line with their reply or as the squares it gives up.
5. The move.
6. The move's jobs.
7. The next step of the plan.
8. A callback or a teaser.

Order on their move: what it hits, then a verdict (sound, passive or rare), then what they want, then what it cost them, then the student's answer.

Several linked thoughts on one move is normal at decisions, and only there.

They find the correct answer, the queen to d7 first (n63). -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124 frames it as prevention ('so ... isn't possible'). positionTrapScan.ts:126 detects a trap only with enough recreational games and a loss of at least 200cp. MISSING: the 'trap set, now see if they fall in' framing, and the follow-up when they avoid it.

Instead of defending it, push it forward and kick the knight (n1-2). You threaten mate, and only the rook to e1 holds it (n29). -> COVERED by detectNewThreat (groundedAnswer.ts:6890) plus threatAnswer (threatAnswer.ts:58), whose kinds are take, step-out, with-gain, kick, block, guard and wait (threatAnswer.ts:21). The sentence does not name the passive alternative ('instead of defending it').
- What their move cost them (Their pawn moves and passive developing moves) e.g. That h-pawn push only loosens their own king (n15). Offering to trade their fianchetto bishop shows the setup's weakness, because the holes it covered stay (n36). Their bishop now just props up a pawn (n40). Their quiet d6 shuts in the bishop on e7 (n130). A pawn on d3 instead of d4 hands you d4 (n176). -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 covers hole (:72-91), bishop-shut (:94-115), castling and structure. It deliberately strips 'pawn cover thinned' (theirMoveCost.ts:144), and kingAttack.ts:71 fires only on the attacker's own move, so their self-weakening h-pawn push (n15) has no Learn lane. describeNotableMove (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:557) is Review-only, called at coachFeatureService.ts:3206. The knight jumps to h5, aiming for f4 (n87). They take on c5, which was the point of their bishop move, and now they are tied to that pawn (n44). -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:124, run from their seat (theirIntent lane, computerRoles.ts:84), states the purpose at the time of the move. stepArc (planArc.ts:236) tracks aims across moves. MISSING: the look-back 'that was the point of their earlier move', said on the move that pays it off.

But once the pawns and pieces trade on f5, your g-pawn forks their rook and knight at the end (n88). -> PARTIAL. buildOpponentIntent (opponentIntent.ts:55) gives their top ideas plus your reply, taken from ply 2 of each line. proofForMover (exchangeLedger.ts:481) counts the trades. latentFork.ts:161 handles knights only (latentFork.ts:27), so a PAWN fork at the end of an exchange sequence is not found. MISSING: composing their idea, then the exchange line, then the fork that ends it.

Inventive, but it doesn't hold up (n17). You could stop the pin with h3, but it bites on nothing here because their pieces are too passive (n76). Their h-pawn lunge threatens nothing: meet h4 with g4, and a sacrifice would fail with too few attackers against your king (n140). The check is harmless because g1 is free (n154). -> PARTIAL. bluffDetector.ts:37 handles PIECES only (knight, bishop, rook, queen; bluffDetector.ts:43), so pawn lunges are left out. falseAlarm.ts:37 needs a real threat. countKingAttack (kingSafety.ts:297) has the attacker and defender counts. A solid way past the traps (n118). -> PARTIAL. threatStoppedBy (opponentMovePurpose.ts:58) feeds the theirPurpose lane (computerRoles.ts:83) and says which of the student's threats their move stopped. MISSING for the opponent's seat.

This is the key decision, the one most people miss (n66). It is harder than it seems (n124). Careful here (n139). -> PARTIAL. criticalMomentStatement (criticalMoment.ts:287) fires only on the count of engine moves that hold (criticalMoment.ts:6-11). anyMoveFine (speedRunReads.ts:68) says the opposite, 'no move here is a big decision', whenever the top three moves sit inside the inaccuracy bar after move 8 (speedRunReads.ts:70-74). - List the candidates, then the one board feature that decides between them (Every real choice in the opening and early middlegame) e.g. You could keep developing or castle long, but their whole queenside is still asleep, so start the attack now with h5 (n13-14). e5 is possible, but e6 keeps the centre closed on purpose (n43). The ask-first form is MISSING, and per F05 it may only be asked for a long-standing weakness.

- King hunt: herd the king with checks, don't chase the fastest mate (A king hunt in a won position) e.g. A check drives their king up the board. Don't spend time hunting for the shortest mate; keep checking and the mate will come (n167-171). -> MISSING. classifyMatePattern (matePatterns.ts:341) names only the final mating pattern.

A neat finish is on the board (n24-25). -> MISSING. payoffFor (learnBoardTeaching.ts:917) closes a promise only on the STUDENT's move (piece plus square), never when the OPPONENT's move triggers the reveal. moveIntent states a purpose immediately.

Worried about the sacrifice on h4? The knight takes, the pawn takes, the queen checks, your king steps to g2, and the g1 knight guards h3 (n92). You don't mind the trade on c3 (n74-75). MISSING: a move that looks like a self-pin, and a sacrifice that is not the engine's main reply.
