Here the knight on g1 earns its keep by guarding h3 (n92). -> MISSING. readTiming (moveTiming.ts:47) compares the same move one turn earlier, by material only. Nothing ties a move's safety to a specific earlier piece placement.

CORPUS CAUTION: these notes are written in the first person ('I missed it'), which V1 bans; see the summary.

## Source 12
Close second reading of voiced-teachings.json notes[187..373]: 187 notes from 8 videos (KID fianchetto game, Najdorf lecture, Italian Bb4+/Nxe4 line, Rossolimo with dxc6, Scotch, a deliberate knight-sacrifice defence lesson, an early-Qh5 game, plus the tail of an English game). The insight catalogue had already mined part of this slice (it read 0ipLPOAN_m8 as game 8; its A1 and A12 entries come from 1PI3 and 1671), and four built computers cite these notes in their headers: moveTiming.ts:1 (#310), moveContrast.ts:1 (#312), recaptureChoice.ts:2 (the dxc6 idea), and the census build status (the Kh1-prepares-f4 move from 1PI3). I catalogued 77 distinct acts. About 18 have no computer and no entry in the catalogue, census or speedrun-target doc (grep-checked).

NEW acts with no computer:
- a counterfactual pattern: 'if their queen stood here, the knight jump would fork' (#284)
- their good move's future drawback: the knight is left with no home after their own e4 (#203)
- their piece placement hands you a tempo later: the queen on f6 invites a knight to d5 (#342)
- a threat met by making it cost them: h3, so if they play the skewer anyway you take the other bishop (#363). threatAnswer.ts:7-13 has no such class.
- the quiet strengthening move is the real danger (#371)
- their move made your break possible (#289). theirMoveChanged (moveInsight.ts:573) and readTiming (moveTiming.ts:47) miss this.
- material arithmetic toward level: a piece is worth three pawns (#349-350)
- a trade that thins their attack helps the defender (#361)
- a numbered argument carried across plies (#264-266)
- temporary vs permanent drawback (#302)
- a two-sided ledger between pieces (#309)
- a modest square justified by its duties (#290-291)
- the best defence both improves and sets a trap (#343)
- a pin that only looks like a pin. pinGeometry.ts:135 decides it, but nothing says it (#196).
- surprise value of a sound but rarely known move (#278)
- an indirectly defended pawn (#216). takeTheSting (speedRunReads.ts:400) and heldByTactic (:162) both skip pawns.
- the drawback → condition → remedy composite (#295). The pieces exist; no composer joins them.

Conflicts and decisions for David (B6):
1. #361 conflicts with code. 'Behind → keep pieces on, every trade helps them' is stated unconditionally in 5 places: moveInsight.ts:1012, tradeJudgement.ts:78, positionCharacter.ts:103, principleVoice.ts:437, reviewConcepts.ts:123. tradeJudgement reads only trades the student starts and ranks 'behind' (:78) before 'attacker-gone' (:91). In #361's situation that is false teaching risk.
2. Repertoire advice is stripped. openingGenerator.ts:2246 strips 'easy to learn' as filler (V4), yet learnability advice is a real act of the reference coach (#195, #270, #330; the census counts about 250 such lines).
3. Rhetorical questions vs F05. All 7 questions in the slice are rhetorical and answered by the coach within one ply. F05 should be read as governing blocking asks only. The only question device in code is methodBeat.ts:145/309.
4. V8 vs material arithmetic. Is 'a piece is worth three pawns' a forbidden number?

Compliance finding (verified): 16 of 187 slice notes, and 679 of 7,477 in the whole corpus, keep the reference coach's first person (I/my/me). That breaks V1 and F0d. The perspective gate scans this corpus (src/data/perspectiveVoice.test.ts:69) but bans only we/our/us (:28) and explicitly allows I/my (:11-12). The notes are spoken in 'teach me X opening' and chat (S6/S7).

Caveats:
- The corpus is distilled. One video keeps only 37% of plies, the phase field mislabels (#219-#230 are tagged endgame with queens on), and no raw transcripts for these 8 videos are on disk.
- Another agent is editing this worktree live (learnBoardTeaching.ts and gemCrushLines.ts are modified). All file:line citations were re-verified in a final pass.
- Scratch outputs: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-chess-academy-pro/61fdf752-44c7-57cb-be1e-44a85a8d5754/scratchpad/slice.txt (the slice with chess.js context), stats.cjs, rhythm2.cjs, rhythm3.cjs.
RHYTHM: Median 17 words per move across 187 notes. 20% are bare move statements of 8 words or fewer (castling, recaptures, opponent shuffles), and 11 notes run 40+ words.

Coverage: 82-100% of plies in 6 of 8 videos, so no move passes in silence (V11 holds). Routine plies get one clause that names the move; this is description, not teaching.

Opening density depends on the video type. Lecture games run 19-26 words a move in the opening (menus of named roads, reasons, warnings, line reputations). A casual game runs 11 words: name the system plus one clause.

Decision moments get 30-70+ words. Once a game is decided, the talk collapses to the move plus a material status (KID game: median 14 words while contested, 12 after the queen trade, with reasons almost gone). Under fire it grows (defence game: 18 words in the set-up, 23 under attack).

The unit is the THOUGHT, not the ply. 12 thoughts span 2-4 plies: the note ends on a dash and the next ply completes it, all in the two lecture videos. Our composer works per ply (thinkAloud.depthClauses).

On the opponent's ply he often starts the student's next decision (17 of 81 opponent-move notes): menus, 'choose carefully', a rhetorical 'what should you take?'.

Order inside a thought: their move and what it wants or changes → the student's answer → the reason → the tempting alternative and why it fails → sometimes the plan's next step. 18% of notes carry a but/rather/instead turn, and 13 name a rejected alternative.

All 7 questions are rhetorical and answered within one ply.

Across a game he threads ideas: arguments numbered over plies, a move rejected three times then played when its reason arrives, payoff callbacks, plan milestones.
- Name the opening or system the moment it is reached, including the opponent's setup and transpositions (opening, on the ply the name becomes true (often the opponent's move)) e.g. When the queen's pawn and c-pawn advance and the student answers with the knight, the coach says the game is heading for a King's Indian; when White fianchettoes too, it names that as a highly respected try against it. -> BUILT: openingAnnouncement.ts:54 openingAnnouncement (transpositions at :82)
- Anticipate the coming variation as an open question before it is committed (early opening, where the student's own repertoire makes one road likely) e.g. After the king's knight comes out against the Sicilian, the coach wonders aloud whether this will be a Najdorf, and confirms it a move later. -> PARTIAL: amateurPlayLookup.ts:76 lookupAmateurPlay + homeOpening.ts:98 rankHomeOpeningCandidates could predict the likely road; nothing voices the anticipation
- Survey the menu at a branch point: name each main road, give each a one-line verdict, then choose (opening branch points, often spoken on the opponent's move to prepare the student's choice) e.g. In the open Sicilian the coach lists the Dragon, the Classical, the e6 and e5 setups, says the early e5 is not great, then plays a6 and gives its first reason (it keeps the knight off b5). -> PARTIAL: openingBranches.ts:56 branchesAt computes the named roads, but they surface as picker tiles (CoachTeachPage.tsx:1214), not speech, and no per-road engine verdict is attached
- Characterize a line's standing and nature: respected try, old main line, what top players choose, theory-heavy, quiet but not boring, colorless (opening, on book moves of either side) e.g. On d4 in the Italian the coach calls it the traditional old main line leading to heavy theory and notes that top players prefer d3; on Be2 against the Najdorf it says quiet does not mean boring. -> PARTIAL: openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine (sharp and theory-heavy :139, played at top level :145) works per OPENING; openingAnnouncement.ts:166 theirOpeningVerdict flags only dubious sidelines. - Keep your best piece when better, and name it as your main asset (trade offers when you stand better) e.g. Close to winning, you keep the dark bishop instead of trading it; later recapturing on e5 with the bishop keeps your best piece centralised. -> PARTIAL: pieceValueRead.ts:148 strongestByDelta; tradeQuality.ts:124 readTrade ('gave-best')
- Name the imbalance a trade creates (minor-piece trades) e.g. Taking on f6 gives up the bishop pair, and with their dark bishop gone the dark squares are yours. -> BUILT: tradeQuality.ts:178 (bishop pair given up); the colour-complex consequence is partial
- Outposts and what a piece sees from them (middlegame and endgame manoeuvres) e.g. The knight heads for the e5 outpost; on d6 it eyes c4 and e4; the rook lands on d3 deep in their camp and freezes their pieces; b5 makes c4 a home for a minor or the queen. -> BUILT: outpost.ts:39 isOutpost; moveInsight.ts:1067 knightReach; speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole
- Anchor a piece with a pawn so it can never be chased (consolidating a well-placed piece) e.g. a6 supports the bishop on b5, so nothing can drive it off the diagonal. -> PARTIAL: outpost.ts:39 isOutpost(requirePawnSupport) tests the square; the move that CREATES the support is not named
- A buried piece counts as missing material (domination and restriction) e.g. c4 walls in the rim knight on a3, so in the fight for the d-file you are effectively a piece up. -> PARTIAL: pieceQuality.ts:209 explainEvalByPieceQuality (bad piece by ablation); reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789 findTrappedPiece fires only when the line captures it; 'effectively a piece up' is MISSING
- A two-sided ledger between pieces (weighing a mutual restriction) e.g. Their knight on the rim blocks your light bishop, but a knight stuck on the rim is a fair price for that. -> MISSING — no read weighs your piece's cost against theirs for one placement
- A trapped piece as a consequence, then collect (after an opponent move that removes a piece's escape) e.g. Their knight move leaves the rook on a1 trapped, so you win the exchange. -> BUILT: reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789 findTrappedPiece
- Name the structure reached and its thematic break (the move that fixes the centre) e.g. d5 makes it a Benoni structure, so the bishop retreats ready for the classic queenside break; with e6 instead it would have been a Scheveningen. -> PARTIAL: positionReadingService.ts:1060 namedPawnStructure knows the French chain, closed centre, IQP and hanging pawns only; no Benoni, Scheveningen or Najdorf structure
- A pin that only looks like a pin (a bishop aims at a piece with a blocker behind it) e.g. Their bishop to g5 eyes your knight, but the e7 pawn stands between the knight and the queen, so it is no real pin. -> PARTIAL: pinGeometry.ts:135 isRealPin decides validity; bluffDetector.ts:37 covers harmless attacks; nothing says 'this only looks like a pin, and here is why'
- Line geometry against your queen: x-ray, battery, frozen defenders (middlegame line play) e.g. Their bishop on d2 x-rays your queen, so move it first; line the queen up behind the rook on the c-file; doubling against the c3 knight freezes it because pieces would fall behind it. -> BUILT: latentDanger.ts:87 detectLatentDanger; deliberation.ts:386 x-ray lineup; tacticsDetector.ts:726 battery; pinPressure.ts:138 pinPressureThreat
- Name the thematic sacrifice and what it buys (structural sacrifices) e.g. The rook sacrifice on c3 is a standard Sicilian idea; later the exchange is given for a protected passed pawn on d3 worth more than the rook. -> PARTIAL: reviewSacrifice.ts:44 sacrificeCompensation names only king-in-centre and development lead; a passer as compensation and named structural sacrifices are MISSING
- Offer the queen trade as the weapon when your structural trump decides (conversion with a structural edge) e.g. Instead of the quiet bishop move, offer the queen trade; once the queens are off, their position collapses against your passed pawn. -> PARTIAL: conversionMethod.ts:44 readConversion (trade pieces when ahead), not tied to a structural trump such as a passer
- Your sole trump, so the plan (defence or imbalanced positions) e.g. Your only asset is the central pawn mass they do not have, so advance it: c3, then d4, then e4-e5. -> PARTIAL: boardPlan.ts:84 structurePlan; nextPlans.ts:161 deriveNextPlans
- Grade their move and punish it (after an opponent error) e.g. Their knight jump is a serious inaccuracy and you simply take the piece; their knight to c3 is a poor reaction that hands you a favourable trade. -> BUILT: accuracyService.ts:122 gradeMove; inaccuracyCall.ts:493 callInaccuracyDetailed (both sides); openingAnnouncement.ts:166 theirOpeningVerdict
- Credit their strong resource honestly (after a strong opponent move that upsets your plan) e.g. They found a different and even stronger way to hit your bishop; that knight leap was a nasty shot. -> PARTIAL: coachFeatureService.ts:1175 (Review, brilliant/only moves); a 'great' opponent move returns null (coachFeatureService.ts:1183); Learn has none
- Take what they left undefended (after an opponent move that leaves material loose) e.g. They did not defend the pawn, so the knight takes on d4. -> BUILT: loosePieces.ts:35 findLoosePieces; moveInsight.ts:573 theirMoveChanged
- Lesson thesis up front (start of a game or lesson) e.g. At move one the coach announces a defensive lesson, a knight given up on purpose to show how to fight on, then says the sacrifice comes later, not yet. -> PARTIAL: teachingSelector.ts:347 renderThesis (Review, Openings, phase narration); per the census Learn has none
- A numbered argument carried across several plies (opening lectures, while routine moves are played) e.g. Why the d5 hole is not fatal: first, enough pieces contest it (said on one move); second, there is counterplay on both wings (said two moves later). -> MISSING — planArc.ts:236 follows aims and learnBoardTeaching.ts:917 payoffFor closes one promised move; nothing carries an argument with numbered reasons across plies
- Payoff callback: reveal why an earlier move was played when it bears fruit (when an earlier quiet move's purpose becomes visible) e.g. That is why you wanted their knight off e7: it guarded d5, and now your knight lands there; your earlier c3 now pays off because it covers d4. -> PARTIAL: learnBoardTeaching.ts:917 payoffFor fires only for a move the coach announced in advance, matched by piece and square (GamePromise at :883); a defensive payoff or a goal reached by another route is not caught
- Plan milestones (as a multi-move plan advances) e.g. The bishop reaching a6 is the first half of the plan; now the final stage on the queenside; f4 is the first real progress; now you are ready for f4. -> PARTIAL: planArc.ts:236 stepArc (emerge / advance / arrive / drop)
- Re-evaluate when the board shifts; an old plan is not binding (after an opponent move that changes the position) e.g. After their knight move, do not grab on e2 just because that was the plan three moves ago; the position now asks a new question. -> PARTIAL: moveInsight.ts:573 theirMoveChanged reports the change; no method beat states the habit (methodBeat has no such stem)

- Teach a pattern by a counterfactual (to teach a fork shape the board almost has) e.g. If their queen stood here, the knight jump to e4 would hit it and the other knight at once, so choose your bishop move with that in mind. -> MISSING — latentFork.ts:161 looks two moves ahead with real targets; no read substitutes a hypothetical piece
- Analogy between openings (naming an opening that borrows another's idea) e.g. The Rossolimo bishop pin is the Ruy Lopez idea moved into the Sicilian. -> MISSING — structureSignature.ts:1 matches note structures for transfer, not openings
- A placement that is right whatever they do (opening choices against an annoying option) e.g. Fianchetto anyway: the bishop belongs on the long diagonal whether or not they take on c6. -> BUILT: speedRunReads.ts:383 goodInEveryBranch
- Self-critique: honesty about what the coach missed (after the opponent refutes the coach's own idea) e.g. The coach admits its trick failed yet half-worked, and that it missed their knight leap. -> PARTIAL: concessionBeat.ts:1 (the coach's own worse moves, no apology); V1 forbids first person, so this needs a non-I phrasing

## Source 13
Read all 444 notes in voiced-teachings #374-817 end to end: 18 videos, 170 opening / 172 middlegame / 102 endgame notes, student White in 295. Mapped 79 distinct teaching acts against src/services (653 modules: headers read, key ones read in full, every MISSING verdict confirmed by grep). Result: 32 acts are produced by a computer today, 29 only partly, 18 by nothing.

ACTS THE COARSE READERS MISSED (none is in the 2026-09-27 census list or the insight catalogue's built list; the few already catalogued but still unbuilt are marked):
- The pin that is broken by kicking the PINNER (h6, then g5), so piling on does not win the pinned piece. Found by probing for it; a 4th member of the family in questions.md item 7.
- A rule's real exception test. The early queen is safe when no enemy minor can hit it with tempo. The other rules with exceptions: develop every piece, defend with the least valuable piece, losing castling, the knight on the rim.
- Tempo arithmetic across a line ('not to win a pawn but to gain two tempi'; 'let them take, a3 would lose a move').
- Comparing candidate checks by where each drives the king.
- One move answering two threats.
- Choosing the king's square by a future check (a1 not a2).
- A capture that opens a file for the DEFENDER.
- The key pawn, and the chain that falls with it.
- Switching between two targets when the first is covered.
- Endgame king technique: hide from rook checks; walk to the centre once they have no pieces.
- Rook-against-pawn technique: a lateral pin, then a pawn attack; a pawn majority used to deflect the defending rook.
- Keeping the opponent's awkward piece on the board by refusing the trade that frees it.
- Blunting a fianchetto with a pawn chain, and structures that defend themselves.
- Recognising a setup family (the Hippo) and its antidote.
- Setting a middlegame trap ('dare them into b3').
- 'Their normal reply is tactically unavailable here'.
- Rejecting a line because a piece ends up misplaced.
- Taking off an advanced enemy pawn near your own king.
- Denying the only blockader of your passer.
- Voicing the student's objection before answering it.
- A teaser now, revealed later.
- Saying out loud that an earlier principle has reversed because the circumstances changed.
- Crediting the opponent's only-move defence.
- Already catalogued but unbuilt: what the opponent wrongly expected (catalogue #16); closing the centre before a wing attack (catalogue A7).

Files: slice dump /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-chess-academy-pro/61fdf752-44c7-57cb-be1e-44a85a8d5754/scratchpad/teach-374-817-18882-1026.txt (compact copy: teach-374-817-compact-18882.txt). Probes in .../scratchpad/probe-18882/: pin487.ts and hook591.ts. No repository file was edited.
RHYTHM: Measured on the 444 notes, which carry 18 videos.

SIZE PER NOTE: median 17 words, mean 22. A quarter (113) are bare move narration with no reason attached.

STUDENT'S MOVES VS THE OPPONENT'S:
- Student moves: median 17-19 words in every phase; 11-22% bare.
- Opponent moves: median 12-15 words; 32-44% bare (endgame opponent moves 44% bare).
- So the student's move almost always gets its job in a clause. The opponent's move is often only named, unless it wants something or costs them something.
- The fat tail is middlegame student moves: mean 33 words, 7 notes of 60+ words.

TWO REGISTERS BY VIDEO TYPE:
- Running blitz commentary: 83-95% of plies get a line, median 11-13 words, a quarter to half of them bare.
- Lesson-style games: only 39-60% of plies get a line, but at 20-25 words. All 57 separate one-line takeaways in the slice sit in the 4 lesson videos (9/13, 17/26, 17/28, 14/20 notes).

OPENING: one clause per move (the move's job, or the opening's name). It swells to about 100 words only at a theory-defining moment: why not the obvious c4; why the bishop that block on d7 is misplaced.

DECISIVE MOMENTS: five notes of 100-545 words (#492 #640 #711 #717 #718), each compressing the rest of a game. They follow a fixed order:
1. status;
2. inventory every threat;
3. the one move that meets them, and why;
4. ready answers to each of their tries;
5. the next step of the plan;
6. king prophylaxis;
7. switch to attack once safe;
8. finishing method (do not give the first check, map the flights);
9. the mating net square by square;
10. a closing generalisation.

ORDINARY BEAT: move → its job (so / which / to) → if the choice is real, the natural alternative and its refutation → the line with their reply in words → the takeaway.

DRAWBACKS: always stated for the opponent's moves. On his own good moves they are stated and then discounted. Weaknesses come with the lever and the piece that will use them.

NUMBERS: only small board counts (attackers, defenders, moves to a crush).

QUESTIONS: never quizzes the student here. He voices THEIR likely question and answers it.
- Name the opening or system as it appears, with what it is trying to do (Opening, on the ply the system becomes identifiable or transposes) e.g. They've chosen the knight-first defence; you take the whole centre with pawns, and if they don't know the theory this is where they get run over. -> src/services/openingAnnouncement.ts:54 openingAnnouncement (the name). The system's aim is only partly computed: mastersPlanRead.ts:83 gives the key pawn break from master games (Learn only)
- Say why a theory move is THE move (its defining job), then point back to it when it pays off (Theory-defining opening moves, and again when the payoff arrives) e.g. The rook-pawn step takes b5 away; with your knight already covering d5, the light squares round c7 are sealed, so your king can walk there later. Twenty moves on, that is exactly where it goes. -> PARTIAL: src/services/moveIntent.ts:124 moveIntent (prevents/prepares, one move deep) + mastersPlanRead.ts:83. Nothing states a theory move's defining job or links the later payoff back to it
- Lay out the opening's plan as numbered stages, then mark progress on each later move (Opening into the early middlegame) e.g. Against the fianchetto defence: first lock the centre, then put the queen on d2 and castle long, then storm their king; later moves are called step one done, second stage complete. -> PARTIAL: src/services/planArc.ts:236 stepArc tracks aims (emerge/advance/arrive) read off engine lines; there is no multi-stage opening plan for it to track against
- Repertoire and opening-choice advice (Moves 1-4, when the first moves leave a choice of system) e.g. This system also covers another defence, so there is less to study; against a hypermodern setup pick the sound positional line, not a theory race; a less-known but reputable reply is fine. -> MISSING. Nothing sets material against development lead in one sentence
- Name what the opponent's move wants (After the opponent's move, whenever it carries an idea) e.g. Their queen on e4 is eyeing your pawn on c5; they want the d-pawn trade and then g5 and g4 to kick your knight off the defence of d4. -> src/services/opponentIntent.ts:55 buildOpponentIntent + moveIntent.ts:124 read from their seat + opponentMovePurpose.ts:58 threatStoppedBy. A three-move chase of a defender is only partly read (opponentIntent looks 2 plies deep)

- Read the bait in their move (When the opponent offers material that leads into their idea) e.g. Their f-pawn push is an invitation: take it and their bishop comes out with check and spoils your king's square. - Name what the opponent missed and what they were expecting instead (Right after the opponent's error) e.g. They were guarding against your knight going to a5 and never saw the fork on d7. - The alternative they did not play, and the answer you had ready (After the opponent's choice, or before their reply) e.g. Where their queen went mattered: had it dropped to e3, your d-pawn would have hit it with tempo. ## Source 14
I read all 444 notes in the slice (notes 818 to 1261 of /home/user/wt-work/public/data/voiced-teachings.json, 24 videos) and catalogued 112 distinct teaching acts. Each act is matched to a computer in /home/user/wt-work/src/services, with file:line confirmed by reading the code. Tally: 39 have an existing computer, 46 are partly covered, 27 have no computer at all. Note numbers in brackets point back into the slice.

WHAT THE CLOSER READING FOUND
The coarse readers probably missed these acts:
- A trap's move order taught from inside the trap (the obvious knight check fails here because a pawn can block) [1168-1169].
- A line branched on both of the opponent's possible recaptures, with what each leads to [1169].
- Honesty about how much a trick actually gains (only a small edge, not a trap) [1170].
- A popular pattern taught together with the condition that makes it fail here [1027-1031].
- A pin that turns out to be an illusion because the pinned queen escapes by capturing with check [1040]. This is a concrete case for brief item 7.
- Reconciling an apparent contradiction: we avoided trades a moment ago, but this trade removes their best piece [1204].
- Giving a piece a new job once its old one is done [885, 1040].
- Raising the student's obvious objection and then answering it [1214-1215, 1228].
- Flagging a move as mysterious now and explaining its point a move later [825-826].
- Trading on your own terms: putting the knight on h6 so it is the piece that recaptures on f5 [899].
- Grabbing free material during an attack as insurance in case the attack fails [1040].
- Converting one advantage into another [1040].
- An exchange sacrifice made to keep the key attacking piece [1146].
- The king makes a poor defender [1232].
- Pawn storms are overrated; in opposite-side castling the pieces can lead the attack [879-882]. `splitPosition.ts:14` teaches the opposite (a pawn race where speed beats a pawn). Under one coach the two must agree on when each applies.

BIGGEST GAPS (to bring to David as new computers, per B6)
1. Patterns taught with their conditions (rule F04). No computer teaches when a pattern works and when it fails. `whyItFailed.ts:170` only explains the student's own failed move afterwards.
2. A pin broken with tempo. `pinGeometry.ts:135` (`isRealPin`) and `whyItFailed.ts:134` (`pinnedToMore`) never test whether the pinned piece can leave with check or with a bigger threat.
3. Interference, deflection/decoy and in-between moves have no board detector. They exist only as puzzle-theme labels in `tacticClassifierService.ts:39-58`. `TacticPatternType` (/home/user/wt-work/src/types/tacticTypes.ts:39) does not include them.
4. Strategic rules with no computer:
   - the principle of two weaknesses;
   - a pawn clamp is worth keeping (`speedRunReads.ts:54` deliberately excludes en passant from the keep-the-tension read);
   - blunting a fianchettoed bishop with a pawn wall;
   - stopping the opponent's pawn break with your structure;
   - fixing their pawns on your bishop's colour;
   - lining up the recapturing piece in advance;
   - pieces are poor at holding up a pawn chain;
   - development order by how sure you are of each piece's square;
   - keeping a piece on its assigned job.
5. Ways of teaching the shared reasoning composer (F0c) lacks: the objection role, a mysterious move paid off later, dropping a plan when the reply changes things, re-evaluating an earlier judgement, numbered multi-step plans, a clean line versus a trap-setting move order, comparing an opening with its sibling, and which openings this move order can still transpose into.

COMPUTERS ONLY ONE SURFACE USES (F2/S1 parity)
- `moveOrder` and `moveIntent` are imported only by `CoachTeachPage` (Learn).
- `danyaBehaviors` is imported only by `CoachTeachPage`.
- `latentFork` is imported only by `positionFacts`.
- x-ray is computed three separate ways: `groundedAnswer.ts:183`, the x-ray relation at `positionReadingService.ts:799`, and `deliberation.ts:386`.

PROBLEMS IN THE CORPUS ITSELF (these matter wherever library notes are spoken, rule S7)
- 46 of the 444 notes are written in the first person ('I'), which breaks rule V1.
- 8 notes name real people or opponents: 862, 870, 872, 874, 884, 887, 1048, 1181 (rule F0d risk).
- Note 1040 (vc-4e6zHMBUgvg-10) is 1,443 words, a whole game's commentary attached to move 5. Seven notes in the full corpus run over 500 words.
- Note 1260 restates note 1253 ten plies later. At that ply its claim is false on the board, because Black already captured on d4 at ply 18.
- Across the corpus, 159 note texts repeat, for 343 extra copies (rule V13).
- In video 4_Ev1a1_2Mg, 56 of 57 notes are bare move calls, about 6 words each.

The frequencies below are counts from my reading. Read-only throughout; nothing was edited.
RHYTHM: Measured over the 444 notes (word counts; 'bare' means no reason clause, by a rough regex):
- Opening: on the student's move, mean 37.6 words, median 20; on the opponent's move, mean 24.3, median 16.
- Middlegame: student mean 25.0, median 22; opponent mean 25.5, median 18.
- Endgame: student mean 15.3, median 12; opponent mean 13.9, median 9.
- 237 of 444 notes are bare and only 37 carry a separate teaching line. Outliers in both directions are distillation artifacts: one video of 6-word move calls, and one 1,443-word note.

The shape across a game:
- The opponent's moves usually get one short clause; the student's moves get the reason.
- At a decision point he speaks at length (60-150+ words) in a fixed order:
  1. what their move did, or that it threatened nothing;
  2. the candidates, each with what it costs;
  3. the tempting move and why it fails;
  4. the chosen move and every job it does;
  5. the line with their reply;
  6. a closing general lesson ('the broader lesson…', 'defensive pieces are underrated…').
- In the opening he explains to the hilt, sometimes three or four points on one move. A quiet move that allows a trick always gets the trick (centre fork, note 1188).
- Endgame conversion turns terse: collect, simplify, the simplest win.
- He stops to say 'pay attention' only at instructive moments, and flags critical moments in one line ('only one move holds').
- Names the opening when it appears and gives its one-line reason for existing (the problem its move order solves) (The move that defines the opening) e.g. This defence exists so your light bishop gets out to f5 before e6 shuts it in. Gap: the reason in move-order terms ('develop it before the pawn buries it') would need boardDelta.ts:65 BLOCKS joined to the identity; no computer joins them.

## Source 15
Second close reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[1262..1705]: 444 notes from 26 videos (14 with the student as Black, 12 as White). Phases: 216 opening, 198 middlegame, 30 endgame. Only 52 notes fill `teaches` and 3 fill `plans`, so the teaching is in `explains`. Coarse Readers 2 (750-1499) and 3 (1500-2249) covered this slice. I grepped all 12 readers' output (digests/teach.md) before marking anything [NEW]. Every code claim below was checked against the file. The reference coach is never named.

WHAT THE COARSE PASS MISSED (tagged [NEW] or [NEW NUANCE] in the list):
(1) "Can you play it anyway?": testing whether the opponent's prevention really prevents your break. moveIntent.ts:383 only works in the student's direction, and speedRunReads.ts:267 playAnyway skips plain trades (:278-283).
(2) Clearance with tempo: "if my own piece weren't there, there would be a pin".
(3) Interception and deflection named live. Clearance, x_ray, deflection, interference and zwischenzug are all 'theme-only' in missedTacticService.ts:724-741, which means no live detector produces them.
(4) X-ray through an ENEMY pawn onto a loose lower-value piece, and luring the target onto your line. positionReadingService.ts:818 findXrays requires a friendly blocker (:860) and a target worth more than the slider (:851).
(5) The masked weakness: a strong piece hiding a structural hole.
(6) The mirrored-square asymmetry.
(7) Don't assume the opponent will make the trade you want.
(8) Keep tactical options alive in a closed position.
(9) The pawn-storm lock standoff (push g5 and they answer h5; push h5 and they answer g5).
(10) An open file is harmless when you cover its entry squares.
(11) Don't block the c-pawn in queen's-pawn openings.
(12) The tempo gift, both ways: a move whose natural answer is one they wanted anyway, and their move that walks into one you wanted anyway.
(13) A fork that wins no material but still serves a positional purpose.
(14) The 'look again for a better move' habit. It is absent from methodBeat.ts:296; Reader 2 mapped similar habits there wrongly.
(15) Converting edges smaller than a piece: a pawn up, or the exchange up, so trade and keep developing. conversionMethod.ts:41 sets CONVERSION_EDGE=3; tradeJudgement needs a two-point lead.
(16) Move orders that deny a resource but cost less than a pawn. moveOrder.ts:29 gates at 100cp, so none in this slice would fire.
(17) The quiet move a combination depended on.
(18) The 'same structure, one difference' comparison. structureSignature.ts:132 detects the Maroczy bind but feeds only corpus-note transfer; the spoken namedPawnStructure (positionReadingService.ts:1060) knows four shapes.
(19) The risk of delaying a pinned capture: a pin to the king dissolves when the king steps off the line. This is a fourth case for brief item 7.
(20) Keep an enemy pawn alive because it walls off their rook, and choose between winning captures by the defender's resources.
(21) Non-recapture capture choice. recaptureChoice.ts:103 handles immediate recaptures only.
(22) Decline material that would free their bad piece.
(23) Explain why the opponent's system normally starts with a different move: the one they skipped is what lets your break in.

CORRECTIONS TO THE COARSE MAPPING:
- 'A threat must be meaningful' is computed: moveInsight.ts:909 emptyThreat, called inside moveMissed at :430, reaches Learn and chat. The coarse pass said MISSING.
- 'The right move one turn too early' is moveTiming.ts:47 readTiming.
- methodBeat has none of the x-ray, weakness-list or look-for-better habits mapped to it.
- positionReadingService.ts:787 pieceScope already counts the squares a piece attacks. That is the raw material for the 'centre knight sees eight squares, corner knight two' nugget; it is never spoken.
- moveInsight.ts:947 removes the queen from looseOwnPieces. That is the opposite of the taught rule that a queen always counts as loose.

STRUCTURAL FINDINGS:
- Capability parity (F2/S1): several computers reach a single surface. findXrays, findRookLift, findBlockade, computeSpace and findFianchetto reach only chat plus the Learn behaviour list (CoachTeachPage.tsx:293). structureSignature reaches only note transfer.
- Dual-use gaps (F4): some computers run one direction only. moveIntent.stopReason explains your prevention but nothing tests theirs. latentDanger guards your own king and queen only. findXrays attacks only through your own blocker.
- F04: nothing computes when the f7 sacrifice works or fails. The slice has a clean 'fails' case (#1555-1558: they are out of attackers). moveInsight.ts:668 greekGift checks no conditions.

DO NOT COPY from this slice:
- F0d: a grandmaster's 'question' credited by name (#1271); a streamer shout-out (#1416).
- V1/F18: the coach talking about itself or its own uncertainty (#1486-1489, #1512, #1523); first-person recommendations and 'a line I grew up on' (#1505, #1507). Credit a real game only.
- V8: a number in speech (#1694 'plus three').
- Off-board: scouting a specific opponent (#1634-1637).
- F10: 'at this level' framing must come from the student's measured play, never a rating.
- F01: two near-silent videos (#1638-1678, #1351-1376) are pure move calls; do not model on them.
RHYTHM: Measured on notes 1262-1705 (444 notes).

OPENING (216 notes): median 18 words, mean 26. 49 notes (23%) are 8 words or fewer, almost all the opponent's reply or a routine recapture. The student's own opening moves get the name plus the point, often two points (what it prepares, what it stops, its drawback, the trap around it). The 9 notes of 60+ words all sit at tabias or structural hinges; one structure lecture is 289 words on a single ply (#1329, the isolated queen's pawn).

MIDDLEGAME (198 notes): median 21 words, mean 27. 40 are short and 18 run 60+ words. The long ones come at decision points, in this order: the question, the candidates, why-not, the line with their reply named, then the habit. One 947-word strategy lecture sits on one ply (#1477) and makes about a dozen sub-decisions.

ENDGAME (30 notes): median 19 words. Mostly directives (bring the king, push it, check then queen) plus counterplay checks. One long note (#1418) is a whole-board check before the last push.

A THOUGHT SPANS PLIES: 78 of 444 notes (18%) are halves of one sentence. A note begins on one move and is finished after the reply (a claim about the threat, then 'it forces the king up'). So the unit of teaching is the thought, not the ply; the composer must let a clause straddle the opponent's move.

QUESTIONS: 25 notes pose about 30 questions. All but two are answered in the same note or the next. They are rhetorical thinking aloud (F18), not pauses for the student (F05).

WHERE IT GOES QUIET: whole replayed games told as bare move calls. #1638-1678 averages 5.8 words with 88% bare; #1351-1376 is 54% bare. That is description, which F01 cuts. Where the coach is teaching, routine moves still get a short clause.

## Source 16
SLICE: notes[1706..2149] of public/data/voiced-teachings.json. That is 444 notes from 22 videos (189 opening, 158 middlegame, 97 endgame; 235 with the student as White, 209 as Black). I read every note in full, with its line. Before calling anything 'missed', I checked it against what the coarse readers already catalogued: the 2026-09-27 teaching census (docs/plans/2026-09-27-*-teaching-census.md: M#1-15, the P and C lists, the 'Beyond' list), the insight catalogue (docs/*-insight-catalogue.md: types 1-39, A1-A12, B1-B11, C1-C11, D1-D8, and the build queue), and docs/plans/2026-09-24-speedrun-target.md (L1-L11, H1-H14). Every MISSING claim below was grepped across src (non-test). Two of my slice's videos (C2unZJEz01o, DO28z1MTaC8) were already read by the catalogue.

WHAT THE COARSE READERS MISSED (not in any list, confirmed absent in code):
(1) Prevention by having the answer ready instead of stopping the move. moveIntent.ts:124 has PREVENTS and PREPARES, but PREPARES covers only your own next move.
(2) Not spending a move to stop a harmless pawn push, and recording the student who does. Seen 5 times.
(3) Holding an unstoppable plan move until it lands with tempo. A four-note arc; the only tempo code is the defensive half at moveInsight.ts:421.
(4) Castling legality as geometry: your piece covers their king's landing square. No computer for it.
(5) The two-weaknesses / second-front principle. It exists only as note-lookup keywords (danyaTeachingService.ts:1369, endgameLessonsService.ts:106).
(6) Comparing the ways to meet a pin and what each one concedes. Only "it unpinned" after the fact: reviewMoveTeaching.ts:205, deliberation.ts:453.
(7) Before allowing a discovered attack, listing every square the front piece can jump to.
(8) The other half of meeting a check: the block hangs something to the next check, so the king move is right. checkMethod.ts:50 exits whenever the best move IS the king move.
(9) Getting the bishop out before the pawn chain closes.
(10) Denying the opponent's opening the exchange or break it is built on.
(11) Reading the opponent's move-order intent before it lands. Transpositions are only named afterwards: openingAnnouncement.ts:82, coachFeatureService.ts:3124.
(12) Naming the other opening where the same maneuver is standard (cross-opening transfer). structureSignature only retrieves notes.
(13) A piece aimed through your own piece is loaded, not wasted.
(14) A live interference/interception detector. Today it is only a puzzle-theme label (tacticAlertService.ts:100).
(15) Standard piece squares for an opening system, and a verdict on how sound the opponent's opening choice is. openingIdentity has no soundness field.

THE CATALOGUE CLAIMS MORE THAN THE CODE DOES. docs/*-insight-catalogue.md:693 says 'Nothing on the owed list remains', but:
- #18 'do it while you can' is not built. moveOrder fires only when the swapped order loses at least a pawn to a material or mate refutation (moveOrder.ts:91, :126). moveTiming reads the reverse direction (moveTiming.ts:47).
- #29 'finishing an attack' (turn the king's weakness into material; split the attackers' jobs) is not built. conversionMethod's attack-king step says the opposite (conversionMethod.ts:115-120).
- Several built reads are narrower than this slice's examples:
  - goodInEveryBranch looks at material only (speedRunReads.ts:383-395).
  - usefulWaiting fires on rook-pawn steps only (speedRunReads.ts:310).
  - castleSide reads your own pawn shelter only (speedRunReads.ts:113-119).
  - pawnHook stands down when your own king is on that wing (moveInsight.ts:793-794).
  - forceConcession names lost castling or an isolated/doubled pawn only (speedRunReads.ts:524-539).
  - ruleException has exactly three rules: same minor twice, shield pawn, early queen (ruleException.ts:87-125).
  - theirMoveCost has four kinds: hole, bishop-shut, castling, structure (theirMoveCost.ts:23).
  - zugzwang uses the tablebase only (zugzwang.ts:38).

CORPUS QUALITY in this slice, all measured:
- 54 of 444 notes (12%, the whole video vc-CQFSXmfxMV8) are a bare move log, at most 11 words, and teach nothing (F01).
  - Nothing blocks them. noteAtPosition takes the first note after preferReachable (danyaTeachingService.ts:526, :645). scoreNarration only breaks ties: 'a preference, never a blocker' (:616-621).
  - Its bare-move penalty (narrationQuality.shared.mjs:291-293) does not even match forms like 'You play d3.' or 'Black plays e6.'
  - Where a log note is the only one at its position, it would lead a 'teach me' beat on that Sicilian line.
- 56 notes speak in the first person (V1). The first-person gate scans only voiced-matchups and voiced-walkthroughs (voicedCorpusRegister.test.ts:2-3, :47-50). public/data/corpus-spoken.json holds 0 'vc-' ids. spokenBeatText speaks an anchored note's explains with fragment pruning only (danyaTeachingService.ts:1728-1800).
- 6 notes name a person. Two attribute a style or method to a player (vc-D7sbbap9lIc-24, vc-DO28z1MTaC8-6), which F0d needs sorted; four credit an opening name or a move, which is allowed.
- 6 notes end mid-sentence (vc-BzN6MEleBlQ-15/16/17, vc-C6vYlx-lS6g-13, vc-CZC9BI_joNU-4/8).

LATENT ROT FOUND ON THE WAY (not in the duplicate census; read-only, so reported, not fixed):
- The 'pass the move' FEN flip has 8 named copies (speedRunReads.ts:354, zugzwang.ts:20, moveIntent.ts:90, coachFeatureService.ts:3802, arrowEngine.ts:51, learnBoardTeaching.ts:504, coachMoveCommand.ts:65, narrationArrows.ts:90) plus about 10 inline copies, and their in-check guards disagree.
- threatOut.flipSideToMove (threatOut.ts:36) checks inCheck AFTER flipping (:44), which tests the wrong side.
  - Verified with a scratch chess.js run: a White-in-check position flips cleanly, inCheck() reads false, and Black's legal moves include Rxe1.
  - computeMustDefend pre-checks before calling it (threatOut.ts:83), so it is safe.
  - liveTacticsContext.dangerLevel (:782) and forkTrick.trickSidestepped (:138) call it with no pre-check.
- openingGenerator.ts:3001, in the fallback LLM stage-generation prompt, tells the model to use a first-person coach voice, which contradicts V1.

Each teaching act below carries its F01 verb, its frequency in this slice (bracketed numbers are indices into notes[]), and the computer that produces it (file:line) or MISSING with a build sketch. Order: opening acts first (F02), then prevention and timing, then strategy, then confirmations of what is already built.
RHYTHM: MEASURED on 444 notes.
- Median words per note: opening 21, middlegame 24, endgame 11. Longest: 206 words, at a middlegame branch point [1804].
- 255 notes sit on the student's own move, 189 on the opponent's. Two videos annotate almost only the student's moves (20 vs 1 and 19 vs 4); the opponent's move is then named inside the next note.
- 167 plies within videos have no note of their own.

THE SHAPE:
(a) Routine book moves get a bare move name or a one-clause principle. This happens even in the opening: [1720], [1726], [1789], [1790], [1794], [1795]; [1806]-[1859] is an entire video of move calls. So the corpus does NOT explain every opening move. V19 asks for more than he does, which means the opening's teaching density must come from computers, not from the notes.
(b) The move that DEFINES the opening gets its name, often by contrast ('with ...Nf6 it would be the other defence'), plus the opening's purpose in one line.
(c) The first real decision gets the longest note, in a fixed order:
  1. what their move did or gave up;
  2. what they want;
  3. the natural or tempting move and why it is premature or fails;
  4. two or three alternatives, each played out with their reply, plus 'the move to be aware of' inside a line;
  5. the choice and its reasons, often enumerated 'first ... second ...';
  6. it closes on the general principle.
This matches F18 closely. F18's step 5, 'what the opponent keeps doing wrong', is nearly absent here.
(d) Follow-through moves get a few words ('and the follow-up'). Then a look-back ('that was the point of the earlier move') when the earlier purpose shows.
(e) In tactical sequences under time pressure he explicitly goes quiet [1752] and defers detail to after the game [1759].
(f) Winning conversions are mostly move calls, with an occasional verdict ('two passers, this wins') and a single technique tip at the end (stalemate safety [2073]).

HOW HE WEIGHS CHOICES:
- 'X is fine, but Y because...'
- 'it doesn't much matter, so...' (equal choices named as equal)
- honesty when the engine and practical results disagree [1800]
- 'a hard call between A and B' [1804]
- 'many good moves here; one approach is...' [1896]

HOW HE STATES CONSEQUENCES:
- 'if they X, then Y, and Z', always including their best reply
- the cost of NOT acting: 'otherwise g4 crashes through' [1733]
- the consequence of THEIR natural option: 'so e4 is over-ambitious' [1737]
- drawbacks are named even for sound moves: 'not a mistake, just a trade of activity for solidity' [1987]

Golden nuggets come as the closing generalisation. Rhetorical self-questions ('what did that weaken?', 'where should this bishop go?') model the method and are answered at once, so they are not student quizzes (relevant to F05).
- [NEW] Reads the opponent's move-order trick BEFORE it lands: their move tries to steer you into an opening you don't want; names the escape (Early opening, at the move that keeps or closes a transposition) e.g. After 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3, Black plays ...d5 so White can't steer the game into a Pirc. In a 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 game, White's 3.Nc3 sidesteps the gambit Black wanted, but ...Bc5 can still steer back toward it. -> PARTIAL. After the fact: openingAnnouncement.ts:82 ('transposed by a different move order'), coachFeatureService.ts:3124 ('your opponent steers into ...'). The predictive read is MISSING. Sketch: from openings-lichess.json, list the named openings still reachable from this position; say which one their last move makes likelier and which one the student's candidate rules out. The census lumped this as 'transposition 63' (docs/plans/2026-09-27-*-teaching-census.md:76).
- [NEW] Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before the pawn move that would shut it in (Opening, when a chain pawn (...e6/...d6, e3/d3) is about to close a bishop's diagonal) e.g. In the Alapin, after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 d5 4.e5, Black puts the bishop on g4 before ...e6. The result is a French-type structure with the problem bishop already outside. -> MISSING (no grep hit). Building blocks: boardDelta's BLOCKS clause names a buried bishop only after the move (boardDelta.ts header); theirMoveCost 'bishop-shut' covers the opponent only (theirMoveCost.ts:23). Sketch: the student's planned chain pawn would cut a still-home bishop's mobility by 3 or more, and the bishop has a safe developing square now. Then say: bishop first, pawn second.
- [NEW] Denies the opponent's opening the exchange or break it is built on, even with an ugly-looking move (Opening, against a defence defined by one exchange or one break) e.g. Against the Grünfeld, a knight to a4 looks misplaced, but it stops the exchange on c3 the defence relies on and also the ...c5 break. Likewise, Black shouldn't grab on c4, because the opening's point is fast development against the centre. -> MISSING. openingIdentity has provokes/aims/gambit/sharp/famous but no 'built on' fact (openingIdentity.ts:1-11). Sketch: take the defining break or exchange from openingIdentity's main master line, then ask moveIntent PREVENTS (moveIntent.ts:124) whether the candidate takes it away. This also adds a fourth rule to ruleException (knight on the rim).
- [NEW] Names the standard square a piece goes to in this system (Opening/early middlegame, when a piece is still undeveloped) e.g. In this Austrian-type setup the light bishop almost always comes to d3 before castling. In the Grünfeld ending the bishop's good square is e6. -> MISSING (no grep hit for typical squares). Sketch: from master or model games in the opening family, compute the most frequent destination of each minor by move 12. Spoken as words, never percentages (V8).
- [NEW] Gives a verdict on the opponent's opening choice: passive but sound, or dubious but demanding precise play to refute (Opening, right after the opponent's defining move) e.g. The Steinitz-style ...d6 against the Ruy is passive but sound. The early ...Nf6 against the Queen's Gambit is objectively dubious, yet White must find e4 and then Bd3 to prove it. -> PARTIAL. Data exists: explorerTeachLine practical score (explorerTeachLine.ts:59) and engine evals. No soundness field in openingIdentity (openingIdentity.ts:1-11). Sketch: masters score plus engine eval at the defining move, turned into a word band.
- [NEW-ish] Names which treatment of an opening this is (quiet vs sharp) and sketches the other branch (Opening, when the opponent picks one of two known setups) e.g. Be2 is the calm, positional way to handle this London-type system; the sharp way goes for an early flank pawn push. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity 'sharp' covers one main line (forcing rate plus theory depth, openingIdentity.ts:9). Contrasting two treatments of the same opening is MISSING.
- [REFINES] Gives a fallback principle when the opponent leaves the memorised line: develop the piece still at home (if only one minor is left, that's the one) (The ply the opponent departs from book, in a line rehearsal) e.g. In a rehearsal the coach (as White) deviates with Nc3 or h3. If you don't know the book reply, find the minor still on its home square and develop it. -> PARTIAL. The departure is named with the usual move (openingAnnouncement.ts:106). development.ts is the one reading of minor development (development.ts:1-14). No line joins the two at the departure moment.
- [REFINES] Calls a pawn sacrifice that is won straight back not a real gambit (Opening gambit lines) e.g. In an anti-Benko line, after ...bxc4 White answers e4, offering a pawn back that it regains at once. -> PARTIAL. reviewSacrifice.sacrificeCompensation covers real sacs (reviewSacrifice.ts:44); openingIdentity 'gambit' covers an imbalance that lasts. The converse ('regained within N plies, so not a sacrifice') is not stated.
- [REFINES] Says plainly when engine and practice disagree, and teaches both (Opening plan choice) e.g. One plan in the Glek System is disliked by the engine but scores well in practice; the main plan is the slower f4 setup. -> PARTIAL. The practical score exists (explorerTeachLine.ts:59; openingGenerator.ts:1829 'soundness by practical score'). No sentence contrasting engine and practice was found.
- [COVERED] 'The move you have to know': the natural developing move is the known mistake at this point in theory (The critical opening fork) e.g. In the line above, the natural Nc3 runs into ...e5 and a queen trade with check, so Bd3 is the move. Against ...b6/...Bb4 setups, a routine Nf3 lets the pin pile up on e4. -> refutedAlternative.ts (header: the most-played alternative, its cost and the punishing line); safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42) after the fact; forkTrick.ts:81 for the pawn-fork case in [2117].
- [COVERED, contrast form partial] Names the opening at its defining move, often by contrast with its neighbour (Defining move of the opening) e.g. 1.e4 Nc6 is a different defence from the one ...Nf6 would give. The Grünfeld meets Nc3 with ...d5 where the King's Indian plays ...d6. -> openingAnnouncement / detectOpening (openingAnnouncement.ts:82, :106). The contrast with a sibling opening is not computed.
- [NEW] Prevention by having the answer ready, not by stopping the move: allow their plan because your reply is prepared (Middlegame, when the opponent's next plan move is visible) e.g. In a Ruy line Black wants ...c5 to kick the d4 knight. Stopping it with b4 is artificial, so Qf3 prepares Nf5 for the moment ...c5 comes. Similarly, ...Qc7 is picked so that recapturing on c6 is comfortable if White trades. -> MISSING. moveIntent PREVENTS takes their reply away; PREPARES is about your own next move (moveIntent.ts:3-12, :124). Sketch: null-move probe for their plan move P (moveIntent.nullMoveFen, moveIntent.ts:90); compare your best reply to P before and after the candidate; fire when P stays legal but is now bad for them because your reply works, and the stopping candidate costs more.
- [NEW] Don't spend a move stopping a harmless pawn push (and catch the student who does) (Opening/middlegame, facing a flank pawn expansion) e.g. Facing a coming ...b5, don't spend a move on a4: the push is harmless, so keep developing. In the Italian, castle rather than spend the move on a3. -> MISSING. Neighbours don't fit: bluffDetector handles piece moves that hit pieces (bluffDetector.ts:37); falseAlarm needs a real threat (falseAlarm.ts:37); usefulWaiting needs a rook-pawn step (speedRunReads.ts:310). Sketch: the candidate's only PREVENTS output is a push the null-move engine read scores as no threat, and the move costs development. Dual-use: record when the student plays it.
- [NEW] Holds an unstoppable plan move until it lands with tempo (Middlegame, when the plan move can't be prevented) e.g. With b4 unstoppable, White plays d3 and waits, avoiding Bd2, which would let the black queen leave a5 first. When b4 finally comes, it hits the queen. -> MISSING. Only the defensive half exists, 'their reply comes with tempo' (moveInsight.ts:421). moveTiming reads the opposite direction (moveTiming.ts:47); skipMiddleman says play the break now (speedRunReads.ts:294). Sketch: M is engine-good now and next move, their null-move best doesn't prevent it, and next move M attacks a piece while now it doesn't.
- [CATALOGUED #18, NOT BUILT] 'Now, while you can': play it before their natural reply takes it away (Opening/middlegame, when a square or diagonal will be denied) e.g. Black slips ...Bg4 in now; if the knight develops first, White plays h3 and the bishop never gets there. -> NOT BUILT, despite docs/*-insight-catalogue.md:693. moveOrder needs a material or mate refutation of at least a pawn (moveOrder.ts:91, :126); moveTiming is the reverse direction (moveTiming.ts:47). Sketch: moveIntent PREVENTS from the opponent's seat; their natural reply R would make the student's move M illegal or bad, so say 'M now, before R'.
- [NEW] Compares the ways to meet a pin and what each concedes (When a knight gets pinned to the queen or king in the opening) e.g. Against ...Bg4 pinning a knight, unpin with Qe1 rather than weaken with f3 or give the bishop for it. Against ...Bb4, Ne2 connects the knights so ...Bxc3 costs no structure, better than a3 or f3. -> MISSING. Only after the fact: reviewMoveTeaching.unpinPoint (reviewMoveTeaching.ts:205), deliberation 'breaks the pin' (deliberation.ts:453). The catalogue's C9 'pin quality' is unbuilt. Sketch: enumerate unpin, defend/connect, kick with a pawn, and give the piece; read each one's concession with boardDelta and the engine.
- [NEW] Before allowing a discovered attack, lists every square the front piece can jump to (Your candidate creates an alignment that their piece can unmask) e.g. c3 kicks the knight but allows a discovery. Before playing it, count each square that knight can land on and what it hits from there. -> MISSING. safetyHabits.blunderCheck fires only after a loss of 150 or more with a piece left en prise (safetyHabits.ts:25). Sketch: an enemy slider behind an enemy piece on a line to your piece or king; enumerate the front piece's legal landings that hit something. Dual-use: record when an allowed discovery won material.
- [REFINES] Before a natural block or retreat, checks it doesn't put two of your pieces on one enemy line (Choosing a retreat or block square) e.g. Retreat the knight to c3, not e3, where both knights would stand on the queen's line and one would fall. -> PARTIAL. Caught after the fact by moveMissed (moveInsight.ts:368) and detectNewThreat (groundedAnswer.ts:6890). A pre-move habit line is not computed.
- [NEW HALF] Meeting a check: the natural block hangs something to the next check, so the king move is right (Student in check with both block and king moves available) e.g. In check on b4, blocking with the knight lets the queen check again and take on b2; tuck the king to c1 instead. In another game the block would bury the bishop and drop c2, so the early king walk is the exception. -> PARTIAL. checkMethod.ts:32 teaches only 'don't reach for the king'; line 50 returns null whenever the best answer IS the king move. Sketch: same function, keep that case and phrase the block's refutation from the engine line.
- [NEW] Castling legality as geometry: your piece covers the square their king must land on (Middlegame with an uncastled enemy king) e.g. If White plays e4, the bishop on h6 sees c1 and White can no longer castle queenside. With White's queen on g7, Black cannot castle short. -> MISSING. Only a stuck-king route check (danyaBehaviors.ts:294) and castleByHand (moveInsight.ts:840). Sketch: chess.js castling legality with and without the student piece's coverage of c1/d1/f1/g1 (c8/d8/f8/g8); name the covering piece. Dual-use: record when the student lets the bind go.
- [NEW] Chooses the castling side from the attack you want: castle opposite their hook and race; predict their castling side from their pawn storm (Before castling, once a flank pawn has advanced) e.g. After ...h6 the pawn is a hook for g4-g5, so castle queenside and storm; the bishop pair and more centre make the race favour you. White's early h4 says they'll castle long. -> PARTIAL. castleSide reads only your own pawn cover (speedRunReads.ts:108-119); pawnHook teaches the hook as a lever and stands down when your king is on that wing (moveInsight.ts:782, :793-794). The race-based choice and the prediction are MISSING.
- [REFINES #27] Opposite-side castling as a race of tempi: a pawn push that is useful whichever way they castle (Before the opponent commits their king) e.g. ...b5 costs nothing if White castles short and is a tempo ahead in the race if White castles long. -> PARTIAL. goodInEveryBranch is material-only (speedRunReads.ts:383-395, leavesSomething :357-366). planRace has no pawn-storm kind (planRace.ts:180). Sketch: count pushes to open a file at each king, per castling branch.
- [NEW] Two weaknesses: stretch the defence with a second front (Middlegame/endgame with a fixed target on one wing) e.g. Fix the d6 pawn with one rook and swing the other toward the king; the defender can't cover both and the kingside gives. There's a second weak square on c5 as well. -> MISSING as a computer. It exists only as note-lookup keywords (danyaTeachingService.ts:1369, endgameLessonsService.ts:106) and in plan prose (nextPlans.ts:335). Sketch: findWeakPawns/holes per wing plus where their defenders sit, and say the second front when the targets are on both wings.
- [CATALOGUED #29, NOT BUILT] Division of labour: each attacker gets its own job (Attack against the king) e.g. One rook takes the h-file, the other heads to the b-file, the king steps to g7, and mate appears. -> NOT BUILT (catalogue #29 at docs/*-insight-catalogue.md:236-242, still owed at :618). kingAttack counts attackers (kingAttack.ts:71) but assigns no roles.
- [CATALOGUED #29, NOT BUILT] Finishing an attack: the king's weakness is a springboard to win decisive material, not only a mate hunt (Winning attack, when mate is not forced but material is) e.g. Rather than insist on mate, use the exposed king to win the rook with checks, which decides just as surely. -> NOT BUILT. conversionMethod's attack-king step says the opposite ('the attack is the fastest win', conversionMethod.ts:115-120). Sketch: compare the engine line ending in a material gain against the mating try; say it when the material line is shorter or surer.
- [REFINES] Strategic zugzwang / domination: they have no useful move; a piece is asked again and again where it can stand (Middlegame bind, or a piece being driven around) e.g. The opponent is so tied up that any move loses something. Repeated hits leave the enemy queen with no comfortable square. -> PARTIAL. zugzwang is tablebase-only, 7 pieces or fewer (zugzwang.ts:38); a trapped piece is flagged only at zero safe squares (reviewFullData.ts:836-842). Sketch: an engine pass test above 7 pieces (passFen exists, zugzwang.ts:20), plus a read of a piece's safe-square count shrinking.
- [NEW] A piece aimed through your own piece is loaded, not wasted (Developing a bishop behind your own knight) e.g. The bishop on b2 sits behind your own knight on c3. Fine: the knight will move and the long diagonal opens onto e5. -> MISSING. latentDanger covers enemy alignments on your king or queen (latentDanger.ts:87). Sketch: own slider, exactly one own piece on the line, enemy target beyond, so the line opens when that piece moves.
- [REFINES #20] Develops to a role, not as far forward as possible (Choosing a developing square) e.g. The bishop goes to e6, not g4: on e6 it hits a2, stands centrally and keeps White's bishop off c4. On g4 it does nothing. -> PARTIAL. pieceOptions.dutiesOf / computePieceOptions (pieceOptions.ts:63, :126); catalogue #20 is still partial. The 'farther isn't better' misconception and the per-square job list are not computed.
- [NEW] When a piece's defensive job is already done by another, spends it on pressure (Choosing between a defending square and an active one) e.g. d4 is already held by the knight, so the bishop goes to g5 to press, not to e3 to defend. -> PARTIAL. pieceOptions.dutiesOf (pieceOptions.ts:63) computes duties; comparing a redundant defensive square with an active one is MISSING.
- [REFINES] Keeps the bishop pair as a reason for the move choice (Open position, holding both bishops) e.g. Retreat the bishop to e3 to keep the pair; pushing on to c5 would only invite ...d6. -> PARTIAL. The asset is named in verdicts (reviewPositionalAssessment.ts:200-204, read via positionFacts.ts:32), plus plan prose (nextPlans.ts:335). The move-choice reason is MISSING.
- [NEW] Their capture released the tension and handed you something: the centre, or the bishop pair (Right after the opponent resolves central tension) e.g. Black's ...Bxd4 lets go of the tension and concedes the centre; now you hold both bishops and more of the middle. -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost has four kinds only: hole, bishop-shut, castling, structure (theirMoveCost.ts:23). keepTension speaks only for the student's own choice (speedRunReads.ts:49).
- [NEW] Resolves pawn tension by pushing past to lock and keep a protected passer, not by capturing (Opponent lunges with a pawn against your centre pawn) e.g. When Black plays ...c5, don't take: d5 shuts the door and leaves you a protected passed pawn. -> PARTIAL. keepTension says 'keep the tension', not 'push past' (speedRunReads.ts:49-64); the catalogue's 'don't release the clamp' is unbuilt.
- [REFINES A4/C6] Provokes a forced defensive pawn move that opens a line to the king (Attack, when a threat forces a pawn move near the king) e.g. Qh6 with Ng5 coming forces ...f6, which opens the a2-g8 diagonal; a bishop reaching c4 then mates. -> PARTIAL. forceConcession names only lost castling or a new isolated/doubled pawn (speedRunReads.ts:524-539); provokes covers only a pawn fixed in your half (speedRunReads.ts:125-138). A line opened to the king is MISSING. boardDelta's WEAKENS could read it from the forced move.
- [NEW] Lures the king into the attack (invites castling toward your pieces) (Attack being prepared against an uncastled king) e.g. e4 opens the bishop's diagonal, threatens a pin and invites Black to castle straight into the attack. -> MISSING. Attraction exists only as a tactic word (tacticNarrationService.ts:198, calculationDrillService.ts:112).
- [REFINES] Prepares a break by pre-defending the pawn it will leave soft (One move before a central break) e.g. Before ...e5, ...Bb7 looks pointless, but after the trade on e5 it keeps d5 from being a target on the d-file. -> PARTIAL. preparationOf names only 'remove a defender' or 'add an attacker' for a capture target (speedRunReads.ts:463-482); rejectedMoveLater (:486). Pre-protecting your own pawn is MISSING.
- [REFINES] Picks which piece makes the move by the tactic it keeps alive later (Two pieces can do the same job) e.g. Win the pawn back with the queen from c8, not the rook: after c6 and the trades, the queen's placement keeps a fork on e3 available. -> PARTIAL. compareTwoMoves engine ablation (per the census) gives a number; naming the tactic only one placement keeps alive is MISSING.
- [REFINES] Chases a lone, unsupported central piece with a pawn (An enemy piece is centralised without pawn support) e.g. Black's knight on e5 has no pawn behind it. Chase it with f4, since a pawn hit can't be met by adding a defender, or offer a knight trade. -> PARTIAL. tempoCount counts their repeated piece moves (tempoCount.ts:32); 'chase with the pawn, not the bishop' is MISSING.
- [REFINES] Flexible move first, because the best plan depends on how they set up (conditional plan) (Opening/middlegame with two plans whose value depends on the opponent) e.g. Play Nc3 first and see how Black develops: if their knight comes to f6, f4 becomes much stronger. -> PARTIAL. flexibleFirst covers only a piece move vs an equal pawn move (speedRunReads.ts:549-563). The conditional 'if they do X, plan A improves' is MISSING.
- [CATALOGUED in census 'Beyond', NOT BUILT] Prefers the simple, safe win over complications (Winning position, several moves keep the win) e.g. No need for complications: the knight just goes back to f3. Up material in a messy position, consolidate first. -> MISSING as a selector. Only a chat stem (groundedAnswer.ts:1343) and prompt text (coachApi.ts:3256). Census lists it at docs/plans/2026-09-27-*-teaching-census.md:81. Sketch: among engine moves keeping a won eval, choose the one with the fewest forcing replies for them.
- [REFINES] A fixed weakness can wait; take the dynamic chance first (Winning attack plus a permanent target) e.g. Their weak g5 pawn isn't going anywhere, so go after the king first. -> PARTIAL. conversionMethod (conversionMethod.ts:44) has no permanence test on the target.
- [NEW] Cross-opening transfer: 'the same manoeuvre as in opening X' (A standard manoeuvre from another opening appears) e.g. Qe1 heading for h4 is the familiar queen route from another f4 system. h3 against ...Bg4 is the same idea as in the Glek setup. The knight's e7-f5 trip is the Caro-Kann route. -> MISSING as a coach line. structureSignature only retrieves notes between similar structures (structureSignature.ts:1-12). Census 'analogy ~120' (teaching census :73). Sketch: index (piece, route, structure signature) to named openings from the opening DB and model games.
- [REFINES] Models the self-question aloud and answers it at once (method, not a quiz) (Plan-finding moments) e.g. After the recapture, ask what your earlier a3 was preparing; the answer (b4-b5) is the plan. When they lunge ...g5, ask what it weakened: the f5 square. -> PARTIAL. methodBeat habits (methodBeat.ts:116); GamePromise threads the follow-through (speedRunReads.ts:36). The habit 'ask what your last quiet move prepared' is not one of them. F05 limits ASKING the student, but this is modelled thinking (F0).
- [REFINES] Recognises a mating net: count the king's flight squares (The enemy king is walked into a corner) e.g. After the king steps to h3, a net is closing around it. -> PARTIAL. Chat stem only (groundedAnswer.ts:7129); matePatterns is not wired to this phrasing.
- [NEW] Interception/interference: a piece cuts the line between an enemy piece and its target (A tactical moment where a line is cut) e.g. After ...d5, the knight steps into the queen's line and cuts it off from the square it needed. -> MISSING as a live board detector. It exists only as a puzzle-theme label (tacticAlertService.ts:100, puzzleConceptHint.ts:44).
- [COVERED] Move order inside a tactic or exchange: which capture or check comes first (A forcing sequence) e.g. Take on g4 first; pushing e5 first allows gxh5. Capture the knight first and only then does the check fork the queen. -> moveOrder.ts:65 (only with a material or mate refutation of at least a pawn, :91, :126).
- [COVERED] Recapture choice by structure, by what it leaves hanging, and by contact between pieces (Any recapture) e.g. Recapture with the knight; neither pawn capture is worth the structure. It has to be the bishop, or e4 hangs. Take with the queen so it keeps guarding the rook. -> recaptureChoice.ts:56/:103. The payoff two moves later is in causalChain.ts:639.
- [COVERED] What their move cost them (a hole, a shut-in bishop, a loosened pawn) and the route to use it (Right after an opponent pawn lunge or structural move) e.g. Their ...g5 leaves f5 as a permanent hole, so steer a knight toward it. Their f3 leaves the e3 pawn as a target. -> theirMoveCost.ts:60; weakenedBy (moveInsight.ts:523, both colours); computePieceRoute (forwardTeaching.ts:186).
- [COVERED] What a quiet move prevents or prepares (one move, two jobs), with the stopped move counted (Quiet moves, either side) e.g. h3 so ...Bg4 can't come; c6 both clamps d5 and opens the queen's route to a5; Ne4 heads for f6 and stops ...Nb4. -> moveIntent.ts:124 (stopReason :383 counts the stopped move).
- [COVERED] King stuck in the centre, so open lines; castling by hand (An enemy king can't castle safely) e.g. Take on c3 to rule out long castling, then bring the knight back to open the centre while the king is stuck. -> castleByHand (moveInsight.ts:840); the king-in-centre reads (catalogue #28).
- [COVERED] Choose a piece's square so a pawn can't kick it with tempo (Developing a knight near enemy pawns) e.g. In the King's Indian the knight goes to d7, not c6, where d5 would hit it and gain space. -> moveInsight.ts:421 ('tempo-handed'; catalogue #37).
- [COVERED] A rule and its exception (shield pawns, early queen) (A move breaks a beginner rule and is still good) e.g. Pushing pawns in front of your own king is fine when the opponent has no counterplay. An early queen move works when it hits two loose pieces. -> ruleException.ts:70 (rules 'twice' :87, 'shield-pawn' :110, 'early-queen' :123 only).
- [COVERED] Speed-run reads: play it anyway, keep the tension, rook to the file that will open, pawn hook (Middlegame decisions) e.g. f5 still works even though it looks prevented. Keep the rook on e8 rather than snap a pawn. The rook belongs on d1 before the e-pawn trade opens the file. -> speedRunReads.ts:267 (playAnyway), :49 (keepTension); moveInsight.ts:869 (fileToOpen), :782 (pawnHook). Fed only on the student's turn (thinkAloud.ts:257).
- [COVERED] Loose pieces drop off: two loose pieces point to a double attack; move order decides whether the trick works (Undefended pieces on the board) e.g. Both the bishop and the e5 knight are undefended, which points to Qd4 hitting both. -> loosePieces.ts:35; 'two hit at once' (built per the catalogue build queue).
- [COVERED] Count attackers and defenders on a break square before pushing (Before a central break or capture) e.g. e4 isn't possible yet: four defenders against three attackers. -> countMethod.ts:17; exchangeLedger.ts:136.
- [COVERED] When ahead: trade, attack, or consolidate, and why (Material lead) e.g. Up material with a bind, don't chase a queen trade; keep attacking. Up a rook, prefer piece play to grabbing a2. A trade of queens is fine when it speeds up the mate. -> conversionMethod.ts:44; deliberation's 'queen trade throws away the attack' (per the build queue).
- [COVERED] Paper-tiger threats: scary-looking, simple answer (Opponent's aggressive-looking move) e.g. Their Ng5 looks dangerous but ...Qe8 answers it. The real problem is the g-file, not their bishop. -> bluffDetector.ts:37; falseAlarm.ts:37.
- [COVERED] Look-back: 'that was the point of the earlier move' (When an earlier move's purpose shows) e.g. The earlier a3 now shows its point: ...b5 would lose to a capture opening the a-file. -> causalChain.ts:639; planMemory / GamePromise.
- [COVERED] Their move's purpose, including a quiet move's hidden idea (After an odd or quiet opponent move) e.g. The king went to h2 so that after the capture on f3 the king is off the open file and their rook can use the g-file. -> moveIntent both seats (moveIntent.ts:124); opponentIntent.ts:55; opponentMovePurpose.ts:58 (defence only).
- [COVERED] Candidate list with each option's brief verdict, and an honest grade of the move played (Decision points) e.g. Options: drop the knight back to trade the bishop, a sharp c5, or b4 with a central claim; the trade looks sterile, so go dynamic. The knight move was probably a small mistake, but not so bad. -> deliberation.ts:144 / :289 (weighing); accuracyService grading.
- [COVERED] Inventory verdict: the advantages listed (bishop pair, centre, opponent's weak pawns) (After a simplification or at a phase change) e.g. Once the c5 pawn is collected: an intact centre, both bishops working and White's pawns weak. -> reviewPositionalAssessment phaseVerdictLine, via positionFacts.ts:32.
- [COVERED] What most players at this level play here (Opening reply choice) e.g. ...d6 is the most common reply among players who don't know the line; ...h6 is a typical default. -> strongChoice.ts:16; refutedAlternative.ts; amateurPlayCache. Spoken without numbers (V8).
