## Source 17
Close second reading of voiced-teachings notes[2150..2593]: 444 notes from 30 videos, 60% in the opening. I found 112 distinct teaching acts. About 36 are produced by an existing computer today, about 55 are partial, and about 21 are MISSING. Roughly 25 of the acts never appear in the 2026-09-27 teaching census; those are tagged NEW vs census. Every code claim was checked at file:line in /home/user/wt-work/src/services. The source names no person in any act text.

HIGHEST-VALUE GAPS, opening first (F02/F03):
(1) Traps, for the one trap library (F04). Two pieces are missing: (a) reading a trap the OPPONENT is attempting, with its refutation (the Noah's Ark attempt); (b) telling the student that their own sound book move also SETS a trap (the QGD …Nbd7 case). trapLearning.ts:105 only warns the student about traps they might walk into.
(2) Tempo arithmetic, both MISSING. Don't trade a piece that has moved twice for one that has moved once. Delay a capture until the recapturing piece has committed (QGD …dxc4 only after Bd3).
(3) The join between a natural move, its drawback, and the punishment that uses exactly that drawback. Example: …Nc6 shuts in the f8 bishop, so dxc5 cannot be met by …Bxc5. theirMoveCost.ts:60 and refutedAlternative.ts:81 each hold half and never meet.
(4) Reversed-colour and inserted-move opening analogies ("an Alekhine with c3/c5 thrown in"), and warning ahead that a move order allows a transposition. openingDetectionService.ts:246 only names a transposition after it has happened.
(5) The attacking twin of the last-move habit: "their last move gave something up — find the tactic it allows". methodBeat.ts:309-313 teaches only the defensive half.
(6) Tactics: desperado; a live zwischenzug detector (it is theme-only today, missedTacticService.ts:741); planning a piece trap by taking its squares first; naming the covered escape square; why a familiar pattern does not apply here; the cleanest of several wins.
(7) King attacks: line up the heavy pieces before opening the file; race awareness with opposite-side castling (planRace.ts:180 only races passers and file collisions); the hook created by THEIR pawn push (hookCreated at moveInsight.ts:826 is only read on the mover's own push); castling by hand with route, contingency, and keeping the rook off the king's path.
(8) Golden nuggets: a pin is harmless when the pinned piece is pawn-protected; pawns are the best defenders; "the count says you lose it, the line says it's fine"; the plan's floor ("even if they win the pawn back you keep X"); take it now before the target escapes.
(9) Strategy: don't trade off the opponent's cramp or move your dominant piece; no counterplay means no rush; diminishing returns, so stop collecting and convert; whether to lock the centre (by analogy to a known structure, or by the castling sides); develop without blocking your own pawn lever; contest the break square before pushing.

ALREADY STRONG (keep and wire everywhere): moveIntent, moveOrder, theirMoveCost, recaptureChoice, ruleException, falseAlarm and bluffDetector, the speedRunReads family, tradeQuality.findTradeTarget, outpost, findColorComplexWeakness, reviewSacrifice, opponentIntent, planChooser, refutedAlternative, theirOpeningVerdict, deliberation, lineWithReasons, exchangeLedger.

RULEBOOK TENSIONS TO FLAG FOR DAVID:
- His one-clause main-line narration (one video's median note is 6 words) conflicts with V19 unless the student's record shows they know the line.
- His level remarks ("a strong player would…", "the line I'd recommend at this level") must key on the student's measured skill (F10/F17), never a rating.
- F05 limits real questions. His rhetorical question, answered at once, is part of thinking out loud (F0/F18), and the composer (thinkAloud.ts:226) has no form for it.
- Do not copy: opponent names and rating numbers (V8, F0d), and personal asides like "my French games", "my coach's line", "learned from a painful loss" (V1).
RHYTHM: Measured on all 444 notes. Median 21 words a note (p25 11, p75 34, p90 50, max 379, mean 26.8). By phase: opening median 21 (n=264); middlegame median 21 but mean 31 (n=150), because the long tail sits there; endgame median 16 (n=30), so conversion is narrated tersely as plan steps. 58 notes (13%) are 6 words or fewer: the move named with no reason. One model-game video runs at a median of 6 words for a whole main line. 12 notes reach 80 words or more, at four kinds of moment: (1) the opening's tabia, where he lays out the whole fight around one break (about 115 words); (2) a combination, where several lines are walked and compared at a single ply (268 to 379 words); (3) a decision with several natural candidates, each refuted, then the indirect answer (90 to 100 words); (4) explaining the opponent's tricky sideline so the student doesn't take the bait (about 80 words). About 23% of notes carry a but/instead/rather-than turn, about 23% a so/because/the-point link, and about 5% a direct question. ORDER INSIDE A NOTE: their move named first, with a verdict if it left book; then what it wants or what it gave up; then 'so' your answer with its reason (often what the answer does NOT block); then the longer plan or break; and later, when it pays off, a tie-back ('that's why'). AT A TACTIC: pause and pose the find-it question; walk the line ply by ply with a point per move; compare the alternative continuation; choose and give the reason. AT A HARD DECISION: list the natural candidates, refute each concretely, find the indirect route through the drawback of their last move, then state the floor ('even if…'). Caveat: the corpus is a per-ply distillation, so one long note can compress several spoken moves.
- Names the opening at the move that defines it and says what that move aims at (for a gambit, what the pawn buys; for an anti-system, what it sidesteps) (the defining ply, or the first ply that identifies the opening) e.g. At g3 after d4, c4 and Nf3: this fianchetto is what makes it a Catalan; the bishop heads for the long diagonal, aimed at d5 and the queenside. -> src/services/openingAnnouncement.ts:54 openingAnnouncement (names the opening once, refines silently) + src/services/openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine (provokes / aims / gambit / sharp, built offline)
- Names the piece or capture the whole opening is built around, so the student knows what never to give away and notices when the opponent gives theirs up (after the defining move, at the opening's signature capture) e.g. The g2 bishop IS the Catalan; the Nimzo's point is giving the b4 bishop for the c3 knight so White's hold on e4 weakens; in the accelerated setup, never let the fianchetto bishop be traded; once they trade their dark bishop, their opening's best piece is gone. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity.ts:85 (aims/provokes) and mastersPlanRead.ts:83 (PieceHome: where master games put each side's pieces) exist. The opening's KEY piece, and 'don't trade it' / 'they just gave theirs up', is MISSING.
- Names the single pawn break the structure turns on, for both sides, and frames the middlegame as make yours, stop theirs (the opening's tabia is reached) e.g. In this Catalan tabia Black lives for …c5. You spend the middlegame stopping it (Bg5 overloads the piece guarding both f6 and c5), then squeeze the half-open c-file. -> PARTIAL. mastersPlanRead.ts:83 counts the break each side's master games actually play; positionReadingService.ts:400 findPawnBreaks lists breaks. Framing the middlegame as preventing THEIR break, and the overload that does it, is MISSING.
- Reads the opponent's preparatory move and answers it the opening's way, giving the reason the answer was chosen (what it does not block) (the opponent prepares a pawn grab or expansion in the opening) e.g. …a6 means they want …dxc4 and …b5 to keep the pawn. Guard c4 with the queen from c2, which blocks none of your developing pieces, and add a rook on d1 for d4. -> opponentIntent.ts:55 buildOpponentIntent (their idea plus your answer, from the PV) and moveIntent.ts:124 (PREVENTS). The reason 'chosen because it blocks nothing' is MISSING; boardDelta.ts:65 only reports what a move DOES block.
- Gives a verdict on the opponent's opening choice against the main move, and how quickly it can collapse (the opponent leaves book) e.g. …d6 here is an inaccuracy; the main move is …d5. The early bishop to c4 against this defence makes little sense. …Nc6 is popular but already loose: one more slip and things go badly within a few moves. -> openingAnnouncement.ts:166 theirOpeningVerdict (dubious or weaker than the main move, by engine cost) + bookDeparture.ts:49. Built. The risk clause ('one more slip and it collapses fast') is MISSING.
- Takes the move a first-timer naturally plays, names its exact drawback, and shows the punishment that exploits exactly that drawback (NEW vs census as a join) (the opponent plays a popular opening move with a structural drawback) e.g. …Nc6 is what most people play the first time, but it leaves the f8 bishop stuck behind e7. So take on c5: they can't recapture with the bishop, the queen has to, and they lose time. -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 names the cost ('bishop-shut', 'hole'). refutedAlternative.ts:81 gives a popular alternative with its cost and line. Nothing joins 'the drawback is X, so the punishing move is the one that makes X matter'. MISSING.

The natural …Nf6 loses a piece to Nxc6. Play …Qf6 instead, so Nxc6 is met by …Bxe3 with mate on f2 threatened. -> trapLearning.ts:105 trapSpeaks (trap-ahead warning, graded red/green) + openingTrapDetector.ts:79 / positionTrapScan.ts:126 (popular-but-losing moves). The repair with tempo is MISSING.

- Restricts an enemy piece before it reaches its outpost (their knight is angling for a good square) e.g. g3 and then the knight to h4 fence their knight off the squares it is heading for. -> MISSING. moveIntent.ts:124 PREVENTS one move, not a whole route.
- Keeps the opponent cramped: don't trade the piece that would relieve them, don't move your dominant piece, no rush when they have no counterplay (NEW vs census) (you hold a bind) e.g. There is a tactic, but it pulls your knight off its dominant square, and there's no need: they can't move. Don't trade either, so their knight stays stuck at home. Improve slowly, one step at a time. -> MISSING. tradeQuality.ts:124 and tradeJudgement.ts:40 judge trades by piece quality and material, not by whether the trade relieves a cramp. There is no counterplay detector; speedRunReads.ts:68 anyMoveFine is the closest.
- Diminishing returns: once well ahead, stop collecting and convert (a winning position) e.g. The first extra pawns matter most, so at some point stop improving and cash in. Don't go out of your way to trade queens, but take the trade when it comes. -> PARTIAL. conversionMethod.ts:44 readConversion (which conversion step the board is on) and tradeJudgement.ts:40 ('ahead'). The 'stop collecting now' trigger is MISSING.
- Uses a pawn majority and the opponent's tied-down pieces (a pawn majority, or an overloaded enemy piece) e.g. Two pawns up with a big kingside majority: push it with g4. Their rook is tied to the file, so you can expand on the other wing. -> PARTIAL. boardStructure.ts:304-326 (split majorities), reviewStrategicOrientation.ts:549 (majority plans, review only), tacticsDetector.ts:690 findOverloadedPieces.
- Creates a weakness for the opponent, then picks between blockading it and trading their best piece (central tension that can be resolved into a weakness) e.g. Take again on c4 and they are left with an isolated d-pawn your queen can hit at once. Then either route a knight to the square in front of it, or bring a knight to c6 to trade their strong knight. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.ts:1060 namedPawnStructure and boardPlan.ts:88 (IQP plan) exist. Choosing the capture that CREATES the weakness is MISSING.
- Trades by piece quality: their only developed or best piece for your worst, and protects your good bishop from their trade (a piece-quality imbalance) e.g. Trade off their only developed piece, the d7 knight, by routing yours to b6. Welcome the bishop taking on e7: it gives their good bishop for your worse knight. Don't castle short yet, or Qd2 and Bh6 trade off your key bishop. -> tradeQuality.ts:273 findTradeTarget ('their best piece, your worst'), tradeQuality.ts:124 readTrade, tradeJudgement.ts:40. Built.
- Removes the defender of a key square to clamp it, and pictures the trade before making it (fighting for an outpost square) e.g. Picture the f3 knight gone: your hold on d4 grows. So the bishop goes to g4 and takes on f3, trading off a piece that controls the square. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:630 findRemovableGuards (tactical removal only) and tradeQuality.ts:273. A count of who controls the square before and after the trade is MISSING.
- Outposts: a hole no pawn can ever cover, occupied at the right moment, and refilled after a trade (the structure creates a hole) e.g. With c4 and e4 pushed, d4 can never be covered by a white pawn, so it's a home for your knight, but not yet with nothing else developed. If a knight is traded there, bring the other one in. -> outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge and :39 isOutpost, theirMoveCost.ts:60 ('hole'), speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole. Built for the geometry. The 'not yet' timing and the refill are MISSING.
- Supports an advanced piece with a pawn, because pawns are the best defenders (an advanced piece is lightly defended) e.g. Prop up the b5 knight with a4: a pawn guard can't be traded off cheaply. d5 keeps your dominant knight anchored. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:209 overprotect (a second guard for an outpost piece). 'A pawn, because pawns are the best defenders' is MISSING.
- States a weakness with what it now means, then the plan against it (a weakness becomes fixed and reachable) e.g. b7 is a lasting weakness now the file is open: lift the rook to a3 and on to b3 against it. After that rook leaves, e6 is weak too. -> positionReadingService.ts:1176 findWeakPawns + positionalRead.ts:616 attackerCanUseFile + forwardTeaching.ts:236 (rook-lift route). Built in parts (D11's 'what it now means' clause is partial).
- Pushes a pawn to fix an enemy weakness, or levers against their expansion at its base or tip (choosing a pawn lever) e.g. a4 and a5 make b7 backward. Once they have pushed b4, chip at it with …a5: at the base of the chain, sometimes at the tip. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:125 provokes (draw out a pawn commitment you can aim at) + positionReadingService.ts:400 findPawnBreaks. Base versus tip is MISSING.
- Develops a piece where it doesn't block his own pawn lever (NEW vs census) (developing a piece in front of a lever pawn) e.g. The knight goes to e2, not f3, so the f-pawn stays free to charge to f4 and f5 at the e6 chain. -> MISSING. boardDelta.ts:65 BLOCKS covers your own sliders being shut in, not your own pawn levers.
- Contests the key square of the break before pushing (NEW vs census) (the opponent guards the square your break needs) e.g. Their knight on h6 stops f5. Ng3 runs into …g6 and Nd2 is slow, so play h3 and keep g4 in reserve to fight for f5. -> MISSING
- Lets the type of centre set the pace (the centre is locked) e.g. With the centre locked, nothing happens fast against good players, so be methodical. Moving a piece three times costs little while nothing is open. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.ts:1060 namedPawnStructure names a 'Closed centre' with its wing plan (:1093). The pace rule is MISSING.
- Decides whether to lock the centre, by analogy with a known structure or by the castling sides (NEW vs census) (a lock-or-take decision) e.g. Don't answer …d5 with e5: unlike the French Advance, their light bishop isn't shut in yet and gets out first, so take instead. With castling on opposite sides, locking the centre lets their pawn storm run faster, so keep it open. -> MISSING. theirMoveCost.ts:60 'bishop-shut' reads a bishop shut in by their own pawn after the fact; there is no read for 'locking now lets their bishop out first' or for locking with opposite-side castling.
- Colour complexes: warns ahead of time, and builds a battery on the weak colour led by the piece that mates (a bishop is gone or about to be traded) e.g. If they ever add …e6 to …g6, d6 and f6 become weak dark squares. With their light bishop gone, line up queen and bishop on the light diagonal, queen in front, since the queen is the piece that mates on h7. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.ts:676 findColorComplexWeakness (static) and tacticsDetector.ts:732 findBatteries. The advance warning and which piece leads the battery are MISSING.
- Judges a bishop by the pawns in front of it (the pawn structure fixes a bishop) e.g. Their light bishop is now no better than a pawn. A fianchetto bishop here will run into your solid d4 and e5 chain. -> positionReadingService.ts:512 findPieceQuality (bad bishop, rim knight) + theirMoveCost.ts:60 'bishop-shut'. Built.
- Explains a counter-intuitive placement by the line that will open later (NEW vs census) (a piece is placed on a line that is closed for now) e.g. The bishop on c4 seems to hit a wall at e6, but once a knight lands on d5 and is taken, e6 disappears and the diagonal opens. The bishop on d3 is aimed at h7 for when the centre opens. -> MISSING. boardDelta.ts:65 UNCOVERS reports only lines the move itself opens; speedRunReads.ts:224 positionOpened fires only after their move has opened one.
- Names the opponent's best counter-plan from their side of the board (once the student's plan is set) e.g. In their shoes I'd look at g4 for kingside play: with their king uncastled, the h1 rook joins in if the h-file opens. Worried about …c4? No, the rook to c3 answers it. -> opponentIntent.ts:55 + lookaheadPlan.ts:166 SidePlan (both sides). Built. The 'an uncastled king's rook can join on the h-file' point is MISSING.
- Tells a threat from an idea: not every idea needs preventing (the opponent prepares an expansion) e.g. Plenty of players would push …a5 on reflex, but b4 is only an idea. What would it do? Send the bishop back to e7, which ends the pin anyway. e4 is nothing to fear, and …b5 is harmless here. -> PARTIAL. bluffDetector.ts:37 (an aggressive move that wins nothing), falseAlarm.ts:37 (a real threat you needn't answer), opponentIntent.ts:55. 'Their quiet idea is fine to allow' is MISSING.
- Defuses a scary-looking threat with the concrete answer, and welcomes moves that cost them (the opponent makes an aggressive-looking push) e.g. …g4 looks like it rips open your king, but you just move the knight and they lose the pawn, because their h5 bishop is loose. Their rook to f1 would actually please you: it costs them castling for good. -> falseAlarm.ts:37 + bluffDetector.ts:37 + theirMoveCost.ts:60 ('castling'). Built. Welcoming the move in advance is MISSING.
- Meets a flimsy wing build-up by hitting back in the centre (the opponent attacks on a wing) e.g. Their kingside build-up looks imposing but is flimsy. Leave it and it dominates, so strike in the centre now, which also pulls their attention away. -> MISSING. movePlan.ts:57 classifyPlan ('center-break') only contrasts the student's move with the engine's.
- Method for finding tactics: ask what the opponent's last move gave up (NEW vs census as a method beat) (just after a weakening move, before the tactic) e.g. Each of their last few moves weakened something. You find the shot by asking what their latest pawn move stopped guarding. The moment c3 weakens d3, take on e4. -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 and boardDelta.ts:65 (ABANDONS / WEAKENS) compute the drawback. methodBeat.ts:309-313 teaches only the defensive half ('what is their last move doing? answer that first'). The attacking habit is MISSING.
- Pauses at the critical moment and asks the find-it question, then answers (a tactic or decisive idea is on the board) e.g. This is the moment to stop and look: can you find the shot? How could you make it impossible for them to take on e4? -> PARTIAL. methodBeat.ts:60 'slow-down' habit (critical and only-move tiers). A rhetorical question answered at once has no form in thinkAloud.ts:226 depthClauses. Real questions are governed by F05.
- Walks the combination ply by ply with the point of each move, then compares an alternative continuation (carrying out a combination) e.g. Nxg5; if the bishop takes e2, the knight to e6 hits the queen; after they take on d1, Nxc7 with check and the rook in the corner falls. Or drop back to e6 and simply dominate. -> lineReasons.ts:20 lineWithReasons, thinkAloud.ts:114 sayLine, exchangeLedger.ts:193 describeExchange. Built.
- Counts attackers and defenders, then looks one step deeper because the count misleads (NEW vs census) (a contested pawn where the plain count is wrong) e.g. e5 is defended twice and attacked once, yet pushing it as a sacrifice is strong: after the trades your rook comes alive and the pressure on f6 grows. They have three attackers on your pawn against two defenders, but winning it wrecks their structure and you get it back. -> PARTIAL. countMethod.ts:17 speaks the count only when it agrees with the legal exchange; speedRunReads.ts:162 heldByTactic (more attackers than defenders, yet taking loses). 'The count says lose, the line says fine because of structure or regaining it' is MISSING.
- X-ray: a line piece aimed through one blocker at a loose or valuable piece, and alignments noted for later pins (a long-range piece lines up through a single blocker) e.g. The queen on f3 also aims through the diagonal at the a8 rook, which is loose, so e5 gains force. The two bishops on the c5-e3 diagonal face each other through the d4 knight. Note your rook and their queen sharing a file, ready for a pin. -> positionReadingService.ts:818 findXrays + deliberation.ts:354 extraJobs ('lines up an x-ray') + latentDanger.ts:87 (for your own king or queen). Built.
- Zwischenzug: instead of the expected recapture, a stronger in-between move first (a recapture is expected) e.g. Don't take back on e5. First take on c6, hitting the a8 rook and the loose c5 bishop at once; or the in-between capture on f6. -> PARTIAL. kneeJerk.ts:15 teaches the habit only after a recapture that cost 100cp or more; thinkAloud.ts:145 notYet; missedTacticService.ts:741 marks zwischenzug 'theme-only'. A live board detector is MISSING.
- Desperado: a doomed piece takes something on its way out (NEW vs census) (a piece is attacked and can't be saved) e.g. That bishop is lost anyway, so let it take the g7 pawn first; then collect the c5 bishop and you are a full piece up. -> MISSING. exchangeLedger.ts:419 only mentions it in a comment.
- Shows why the defence fails: the escape square is covered (an attacked piece seems to have a way out) e.g. The queen to d5 would save both pieces, but your knight covers d5. After …b5 the queen has nowhere to go: c2 and b3 are covered by the knight, and a3 walks into a pawn fork on b4. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:451 findTrappedPieces (a piece trapped now) and groundedAnswer.ts:6890 detectNewThreat (forks). Naming the covered escape square is MISSING.
- Plans a piece trap: take away the escape squares first, then attack (NEW vs census) (an enemy queen or piece is short of squares) e.g. Knight to d4 first, so their bishop only has d1, and if it goes to g4, h5 chases it. Then …b5 traps the queen. …b5 straight away is inaccurate because the queen slips back to d1. -> MISSING. tacticsDetector.ts:451 only sees a piece that is trapped right now.
- Hunts a knight on the rim, trapping it with a pawn (an enemy knight goes to the edge) e.g. The knight on h5 is out on the rim and asking to be hunted. g4 traps it, a pawn push in front of your king you can afford because it wins a piece. -> tacticsDetector.ts:451 (trapped_piece) + positionReadingService.ts:512 (rim knight) + ruleException.ts:70 ('shield-pawn'). Built.
- Picks the move order that makes the tactic work (a known tactic that only works in the right order) e.g. A queen check on a5 is the standard trick against a king still on e1, but given now it loses a piece to Bd2. Take on e5 first; then the check hits king and knight together. -> moveOrder.ts:65. Built.
- Keeps a hidden tactic as a deterrent when placing a piece (developing a piece that has a tactical side job) e.g. Knight to f6 rather than e7: if they ever push e5, the knight jumps to g4, hits the pawn and wins it. That is what stops the push. And don't fear the standoff: taking on e3 threatens mate on f2. -> moveIntent.ts:124 PREVENTS + :383 stopReason, forkTrick.ts:81 forkTrickFor. Built.
- Spots the new threat that a capture, or a piece landing, creates (right after a capture, or when a piece lands on a forkable square) e.g. You take back on d4, and now …d5 threatens a fork. The moment their rook went to e1, look at the knight jump to c2. -> groundedAnswer.ts:6890 detectNewThreat (one move ahead) + latentFork.ts:161 (two moves ahead). Built.
- Chooses the cleanest of several winning moves (NEW vs census) (several moves win) e.g. Taking on e2 wins and the knight check on f2 wins, but the knight check on g3 is fastest. Recapture with the rook, the tidier choice, and keep the conversion clinical. -> MISSING. MultiPV gives the evals, but no read says 'several win, this one is fastest or cleanest'.
- Explains why a familiar pattern doesn't apply here (NEW vs census) (a pattern is almost on the board) e.g. This isn't a smothered mate, because they can give up the exchange on f2. If a rook does land on f2, you just take it and it's mate. -> MISSING. matePatterns.ts:341 classifyMatePattern only names a mate that has been delivered.
- Aims for the most winning position, not the first queen trade (a tactic offers a queen trade) e.g. Taking on d8 to swap queens isn't best, and grabbing the rook on a8 lets their queen take yours. Find the move that keeps the most. -> PARTIAL. deliberation.ts:66 Shortfall 'trades-queens' flags a candidate that trades queens. The principle itself is MISSING.
- In a mating race, ignores side issues and checks only for their mate threats (attacking with castling on opposite sides) e.g. Do you have to take the knight on c4? No: ignore it and just make sure they aren't threatening mate. The threat of opening the h-file is stronger than opening it. -> PARTIAL. threatOut.ts:71 computeMustDefend (null-move mate threat) and speedRunReads.ts:144 threatStronger. The race rule is MISSING.
- Calculates a poisoned pawn concretely instead of fearing it (a pawn grab with the queen) e.g. People fear the queen getting trapped on b2, but after the rook comes to b1 the queen drops to e5, not c3 where the rook hits it again. And even without e5, taking on a3 is fine. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:267 playAnyway (the scary reply comes and the line still holds).
- Warns that a free pawn is a trap when you're behind, especially a grab that trades queens (a capture is available while behind in material) e.g. Don't take on e5 and swap queens. With their bishop covering e2, a rook landing on d1 is mate; and even without that, trading queens a piece down is far too high a price. -> whyItFailed.ts:170 ('answered by a tactic'), moveAllowed.ts:27, tradeJudgement.ts:40 ('behind'). Built in parts.
- Justifies a sacrifice with a checklist (a speculative sacrifice) e.g. This sacrifice isn't crazy: they're undeveloped, neither bishop is out, castling is far off, and the e-file is open for a rook check and d6. -> reviewSacrifice.ts:44 sacrificeCompensation + :113 enemyKingStuckInCenter. Built.
- Practical choice: a move that leaves the opponent one hard-to-find saving move (NEW vs census as a computer) (choosing between moves of similar objective value) e.g. Start with the knight to d4: only the queen to d1 holds for them, and it's hard to find because the natural reply is the bishop retreat. That's practical, not tricky. -> PARTIAL. criticalityScan.ts:103 scanCriticality could be run from the opponent's side; explorerTeachLine.ts:60 moverScore gives the practical score. Using this as a reason to choose a move is MISSING.
- Gambit mindset: don't defend an attacked piece on reflex; give it, or move it by choice and keep the threats (playing for the initiative) e.g. Let them take the knight; the compensation is real. The b6 pawn sacrifice drives their knight to a8, and it needs several moves to get back. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:267 playAnyway, speedRunReads.ts:144 threatStronger, reviewSacrifice.ts:44. Counting how many moves the exiled piece needs to come back is MISSING.
- A pin is harmless when the pinned piece is protected by a pawn (NEW vs census) (a pin on a minor piece appears) e.g. The bishop pin on f6 isn't dangerous. Quick test: the knight is protected by a pawn, so it can't be won. You can ask the bishop with …h6 later; no rush. -> PARTIAL. pinPressure.ts:85 findPinPressure stays silent when adding attackers can't win the pinned piece; pinGeometry.ts:135 isRealPin. The spoken 'harmless pin' test is MISSING.
- Asks the pinning bishop to decide, and lists what the trade would change (a bishop pins your knight) e.g. Escaping the pin isn't urgent, but h3 gives you the option. If they take on f3, the troublesome bishop is gone, your queen comes into play and castling gets closer; then g4 and g5 is a clear plan. -> PARTIAL. thinkAloud.ts:302 obviousStopFlaw warns when the pawn move creates a hook; ruleException.ts treats h3/h6 against a pinning bishop as routine. The consequences of the trade are MISSING.
- Plays a move that leaves the opponent two bad choices (a pin or an invasion threat) e.g. Bg5 is a nasty pin: either they push …g5 and weaken themselves, or they live with it while the pressure on f6 grows. The rook to e3 forces an unwelcome rook trade or lets your rook into e7. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:512 forceConcession (their best answer concedes something nameable). A read where every option concedes something is MISSING.
- Explains why an earlier choice mattered with a counterfactual (NEW vs census) (justifying an earlier quiet move) e.g. Had your pawn gone to c4 instead of c3, taking on f3 and then the knight to d4 would win: with the queens facing each other on the d-file, you couldn't take the knight. -> MISSING. tempoFen.ts:11 only builds 'what if they got a free move'.
- Pre-empts the student's hesitation about a correct but scary move (a correct move that feels risky) e.g. You might hesitate because it lets them swap queens and chase your king for a pawn, and you might expect to win c5 back easily. You won't. -> speedRunReads.ts:267 playAnyway. Built.
- Eliminates candidates one by one, each with its own refutation, then finds the indirect answer (a difficult decision, such as holding on to an extra pawn) e.g. Be3 runs into the knight to g4; h3 then Be3 runs into the knight to d5; a3 and b4 fail to the capture on b4. So go indirect: …a5 weakened b5, so put a knight there. -> deliberation.ts:144 buildDeliberation + refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63 droppedJob + whyItFailed.ts:170. Built.
- Compares candidates by whether they do both jobs (one move has to solve two problems) e.g. The queen to d3 escapes the pin but leaves d4 undefended; c3 defends it with a pawn and builds the chain. The queen to b3 is exposed and too far from the kingside. -> refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63 droppedJob + deliberation.ts:354 extraJobs + moveIntent.ts:124. Built.
- Slips in a useful, risk-free move before the main break (just before a committal break) e.g. b3 first opens the queen's diagonal and can't hurt before e5. h3 first, so g4 is ready if their bishop goes to h5; it also keeps h2 as a retreat for your bishop. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:307 usefulWaiting + moveIntent.ts:124 (PREPARES).
- Take it now, before the target can leave (NEW vs census) (a capture is available right now) e.g. Take the f3 knight while you can; if you wait, it may move away. Grab the bishop now, calmly. -> MISSING. speedRunReads.ts:144 threatStronger and thinkAloud.ts:145 notYet cover the opposite case (the target isn't going anywhere).
- Keeps or releases central tension at the right moment (pawn tension in the centre) e.g. You don't have to take back at once: with their knight on d5, their capture on c3 isn't a real threat. Now is a good moment to release the tension with the c-pawn. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:49 keepTension. 'Now is the moment to release it' is MISSING.
- Chooses which piece recaptures, and says why (any recapture with more than one option) e.g. Recapture with the knight, not the queen: a queen on d4 gets hit by …c5. Take with the d-pawn to free the bishop fastest while their king is stuck in the centre; the doubled pawns can't be reached anyway. Take with the bishop so the knight stays on its outpost. -> recaptureChoice.ts:103 + moveContrast.ts:64 + tradeQuality.ts:71 recaptureDamage. Built. 'Doubled pawns that can't be reached don't matter' is only partial, via positionalRead.ts:616.
- Weighs a capture that damages their structure against what it gives away (a capture that would damage their structure) e.g. Taking on f6 ruins their pawns, but you give up your good bishop, and their king can step to h8 and use the open g-file for a rook. It isn't as clear-cut as it looks. -> PARTIAL. tradeQuality.ts:124 readTrade. The damaged side gaining an open file is MISSING.
- Decides which side to castle, including castling opposite to unbalance a worse position (before castling) e.g. The big decision now is which side to castle. Long is tempting, but short castling suits a quiet game. A piece down, the simplest way to unbalance is to castle on the other side from them. -> speedRunReads.ts:108 castleSide + kingSafety.ts:202 castleRoute. Built. Castling opposite to unbalance when behind is MISSING.
- Checks a routine move before playing it (before castling or another automatic move) e.g. Careful: castling right now lets …c4 cut the knight off from the bishop that defends it. Plenty of players would push a3 automatically here, but you don't need another queenside weakness. -> PARTIAL. tacticalRead.ts:221 pickTempting (the appealing but losing move, with its refutation); safetyHabits.ts:25 blunderCheck and :42 autopilotGuard fire only after the costly move.
- Doesn't push pawns in front of his own king, or on the wing where he is being attacked (defending on the wing of a pawn storm) e.g. Kb1 is the right answer, not the automatic a3; c3 has already weakened that side. Their …g6 against your storm only hands you a hook. -> boardDelta.ts:65 (WEAKENS near your own king) + moveInsight.ts:826 hookCreated. Built.
- Explains the jobs of a pawn storm (launching a pawn storm) e.g. g4 and g5 first drive away the f6 knight, the key defender of their king. Then h5 and a push to g6 open lines, and the advanced pawns also win squares for your pieces. -> PARTIAL. kingAttack.ts:71 (a shelter pawn taken, a defender removed by capture, a file ripped open) and conceptEngine.ts:783 ('pawn-storm'). A pawn kicking the defender away, and pawns winning squares, are MISSING.
- The hook: their defensive push gives your storm something to bite on (NEW vs census, on the opponent's move) (they push a pawn in front of their own king) e.g. Trying to slow your pawns, they played …g6. Now h5 attacks it and the h-file opens much faster. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:826 hookCreated is read only on the mover's own push (moveInsight.ts:441, thinkAloud.ts:302). theirMoveCost.ts:23 has no hook kind, so on the opponent's move it is MISSING.
- Opening a file against the king: line up first, then open (NEW vs census) (about to open a file in a king attack) e.g. One open file is all you need, but you only get one chance at it. Bring the queen to h3 first, then take on g6. Take first and they recapture with the f-pawn and defend with a rook on f7. -> MISSING. kingAttack.ts:71 only notices a file after it has opened.
- Race awareness with opposite-side castling (NEW vs census) (castling on opposite sides) e.g. You're committed now: keep attacking and be faster. Their …b5 with no rook behind it actually helps you, and closing the centre would free their attack. -> MISSING. planRace.ts:180 detectPlanRace only races passed pawns and file collisions.
- Castling by hand: choose the route, plan for their reply, and keep the king's path clear (NEW vs census) (the king has lost its castling rights) e.g. Your king has been flushed out. Develop first, then walk it to safety: back to e8, or fianchetto and go f8 then g8. If b3 and Ba3 pin it there, step back to e8. Put the rook on e8, not f8, or it blocks your own king. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:858 (walk the king by hand, with a rook coming across) and kingSafety.ts:202 castleRoute. The route choice, the contingency and 'don't block the king's path' are MISSING.
- Against an uncastled king: speed matters more than structure (the enemy king is still uncastled after the opening) e.g. Their king is stuck in the centre, so recapture the way that opens your bishop fastest; you may win before they castle. Rf1 from them would cost castling for good. -> reviewSacrifice.ts:113 enemyKingStuckInCenter + kingSafety.ts:142 detectCentralKingDanger. Built in parts.
- Welcomes trades that strip the enemy king of defenders (an exchange near the enemy king) e.g. If their bishop takes on c3, it only trades off one of their king's defenders. Fine by you. -> kingAttack.ts:71 + tradeJudgement.ts:40 ('attacker-gone'). Built.
- Doesn't commit the queen to the attack too early; builds first (building up an attack) e.g. Not Qh5 yet; …g6 would just stop it. Centralise the knight first. -> PARTIAL. moveOrder.ts:65 fires only when the early order loses material.
- Plays a protective king move before a break that his own pawn move made risky (your own pawn move has loosened your king) e.g. f4 loosened the diagonal to your king. Push e5 now and after the trades their queen checks from d4 and also hits the h4 bishop. So Kh1 first. -> moveIntent.ts:124 PREVENTS + boardDelta.ts:65 WEAKENS. Built.
- Builds the final mating net with pawns, and finds the king's hiding square (turning a won position into mate) e.g. g6 plus h5 is better air than g6 alone, because it also boxes in their f3 bishop. h4 and h5 control g3, and then the queen lands there with mate. Against their checks, the king hides on h6. -> MISSING. moveFundamentals.ts:43 'luft' exists as a reason for a move, not as a choice between ways of making air.

## Source 18
Close second reading of voiced-teachings.json notes[2594..3037]: 444 notes from 26 videos, all read. I catalogued 65 distinct teaching acts and matched each one to code. 20 already have a computer that produces them, 36 are partly covered and 9 have no computer. Ten acts are tagged [missed] because neither the insight catalogue nor the teaching census records them in that form.

WHERE THE GAPS CLUSTER
1. MEMORY ACROSS MOVES. Re-testing an idea that was refuted earlier once the board changes (speedRunReads.ts:486 only looks forward inside one engine line). Keeping an opening's standing danger in view for several moves.
2. FORWARD URGENCY. 'This works only until they develop.' moveTiming.ts:73 only looks backward.
3. OFFENSIVE MIRRORS OF DEFENSIVE COMPUTERS. Their piece has lost its retreat, so kick it now (noRetreat covers only the student's own pieces). Their advanced pawn will be a hook if they castle on that side (pawnHook requires their king to be castled already, moveInsight.ts:789-791).
4. COMPARING CANDIDATES BY PURPOSE. Which candidate prevents more or poses more threats. Preferring the simple move when the line is messy.
5. NUGGETS WITH NO COMPUTER. Opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker in the middlegame. Pawns are the best attackers of pawns. A weak square is not a weak pawn. The second weakness. Decoy into a fork. Clear your own pawn out of your rook's way.

DEFECTS FOUND WHILE MATCHING (each read in code)
- moveInsight.ts:966: noRetreat skips every non-pawn chaser. Its header (moveInsight.ts:952-956) cites the knight-on-h4 case, and both cases in this slice are knight chases, so it can never fire on them.
- conceptEngine.ts:787: says 'an isolated or doubled pawn can't be defended by another pawn, so it's a permanent target'. This is false for a doubled pawn with a neighbour pawn (D10), and the reference coach teaches the opposite here (n2848, n2993). It fires through boardConcepts.ts:272.
- mechanismContrast (moveInsight.ts:459-469) only distinguishes a double attack from a single target. The catalogue's built mark for compare-your-checks (docs/…-insight-catalogue.md:396-397) is therefore overclaimed; the n2722 case cannot be produced.
- Opposite-coloured bishops are known only as a drawish ending (conceptEngine.ts:155), because the class requires the bishops alone (endgameMatchup.ts:52).
- moveOrder.ts:13: its guard excludes the 'recapture hits your other piece' intermezzo (n2639-2640).
- pieceOptions, the choose-a-square-by-elimination computer, is reached only from chat (coach/coachService.ts:1507).
- The fork detector requires victims worth at least a knight (tacticsDetector.ts:136), so a queen hitting two pawns (n2893) is never named.
- obviousStopFlaw is hard-wired to a bishop pinning a knight (thinkAloud.ts:307).
RHYTHM: Measured on all 444 notes. Two shapes of video: 15 full walks (a note on 75-100% of plies) and 11 distilled ones (12-57% coverage, fewer but longer notes).

WORDS PER NOTE
- By phase (mean / median): opening 27/24; middlegame 31/26 (longest 318); endgame 22/20.
- By ply: plies 1-6 average 21 words; 7-12: 27; 13-20: 32; 21-30: 34; 31-45: 25; after that: 23.
- Bare move-naming (6 words or fewer) is rare: 9% overall, 11% in plies 1-12, 8% later. Even a book move usually gets a clause.

LENGTH FOLLOWS DECISIONS, NOT TACTICS
- Notes within two plies of a capture or check average 28.6 words; quiet stretches average 27.5.
- The twelve longest notes (78-318 words) are all decision points. Examples:
  - weighing two knight jumps while building a mating net (n2970);
  - why a pawn should attack the pawn, with both of the opponent's options (n3029);
  - calculation with branches (n3034-3037);
  - whether castling is safe against an x-ray (n2928);
  - 'you won a piece, now what' (n2969);
  - forced win or stabilise (n3019).

OPENING RHYTHM
- Plies 1-3 name the opening and its idea, sometimes spread over three moves (n2629-2631).
- Book moves get a short clause each.
- The opponent's first offbeat move triggers: a grade word, why, and how to punish.
- Coarse measure using the app's named-line DB as the book boundary: plies inside a named line average 21 words; the 2-6 plies after it average 29.

THEIR MOVES GET EQUAL AIRTIME. 193 opponent-move notes average 28.5 words; 251 student-move notes average 27.6. On their move he grades it, says what it wants or cost them, and how to punish it.

ORDER INSIDE A BEAT
- On a normal move: name the move → grade it in a word (39 notes) → its reason, or what it wants or costs → the consequence, often an if-then (32 notes) → the plan → a closing rule or nugget (29 notes).
- At a decision: pose the question → the candidates, each with its concrete refutation → the choice and its second job → the line with their reply → the habit.

DELIVERY
- 34 notes (8%) end mid-sentence: one explanation is spread over 2-5 plies while the moves are played, so a line is narrated as it happens.
- 25 notes ask a rhetorical question and answer it at once.
- 19 make a remark about players at this level, in words, never numbers.

The Larsen's e3 is about piece pressure on the centre, not pawn control (n3025).
