## Source 19
Close second reading of voiced-teachings notes[3038..3481]: 444 notes from 29 games (259 opening, 158 middlegame, 27 endgame). Note numbers below are indexes into notes[].

Most families the 2026-09-27 census marked missing are now built, and this slice confirms them:
- speedRunReads (26 reads, src/services/speedRunReads.ts:49-647). They reach Learn and chat via thinkAloud.depthClauses (thinkAloud.ts:257) and positionFacts.ts:1009.
- moveInsight: castleByHand, pawnHook, noRetreat, pawnCanGuard, emptyThreat, autopilotRecapture.
- Also moveIntent, theirMoveCost, moveOrder, ruleException, falseAlarm, bluffDetector, recaptureChoice, refutedAlternative, forkTrick, conversionMethod, pushOrHold and endgameTechnique.

The earlier readers missed finer acts. Every MISSING item below is a NEW computer under B6 and needs David's yes.

1. OPENING acts, first by F02:
   - The crossroads map, spoken aloud. The database already has it in openingBranches.branchesAt (openingBranches.ts:56), but its only caller is the Learn picker (branchExplorer.ts:55).
   - The opening system's plus/minus ledger, and the ply where you must know the theory.
   - Move-order reasoning from what the opponent has NOT played yet.
   - 'It transposed, and here is what is different in this version' (openingAnnouncement.ts:82 says only the first half).
   - Analogy to another opening, or why its familiar idea does not transfer here.
   - A verdict on their opening choice (openingAnnouncement.ts:166) together with the standard way to punish it.
2. The branched reply map: 'if they play X you answer Y; if Z, then W'. The reference coach uses it constantly in live games. The coach had it, and it was deleted (opponentIntent.ts:93-95). The engine fan it needs is still computed.
3. Anti-prophylaxis ('you could stop it, but you want it'), and 'don't make their planned break easier'.
4. Calculation method:
   - Back up to the last branch point when a line fails.
   - Quiet in-between moves before a recapture. autopilotRecapture fires only when the better move is forcing (moveInsight.ts:654).
   - Look one move past the end of a line.
5. Golden nuggets with no computer at all:
   - Castling is legal while the rook is attacked.
   - Opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker in the middlegame.
   - Two minor pieces versus rook and pawn in the middlegame.
   - Pawn-structure value depends on the phase and on where the king is.
   - Two pawns can hold three; don't over-push.
   - Capture only after their bishop has moved, so it moves twice.
   - Kb1 after castling long.
   - Keep a piece home to block checks.
   - Choosing the square for an exposed king.
   - Trapping a piece by cutting its defender's line.
   - Empty pins, and pins used as a shield.
6. Built computers gated narrower than the reference coach's use:
   - anyMoveFine is off past 300cp (speedRunReads.ts:74).
   - provokes fires only when their reply is a pawn advance (speedRunReads.ts:134-136).
   - escapeSquareFirst excludes checks (moveInsight.ts:704).
   - pawnHook returns null for a central king (moveInsight.ts:791-792).
   - prepare-break covers centre squares only (moveFundamentals.ts:986-991).
   - latentDanger is only called for the student's own pieces (positionFacts.ts:488, moveInsight.ts:138).
   - recaptureChoice ignores passed pawns, queen trades, and files it opens for their attack.
   - Hanging pawns are recognised only as c4/d4 or c5/d5 (positionReadingService.ts:1122-1132), so the c6/d5 pair is never named.
   - materialPlan's 'keep pieces on when down' (moveInsight.ts:1012) is the opposite of his 'trade to relieve pressure' when merely worse.

V1 transformation: the reference coach speaks in the first person ('I like', 'I missed', 'my favourite system'). Every such act must become a board fact, for example 'there was a stronger move here' or 'the usual setup is'.
RHYTHM: Measured on these 444 notes.
- OPENING: median 18 words per note, mean 24, p90 47. 61 of 259 opening notes (24%) are under ten words, just naming a standard book reply. Then 50-190 words land at a crossroads, a sideline, a trap, or the first ply where the theory must be known. Naming the line is the single most frequent opening act (73 of 259 opening notes).
- MIDDLEGAME: median 32 words, mean 55, p90 74; 20 notes run over 60 words. At real decisions there are spikes of several hundred words where the decision is calculated aloud (one note runs about 2,000 words and covers a whole defensive phase through to the endgame).
- ENDGAME: median 19 words, max 43 in this slice. One running plan, said a move at a time (double the rooks on the e-file, the knight via c4 toward a5, probe with the rook), with almost no lecturing.
- THOUGHTS SPAN PLIES: a single explanation is often split over 2-5 consecutive moves while the opponent replies (notes 3121-3122, 3127-3130, 3134-3138, 3236-3245). The teaching is a running thread, not a caption per move.
- ORDER INSIDE A DECISION: what their move changed or threatens; the candidates and why each fails; 'not yet, first this'; the line in words with their reply; what it achieves; then the general habit or principle, sometimes with a self-correction.
- QUESTIONS: 8% of notes ask the student something, and almost all are answered at once.
- VERSUS THE RULEBOOK: in standard book stretches the reference coach is terser than V19's 'every opening move explained to the hilt'. The rulebook is the law, so the coach should go beyond the reference there, not copy its terseness.
- Names the opening or variation on the ply it is reached, and gives its character in the same breath: sharp and theory-heavy, solid but passive, an underrated surprise weapon, or dangerous if you don't know it (The first ply a named line is reached (either seat), and when a sideline is chosen) e.g. This is the Four Pawns setup: a huge centre, and you can be overrun quickly if you don't know the lines. / This is the solid, symmetrical setup: no weaknesses, few winning chances. / Its reputation says unsound, but it is far more dangerous than that. -> src/services/openingAnnouncement.ts:54 openingAnnouncement names it once. openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine adds what the opening provokes, its gambit, its typical structure and famous games, but has only two characters: sharp and theory-heavy, or quiet (openingIdentity.ts:138-141). MISSING: the solid/passive/no-weakness profile and reputation versus reality (surprise value).
- States the opening system's bargain (what you get, what you pay) and flags the exact ply where the natural move is wrong, so the theory must be known (Right after the system's defining move, then at its first critical book branch) e.g. You get a big centre; the bill is slow development, and one careless move starts the centre pawns falling. This is the first moment you must know the move: the natural knight development is not the main line here. -> MISSING as one fact. Pieces exist: criticalityScan severity 'only-move' (criticalityScan.ts:50, ONLY_MOVE_CP at :85) can mark the ply, and refutedAlternativeCore.renderRefutedAlternative (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98) can refute the natural move. Nothing computes the plus/minus ledger, or joins 'in book' with 'only move' into 'you must know this'.
- Maps the crossroads aloud: the 2-3 named roads from this position, which is calm and which ambitious, and which one this game takes (Opening branch points, both seats, often on the opponent's move before the student has to choose) e.g. First crossroads: support the chain with the knight, or grab more space with the c-pawn, the most ambitious road. Taking on d6 is the calm main line; this game goes the sharp way. -> Data exists, voice MISSING. openingBranches.branchesAt (openingBranches.ts:56) returns the database's roads and their names, but its only caller is the Learn picker (branchExplorer.ts:55). theoryDeparture.findTheoryDeparture (theoryDeparture.ts:73) has the masters' and amateurs' main moves for Review. No surface speaks the crossroads.
- Gives each opening move's job against the opponent's setup: it leans on a defender, walls off their bishop with pawns, prepares the central break, or steps away from a pawn kick while keeping its diagonal (Nearly every non-trivial opening move) e.g. The bishop pins nothing yet; it pressures the knight that guards e5. / c6 builds a pawn wall, so their long-diagonal bishop points at a dead end. / c3 quietly prepares d4. / The bishop steps back to b3 and still looks at f7. -> Mostly covered. moveFundamentals ids attack-defender, keep-working, prepare-break and open-diagonal (moveFundamentals.ts:30-71), and moveIntent.moveIntent prevents/prepares for either seat (moveIntent.ts:124). Gaps: prepare-break fires only on core-centre squares (moveFundamentals.ts:986-991), so wing breaks such as a6 before b5 are missed. 'A pawn chain built to blunt their fianchettoed bishop' has no named purpose (MISSING).
- Move-order reasoning from what the opponent has NOT played yet, or has already committed to: which development is needed now and which can wait (Opening, plies 3-16, usually right after the opponent's move) e.g. They haven't put a knight on f3, so nothing hits e5 yet; develop the f6 knight first. / With both knights already out, this order takes away the line you would normally choose. / The c6 knight now would let them push d5 with tempo, so keep it back and start with the queen. -> MISSING. moveOrder.moveOrder (moveOrder.ts:65) only proves 'Y first runs into R' between the student's own engine moves. moveTiming.readTiming (moveTiming.ts:47) is about material only. Nothing reasons from the opponent's absent or committed moves.
- Says the game has transposed AND what is different in this version, and what that changes in the plan (When the game reaches another opening's structure by a different move order) e.g. This is now a Scotch-type position, but with the c-pawns gone your d6 square is sensitive. The usual bishop to c5 runs into a knight jump to f5, so develop the knight to f6, which also hits e4. -> Half built. openingAnnouncement already says 'by a different move order, the game has transposed into X' (openingAnnouncement.ts:82). What is different here, and what it changes, is MISSING.
- Imports a plan from a known structure by analogy, or explains why a familiar idea does NOT transfer here (Unusual setups that resemble a well-known structure) e.g. The hole on d5 is like the one in Najdorf structures with ...e5: your minor pieces can cover it, so it isn't fatal. / It looks like a Dragon but calmer: both kings go short and nobody is mated soon. / That gambit idea fails in this version because their centre pawns are still intact. -> Partial. structureSignature.computeStructureSignature and signatureMatchScore (structureSignature.ts:65, :165) compute structure families (maroczy-bind, iqp, carlsbad, kid-lock, advance-chain) for note transfer. motifLedger links ideas within one game only ('same idea as move N', motifLedger.ts:42). A spoken cross-opening analogy, and the 'does not transfer because' check, are MISSING.
- Warns that the natural, automatic move in this book position is a mistake, and gives the concrete refutation (often the centre fork trick or a pin) (Book positions where the most-played move loses something; said before the student chooses) e.g. The automatic knight to f3 is an inaccuracy here: their bishop comes to g4 and piles on the knight and the e5 pawn, and only the bishop to e3 holds. / The bishop to c4 looks natural but runs into knight takes e4 and d5, a fork. -> Covered. refutedAlternative.refutedAlternative (refutedAlternative.ts:81) with renderRefutedAlternative (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98) says 'most players play X here, and it walks into...'. forkTrick.forkTrickFor (forkTrick.ts:81) handles the centre fork trick. safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42) says it after the fact.
- Names a trap position and gives the correct move, then deliberately plays the wrong one to show the refutation, and calibrates how bad it really is (Known trap positions in the opening; also as a lesson device (play the bad line on purpose, then recover)) e.g. There is a nasty trap here, and the right move is the knight. Take on c3 instead, and the bishop sacrifice on f7 drags your king out while their queen collects the c5 bishop with tempo. Much worse for you, though not lost, whatever older books claim. -> Partial, spread over the systems F04 says to merge: openingTrapDetector.detectTrapInPosition (openingTrapDetector.ts:79), positionTrapScan.scanPositionForTrap (positionTrapScan.ts:126), trapLearning.trapSpeaks (trapLearning.ts:105), with severity words from engineConstants costWords. The 'worse but not lost' calibration and the deliberate walk through the wrong line are MISSING as one act.
- Teaches the opening's recurring tactical motif so the student recognises it again: a knight that keeps harassing the queen and can trap it, or the long knight tour toward f5 (The first time the motif appears in the line) e.g. Remember this idea in this setup: the knight jumps to a4 and hits their queen; it can repeat, and at the right moment the queen runs out of squares. -> Partial. tacticsDetector trapped_piece (tacticsDetector.ts:520) fires when the trap lands, and S7 library notes cover 'teach me X opening'. A per-opening motif spoken live is MISSING.
- Judges the opponent's opening choice (time-wasting, fashionable but planless, dubious) and names the standard way to punish it (The opponent leaves the main line early) e.g. That fianchetto doesn't fit and costs time: develop the knights, then e6 and d5. / This a4 is in fashion, but people who play it often reach the middlegame with no plan. -> Half built. openingAnnouncement.theirOpeningVerdict (openingAnnouncement.ts:166) calls a choice dubious or weaker, with the engine's cost. thinkAloud.opponentHabits (thinkAloud.ts:180) and tempoCount (tempoCount.ts:32) count wasted tempi. The standard punishing plan is MISSING.
- Says where theory ends and switches to the principle that guides the next moves (The ply the game leaves book) e.g. Known theory stops here. From now on the job is to make their centre pawn move, so the knight on e5 loses its support. -> Covered. bookDeparture.bookDeparture (bookDeparture.ts:49). openingAnnouncement says the settled opening name at the departure ply (openingAnnouncement.ts:54).
- Gives the opponent's move its purpose AND its price in one breath, then routes a piece to exploit the price (Opponent pawn moves, especially in the opening and early middlegame) e.g. Their h5 stops your h5, but it gives up g5 for good; your knight goes h3 and settles on g5. -> Covered in parts. theirMoveCost.theirMoveCost (theirMoveCost.ts:60) has a 'hole' kind with a one- or two-jump knight route (:86). moveIntent covers the 'it stops X' half for either seat (moveIntent.ts:124). Joining both halves into one 'X, but Y, so Z' chain is the F0c composer, which is not built.
- Names the harm a pawn move does to its OWN army: it takes its knight's natural square, or opens one bishop and buries the other (Early pawn moves by either side) e.g. c6 is wrong twice: it takes the knight's best square and leaves the e5 pawn without a guard. / d6 frees one bishop but leaves the other only e7. -> Partial. theirMoveCost 'bishop-shut' (theirMoveCost.ts:109) covers the opponent's moves, and principleAttribution's buried-own-bishop rule (principleAttribution.ts:969) covers the mover. 'Takes away your own knight's natural square' is MISSING.
- Labels a structural concession as permanent, with the reason (pawns cannot move back): a backward pawn plus a hole becomes a lasting target (The move that creates the concession, either seat) e.g. That c5 leaves d6 backward and d5 a hole for good. No pawn of theirs can ever come back to cover d5, so a knight there can never be chased. -> Covered. theirMoveCost 'structure' (theirMoveCost.ts:147), outpost.noPawnCanChallenge (outpost.ts:22), speedRunReads.forceConcession (speedRunReads.ts:512), and moveInsight.holeAccess for the mover's own pawn move (moveInsight.ts:1101).
- A threat is not a reason by itself: check the reply first, and prefer a quiet structural move over a tempo move that leaves a permanent weakness (one-move-itis) (When a tempo-gaining move is available, especially while defending) e.g. c5 hits the bishop with tempo, but d6 stays weak for the rest of the game. c6 is quieter and keeps d5 in reserve. / The bishop eyes f7, but b5 is coming to kick it. -> Partial. moveInsight.emptyThreat (moveInsight.ts:909) catches 'the attacked piece simply moves away'. The trade-off of tempo now against a permanent weakness is MISSING.
- Sizes a threat down and names the ready answer, or says it is only a pawn; and says a piece on an attacked square is fine when it cannot actually be won (The opponent's aggressive-looking moves, and positions where the student is ahead) e.g. The knight jump to b4 looks scary, but the rook to c1 answers it. / It only threatens a pawn, so keep your eyes on the whole board. / Your bishop on e8 is attacked, but it can't actually be won. -> Mostly covered. bluffDetector.detectBluff and bluffClause (bluffDetector.ts:37, :115) say 'it wins nothing, no need to react', but do not name the ready answer. falseAlarm.falseAlarm (falseAlarm.ts:37) covers real threats that can be ignored. Also speedRunReads.playAnyway (speedRunReads.ts:267), heldByTactic (:162) and takeTheSting (:400).
- Predicts the opponent's next move and says why their other options do not exist (Before the student's move, when the opponent's reply is narrow) e.g. Ask what they'll play next: the knight goes to h6, because your pawn on d6 takes g7 away from it. -> Half built. opponentIntent.buildOpponentIntent (opponentIntent.ts:55) finds the engine's top try, rendered as 'keep an eye on their X' with no reason (opponentIntent.ts:97-100). Why the alternatives are ruled out is MISSING.
- Branched reply map: if they play X you answer Y; if they play Z you answer W (When the opponent has two or more sensible replies, mostly in the opening and early middlegame) e.g. Where their queen goes matters: if it drops back to e3, d5 hits it; if it stays on h5, your knight comes to c6 and later b5. / A d3 kick doesn't hurt: the knight steps back, and your development was still a free move. -> MISSING because it was removed. opponentIntent's branched form was deleted (opponentIntent.ts:93-95: 'deleted 2026-09-30 (G8.5) ... no demo surface ever called it'). The engine data it needs (ply 2 of each line) is still computed there.
- Reads the opponent's plan from where their piece went, and judges whether that plan is safe for them given where their king is (The opponent makes a committal piece move) e.g. Their knight retreat to h6 gives away the plan, f5 next, and that is a very risky plan while their king is still uncastled. -> Half built. moveIntent reads what either side's move prepares (moveIntent.ts:124; whatItDoes at :423). reviewOpponentCommentary.buildOpponentMoveTeaching (reviewOpponentCommentary.ts:48) works in Review only. The risk verdict based on where their king stands is MISSING.
- Prevents the opponent's next GOAL because the whole plan depends on it, for example stopping them castling so the pressure down the e-file keeps paying (The opponent's king is still central with a half-open file on it) e.g. If they castle, your pressure down the e-file was for nothing. So the queen goes to e8: now castling drops their bishop. -> Partial. moveIntent's prevents half (moveIntent.ts:124) can say 'so ...O-O isn't possible'. speedRunReads.forceConcession (speedRunReads.ts:512) fires when castling rights are actually lost. reviewSacrifice.enemyKingStuckInCenter (reviewSacrifice.ts:113) detects the state. 'Keep their king in the centre' as a standing plan is MISSING.
- Anti-prophylaxis: you could stop their move, but you want it, and here is why (An obvious prevention move exists) e.g. Why not e5 to stop d4? It would cost you d5, and their d4 only helps you anyway. / a4 would stop b5, but you can allow it. -> MISSING.
- Rejects a natural developing square because it would make the opponent's planned break easier (The opponent has a known break and the student is choosing a square) e.g. They are preparing c5. A bishop on d3 would block your own control of the file and make c5 easier, so the knight goes to e2 and on to f4 instead. -> MISSING. moveIntent supplies their plan, but nothing tests whether a student's candidate square makes it easier.
- Keeps a running inventory of everything loose on BOTH sides before choosing (Sharp middlegames with several pieces en prise) e.g. Keep a list in your head of what is hanging: their queen, your rook, the g7 pawn. -> Partial. loosePieces.findLoosePieces (loosePieces.ts:35). methodBeat's 'loose-trigger' names one loose enemy piece at deciding moments (methodBeat.ts:296). moveInsight.looseOwnPieces (moveInsight.ts:940) covers the student's own. A two-sided running inventory is MISSING.
- Target scan: which of your pieces can hit their exposed piece? Counterattack instead of retreating (A student piece is attacked while the opponent also has a loose high-value piece) e.g. Your queen is attacked, but theirs is loose too. Which piece can hit it? The knight to c3, and suddenly three of their pieces and pawns hang. -> Partial. speedRunReads.takeTheSting (speedRunReads.ts:400) fires when the engine's move neither moves nor guards the attacked piece. thinkingTargetsStep and thinkingHitTwoStep teach targets in lessons only. The counterattack scan as a live habit is MISSING.
- Lists the candidate moves and rules out each with its concrete cost before naming the move (Every real decision) e.g. Two approaches. Moving the queen loses the rook, and your king can no longer castle short. Or counterattack. And d3? It loses to a queen capture on e3 with mate. -> Covered. deliberation.buildDeliberation and meaningfulAlternatives (deliberation.ts:144, :306), and methodBeat 'candidates' (methodBeat.ts:296).
- Picks the one line that needs calculating and checks it concretely; when two moves both win, picks the one that keeps more (Converting, or in forcing positions) e.g. Only one line needs working out: their bishop takes f3. Take the rook first and recapture afterwards; that order also keeps your e5 pawn. -> Partial. methodBeat 'forcing-scan' fires at deciding moments only (methodBeat.ts:296). moveOrder (moveOrder.ts:65) handles 'X first'. 'Which winning order keeps more' is MISSING.
- Calculation method: when a line fails, go back to the last move where you had a choice, not to the start; insert the move that secures your piece, then collect (Right after showing a failed line) e.g. Grabbing the rook fails because the knight gets trapped. Don't abandon the idea: go back one move, play the bishop to b3 first so the knight stays guarded, then take the rook. -> Half built. speedRunReads.secureFirst (speedRunReads.ts:178) says to secure the piece first because the capture will still be there. The backtrack method is MISSING.
- 'Not yet, first this': take away a defender, add an attacker or kick a piece first, and then the move works (Whenever the natural move is premature) e.g. Don't put the bishop on d4 yet, because their knight takes it. Trade that knight off with your other bishop first, then the bishop lands on d4. -> Covered for captures and checks: thinkAloud.notYet (thinkAloud.ts:145), speedRunReads.rejectedMoveLater and preparationOf (speedRunReads.ts:486, :463), and moveOrder.moveOrder (moveOrder.ts:65). Quiet moves to a square, like a bishop to an outpost, are not covered: rejectedMoveLater keeps only tempting captures and checks (speedRunReads.ts:499).
- Looks one move past the end of a line for the resource that changes the verdict (Evaluating trades and simplifications) e.g. They can grab a7, but look one move further: you have a check on e1, and with opposite-coloured bishops that is enough to hold. -> Partial. speedRunReads.playAnyway (speedRunReads.ts:267) looks one move past a scary reply. A general end-of-line resource check is MISSING.
- Don't play automatically: before the obvious recapture or reflex retreat, look for the in-between move (even a quiet one), or simply save your attacked piece instead of recapturing (Any recapture or reflex retreat) e.g. The recapture is obvious, but a quiet bishop move wins their queen. / Don't take back with the pawn; drop the bishop back and you are a piece up. / Most players would pull the rook back here; don't rush it. -> Partial. moveInsight.autopilotRecapture (moveInsight.ts:642) fires only when the better move is a check, a mate, or a capture elsewhere (:654). Quiet in-between moves, and saving the piece instead of recapturing, are MISSING.
- Says when a decision doesn't matter so the student saves time, including won positions where any sensible capture wins (Equal-value choices, and trivial decisions in won positions) e.g. Either recapture is fine; decide quickly and save your thinking for a real decision. / Take on g4 or d5, it hardly matters; just take something. -> Partial. speedRunReads.anyMoveFine (speedRunReads.ts:68) is switched off when the evaluation is beyond 300cp (speedRunReads.ts:74) and before move 8, so the 'anything wins here' version never fires in won positions.
- Reconstructs how the idea was found (goal, what is in the way, remove it) so the student can repeat the search (After a non-obvious move) e.g. To win that bishop you have to take away the pawn that guards it. That is why d3 comes first, and then you take on e4. -> Partial. thinkAloud.depthClauses (thinkAloud.ts:226) and speedRunReads.preparationOf ('take away a defender first', speedRunReads.ts:463). The goal/obstacle/remove-it chain is the F0c composer, which is not built.
- Asks the student the question, pauses, then answers it (Before a tactic or a key decision) e.g. What is the tactic here? The knight takes f7. / The check forces their knight out; what do you do with it? d4, and it is lost. -> Partial. Lessons ask questions (thinking steps, hintRegister). Asking in live play is gated by F05 (only for long-standing weaknesses). The 'question then immediate answer' form has no narration lane.
- Reads a geometric alignment as a cue to hunt for a tactic: queens facing each other on a file, a rook-and-queen x-ray behind a shield, an undefended piece inviting a discovered attack. Then finds the move that removes the shield and opens the line at once (Middlegame and late opening, whenever an alignment exists) e.g. The queens share the d-file with pieces in between; if it opens they face each other, and their queen is guarded only by the king, so lure the king away. / Rook and queen stand on one line: if the front piece stepped aside and that pawn were gone, the queen would fall, and the knight capture does both. -> Mostly MISSING on the attacking side. latentDanger.detectLatentDanger (latentDanger.ts:87) takes the seat as a parameter but is only ever called for the student's own pieces (positionFacts.ts:488, moveInsight.ts:138). moveFundamentals 'queen-off-file' is the defensive half. moveIntent's 'two jobs' covers the move that does both things.
- Names the mechanism of a tactic so it can be recognised: an overloaded defender, the queen as the only glue, a battery that freezes a piece, a back-rank discovery, an x-ray (Each time the mechanism appears) e.g. Their king is overloaded, guarding two things at once, so take on f7. / Their queen alone holds both the knight and the pawn. -> Covered. tacticsDetector (battery at tacticsDetector.ts:774, trapped_piece at :520), speedRunReads.queenGlue (speedRunReads.ts:567), moveInsight.heavyTiedDown (moveInsight.ts:1022), and conceptEngine's definitions (conceptEngine.ts:130-141).
- Traps a piece by cutting its defender's line (interference), then teaches that a trapped piece is not going anywhere, so improve first (A piece's only defence runs along a line) e.g. Their queen guards the knight; the rook to f4 cuts the line between them, and the knight has no escape. There is no need to take it yet. -> Half built. tacticsDetector's trapped_piece (tacticsDetector.ts:520) sees the result, and speedRunReads.threatStronger (speedRunReads.ts:144) says the capture isn't going anywhere. Interference as a named mechanism is MISSING.
- A piece with no retreat square is a target for one pawn push, so choose the square that has a way back (Developing bishops and knights in the opening) e.g. Fianchetto the bishop rather than put it on g4: on g4 it has no retreat, and h3 then g4 traps it. / Their bishop has only one square left, so e6 and d5 win it. -> Covered. moveInsight.noRetreat (moveInsight.ts:957).
- Teaches pins with their conditions: an empty pin they break at once; a pin that doesn't bite because the pinned piece is defended and can't be attacked (so remove the defender); and never rely on a pin to keep your queen safe (Whenever a pin is formed or considered) e.g. The bishop on b5 won't pin for long, since they simply put a bishop on d7; the bishop to c4 keeps lasting pressure on f7 instead. / Their rook pins your bishop, but a pawn defends it, so remove the pawn: d3, then take on e4. / Don't let your queen's safety depend on a pin; if the pinning piece is lured away, the queen hangs. -> Partial. pinGeometry.isRealPin and pinPressure.findPinPressure (pinPressure.ts:85) cover piling on a real pin. The empty pin, 'defended pinned piece, so remove the defender', and 'a pin as a shield is fragile' are MISSING. questions.md item 7 already lists the 'pin broken with tempo' family as missing.
- A check whose real point is the square it forces the blocking piece onto, where a pawn then wins it (Checks against an uncastled king in the opening) e.g. The queen check forces their knight to block on c3; it is pinned there, and d4 wins it. -> Covered. speedRunReads.awkwardBlock (speedRunReads.ts:244) together with pinPressure (pinPressure.ts:85).
- Names the parts of the mating net (which flight squares are gone, what seals the last one) and prefers the mate to grabbing material (Attacks on the king when mate is near) e.g. Your knight takes one square from their king, and with the doubled rooks and the queen that completes the net: the rook mates. / Don't take the queen yet; a bishop check first puts a piece on f7 and seals the escape square, then the rook mates. -> Partial. matePatterns.classifyMatePattern and explainMate (matePatterns.ts:341, :379) name a mate only after it is delivered. moveInsight.escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701) excludes checks that seal a flight square (:704). Pre-mate ingredients and 'mate before material' are MISSING.
- Explains why a structure that looks weak is in fact robust: a latent pawn fork punishes the natural attacking move, and the pieces guard each other (Defensive pawn structures with a pawn on d6 and pieces behind it) e.g. d6 looks like a target, but if their bishop ever comes to f4, e5 forks and wins a piece; and every one of your pieces protects another. -> Partial. latentFork.detectLatentFork (latentFork.ts:161) covers piece forks two moves away, and forkTrick (forkTrick.ts:81) the centre fork trick. The 'looks weak but holds' framing is MISSING.
- Teaches what makes an outpost, with the reason: a square no pawn can ever challenge (pawns can't move back), versus an unstable square a pawn can kick (Choosing where to put a knight) e.g. Put the knight on d4: no pawn of theirs can ever attack that square again, so the knight can stay there for good. / A knight on e5 is unstable here; f4 just kicks it away. -> Covered. outpost.isOutpost and noPawnCanChallenge (outpost.ts:39, :22), and speedRunReads.overprotect and rightPieceForHole (speedRunReads.ts:209, :337).
- Isolated-queen's-pawn technique: covering the square in front matters more than standing on it; whether the isolated pawn is good or bad depends on piece activity; and after an exchange the weakness can shift to the neighbouring c-pawn (Isolated-pawn structures (Alapin, Queen's Gambit types)) e.g. Against the isolated pawn, what counts is covering the square in front of it; whether a piece actually stands there is secondary, so the knight heads for b3 and d4. / After the exchange on c6 the weak pawn is now c6, because d5 can never come back to defend it. -> Partial. positionReadingService.namedPawnStructure (positionReadingService.ts:1060) gives the isolated-pawn plan 'blockade it, ideally with a knight, and trade pieces' (:1114-1119). Hanging pawns are recognised only as c4/d4 or c5/d5 (:1122-1132), so the c6/d5 pair is never named. Good versus bad by piece activity, and the shift of the weakness, are MISSING.
- Names the pawn-majority imbalance a recapture creates, and says that in a pawn ending, king placement and who makes a passed pawn first decide it (Pawn exchanges that create majorities; endgames) e.g. Taking back with the c-pawn gives them a queenside majority and you a kingside one. / Both sides have three pawns against two on a wing, so it comes down to whose king is closer and who makes a passed pawn first. -> Partial. boardStructure.queensideMajority (boardStructure.ts:304-307) is used only by Review's reviewStrategicOrientation (reviewStrategicOrientation.ts:490). recaptureChoice does not consider majorities.
- Golden nugget: a pawn structure's value depends on the phase and on the king. Doubled pawns that would be terrible in front of a middlegame king are fine in an ending, because the king guards both from one square. Structural damage matters around the king, not in general. Doubled pawns that open a file are often good (Captures that change the structure; the move into an endgame) e.g. With queens on, doubled f- and h-pawns in front of your king would be awful; in this ending they are fine, because your king guards both from one square. / The capture on h6 is strong because their king lives there, not because it doubles pawns. / If they take on e6, your doubled pawns cover key squares and the f-file opens for your rook. -> MISSING as a judgement. recaptureChoice.readRecapture counts doubling as a minus and an opened file as a plus (recaptureChoice.ts:63-71), and tradeQuality.recaptureDamage has 'king-cover' (tradeQuality.ts:71). Nothing makes the verdict depend on the phase or on where the king is.
- Opposite-coloured bishops: drawish in the endgame, but in the middlegame they favour the attacker. When converting with them, attack the king instead of counting pawns (Any position with opposite-coloured bishops) e.g. Opposite bishops would be drawish in an ending, but with queens on they help the attacker: nothing of yours can cover their bishop's squares. / A pawn up with opposite bishops, don't grind pawns; push the kingside pawns and go for the king. -> Half built. conceptEngine 'opposite-bishops' (conceptEngine.ts:155) and pushOrHold (pushOrHold.ts:28) teach the drawish ending. The middlegame 'favours the attacker' half, and 'convert by attacking', are MISSING.
- Judges material imbalances by phase: two minor pieces for rook and pawn usually favour the minors in the middlegame; queen against two rooks depends on concrete play (Trades or sacrifices that create an imbalance) e.g. If they grab on f2, you get two pieces for rook and pawn. In a middlegame the rooks have no open files yet, so two active minor pieces usually do more. -> MISSING. moveInsight.materialPlan covers 'up the exchange, open files for the rooks' (moveInsight.ts:1006-1007); endgameMatchup classifies endgame matchups only.
- Pawn restraint and pacing in endings: two pawns can hold three, slow their majority down, don't push too fast, and one push can kill your own future passed pawn (Endgames with pawn majorities) e.g. g5 slows their majority: your two pawns can hold up their three. / b4 would mean you can never make a passed pawn on the queenside. / Push too early and the pawns become targets. -> MISSING. endgamePawnReads has passerKinds, outsidePasserDecoy, pawnEndingTrade, spareTempoWasted, kingCourse and findBreakthrough (endgamePawnReads.ts:52-189), but no restraint read.
- Pawn-race arithmetic: count the steps to promotion, and check whether the king can reach the corner or the square of the pawn (Pawn endings and races) e.g. Both pawns queen, but their king cannot reach b8 in time, so your new queen holds on and you win. -> Covered. endgameTechnique.detectRuleOfSquare (endgameTechnique.ts:180), conceptEngine rule-of-the-square (conceptEngine.ts:327-330), and planRace.
- Teaches the king-safety rule with its reason (the farther from the centre, the safer, which is why you castle), and castling by hand: the route, why the immediate first step fails, the preparing move, and keeping a piece home to block checks (The king is stuck in the centre after losing castling rights) e.g. The king walks to g8 simply to get far from the centre; that is the whole point of castling. Kf7 right away runs into Ng5, so h6 first. And the light-squared bishop stays home for now, ready to block a queen check. -> Partial. moveInsight.castleByHand (moveInsight.ts:840) gives the route. kingSafety.detectCentralKingDanger (kingSafety.ts:142) reads the danger. moveIntent can prove that h6 prepares Kf7 (moveIntent.ts:124). 'Keep a piece home to block checks', and the distance-from-centre rule given as the reason, are MISSING.
- Chooses the exposed king's square by looking several moves ahead (a pawn that will become a hook, a file about to open), and puts king safety above clinging to an extra pawn (The king has been forced out of its shelter (for example after a sacrifice on f7)) e.g. Not e8: after d6 that pawn becomes a hook for e5, and the e-file opens on your king, so f8 is safer. And don't grab b2: their bishop comes to b2 and your kingside gets crushed. -> MISSING. moveInsight.pawnHook handles hooks on a castled wing only and returns null for a central king (moveInsight.ts:791-792). endgamePawnReads.kingCourse covers king-and-pawn endings only.
- Which side to castle: away from the wing whose pawns the opponent has already stripped (Before castling) e.g. Their pawns have already been thrown at your kingside; castling there hands them an attack, so castle long. -> Covered. speedRunReads.castleSide (speedRunReads.ts:108).
- Under uncertainty, plays the move that helps whatever the opponent does (whichever side they castle), keeps a square free as a fallback, and commits last to the piece whose best square depends on their setup (The opponent's king is uncastled; flexible middlegame setups) e.g. Their king hasn't castled: a6 is useful either way, starting a pawn storm if they go long and still covering b5 if they go short. / Castle long first and see how they develop; then you know where the bishop belongs. / Keep d7 empty, so the knight can drop back there if they castle long. -> Partial. speedRunReads.flexibleFirst ('piece before pawn', speedRunReads.ts:549), keepSquareForKnight (:316) and usefulWaiting (:307). 'Useful whichever side they castle' and 'commit last to gain information' are MISSING.
- Names standard follow-ups and manoeuvres as typical: Kb1 after castling long, the knight via e2 to f4, the knight via d2 and f1 toward f5, the knight to the square in front of an isolated pawn (After castling long; when a piece is idle) e.g. After castling long, the king to b1 is the standard follow-up: it takes the king off the c-file. / The knight goes e2 and then f4, a standard route for it in these structures. -> Mostly covered. forwardTeaching.computePieceRoute and computeSliderRoute (forwardTeaching.ts:186, :236), and nextPlans.findWorstPlacedPiece (nextPlans.ts:81). The Kb1 habit after castling long is MISSING.
- Chooses captures and recaptures by consequence: toward the centre, which file it opens for you, avoiding a tempo hit, avoiding a queen trade, creating a passed pawn; and between two winning captures, the one that opens no file for THEIR attack (Every capture or recapture choice) e.g. Take back with the knight; the queen there would be hit with tempo. / Take the centre pawn, not on g4, which would open the h-file toward your own king for them. / Take with the rook that leaves you a passed pawn. -> Partial. recaptureChoice.readRecapture and recaptureChoice (recaptureChoice.ts:56, :103) cover the file opened, toward the centre, doubled pawns, an isolated pawn, freeing a bishop, a tempo hit and castling. Creating a passed pawn, avoiding a queen trade, and 'opens a file for their attack' are MISSING.
- Counts attackers against defenders on the key square to show why a pawn holds or falls (Central breaks and contested squares) e.g. After d5 and the exchanges, the pawn is guarded as often as it is attacked, so they can't take it. / You cover d5 three times to their two, so their d5 break never comes. -> Covered. countMethod.countMethod (countMethod.ts:17), moveIntent.stopReason (moveIntent.ts:383), and exchangeLedger.
- States the rule and its exception here, with the board's reason (The engine's move breaks a textbook rule) e.g. Normally you don't spend two moves on one piece in the opening; with this much development in hand, it is worth it for the attack. / Recapture toward the centre, unless your centre is strong enough to ignore the poke. / Don't play both e6 and g6 in one setup; too many squares go weak. -> Partial. ruleException.ruleException (ruleException.ts:70) knows three rules: the same piece twice, a shield pawn, the early queen. Others, such as 'toward the centre, unless...' and 'not both e6 and g6', are MISSING.
- Names the principle the opponent is breaking so the student can punish it (Early unprincipled moves by the opponent) e.g. They developed bishops before knights, so force their knight out with a check and then win it with a pawn. -> Partial. thinkAloud.opponentHabits (thinkAloud.ts:180) and tempoCount (tempoCount.ts:32) count tempi and undeveloped minor pieces. principleAttribution's knights-before-bishops rule (principleAttribution.ts:955) attributes the slip to the mover, not to the opponent.
- Meets a check with the block that develops, not the block that helps their plan or puts the piece on a bad square (Early checks) e.g. Block with the knight from c3, not the bishop from d2. Bd2 only pushes their queen toward the pawn it wants anyway, and d2 is a poor square for that bishop. -> Partial. checkMethod.checkMethod (checkMethod.ts:32) lists the three kinds of answer (king move, block, capture). Which block is better is MISSING.
- A development lead licenses breaking rules and means the position should be opened now (Opening or early middlegame with a tempo edge) e.g. You are ahead in development, so open the position, and take with the bishop because it forks. -> Covered. ruleException (ruleException.ts:70), positionalRead's 'open the position before they catch up' (positionalRead.ts:273), and reviewSacrifice.sacrificeCompensation (reviewSacrifice.ts:44).
- States the plan as stages with checkpoints, and what happens if it fails (The start of the middlegame) e.g. Step one, keep their king from castling; step two, chase it toward f2; then attack. If they do manage to castle, your structure is sound and the game simply goes on. -> Partial. nextPlans.deriveNextPlans (nextPlans.ts:161), speedRunReads' promise threads, and planMemory. The 'if it fails, you are still fine' risk check is MISSING.
- Transforms one kind of advantage into another (a slow positional edge into active play) and states the pros and cons of doing it (A positional edge has stalled) e.g. Capturing on c6 swaps a slow edge for active play. The price: the bishop pair goes, and their d-pawn gets a neighbour, so it is no longer isolated. -> Partial. positionTransformation.detectPositionTransformation (positionTransformation.ts:83) flags bad or missed trades. thinkAloud.lineAchieves notes a transformation into a pawn ending (thinkAloud.ts:86). A voluntary transformation with its pros and cons is MISSING.
- When ahead: simplify and allow trades, put pieces on safe squares (even passive ones) for a concrete reason, win efficiently rather than flashily, take what is free, and steer for the clean mate (Clearly winning positions) e.g. You are a piece up: put the rooks on the open files and let them trade. The bishop goes to f2, the safest square. / Pick the most economical win, not the flashiest. -> Covered. conversionMethod.readConversion (conversionMethod.ts:44), moveInsight.materialPlan (moveInsight.ts:993), and tradeJudgement's 'ahead' case (tradeJudgement.ts:40). The efficiency and mate-first framing is partial.
- When worse: relieve the pressure by trading, take a defensive posture that covers as many squares as possible with the pieces kept near the centre, defend with the cheapest unit, and don't tie a whole rook to one pawn (Positions that are worse but still roughly level) e.g. You are under pressure; trading pieces takes the sting out of it. / Defend c7 with a pawn, not by tying a rook to it. -> Partial. moveInsight.pawnCanGuard (cheapest defender, moveInsight.ts:889) and heavyTiedDown (:1022). 'Trade to relieve pressure' is MISSING. moveInsight.materialPlan gives the opposite advice when down material (keep pieces on, moveInsight.ts:1012): right when lost, wrong when merely pressed.
- Restricts an enemy piece or pawn: take its forward squares with pawns, freeze their pawn, confine their rook (Middlegame squeezes) e.g. c3 takes away the knight's forward squares. / a5 freezes their a-pawn in place. / The bishop on d7 keeps their rook off c8. -> Partial. moveFundamentals 'prophylaxis' ('takes the X square away from their piece', moveFundamentals.ts:754) and 'space'. Freezing a pawn and confining a rook are MISSING.
- Finds the target and the way in (weak lines, a diagonal), and redeploys the piece that has finished its job (Quiet middlegames) e.g. That pawn is weak; how do you hit it? The bishop on c3 has done its work, so bring it round to attack the pawn. -> Covered. forwardTeaching routes (forwardTeaching.ts:186, :236), positionReadingService.findPieceQuality (positionReadingService.ts:512), nextPlans.findWorstPlacedPiece (nextPlans.ts:81), and moveInsight.diagonalContest (moveInsight.ts:1137).
- Tempo technique: capture only after their bishop has moved, so it has to move twice; keep a useful move in reserve until it counts; make the opponent commit when it costs you nothing (Tension in the opening and middlegame) e.g. Don't take on c5 yet. Wait until their bishop leaves f8, then take, and they have spent a move. / Keep a6 for later; nothing bothers you right now. / h3 makes the knight decide where it is going, and costs you nothing. -> MISSING for the capture timing and the reserve move. endgamePawnReads.spareTempoWasted covers pawn endings only (endgamePawnReads.ts:147). 'Make them commit' is partial: speedRunReads.provokes (speedRunReads.ts:125) fires only when their reply is a pawn advance (:134-136); usefulWaiting (:307).
- Separates how a position looks from what it is, and explains a verdict by listing the opponent's assets (Middlegame assessments) e.g. It looks bad for you, with less space and d6 a target, but every one of your pieces protects another. / You are still worse: their e-pawn can advance, and the bishop-and-queen battery keeps your knight frozen. -> Partial. positionFacts' phase verdict and pieceQuality.explainEvalByPieceQuality. The contrast between appearance and reality is MISSING.
- Reveals the second purpose of an earlier move when it pays off (A previously prepared move gets used) e.g. c3 had a second job: now d4 blocks their bishop and gains time, using the same pawn that prepared the break. -> Partial. speedRunReads' promise threads (the GamePromise field, speedRunReads.ts:36), planMemory, and causalChain.buildCausalChain (causalChain.ts:639) for backward tactic chains.
- Separates the objective verdict from practical chances: the engine slightly prefers them, but it is hard to prove at the board; or players often bluff each other into a line (Opening choices and sharp sidelines) e.g. The engine slightly prefers them, but finding the proof over the board is hard, so it is a fair practical choice. -> MISSING as a computer. The earlier census rated practical play as authored judgement; amateurPlayLookup holds amateur frequencies that could ground 'people often...'.
- Credits the opponent's good or only moves, and names a better move the game missed (After good opponent play; in Review) e.g. They defended well; the knight move was the only way to keep the pawn, and the position still falls apart. / The bishop to d5 was even stronger here. -> Partial. coachFeatureService.ts:1175 'Their only move, and they found it' (Review only), and strongChoice.strongChoice (strongChoice.ts:16) for a stronger move that strong players play here.
- Uses a short, vivid comparison to make a principle stick (for example, a modest square can be the right square, or there is no point worrying about tidiness when you are winning) (Right after a principle is stated) e.g. A quiet square that guards your centre beats a flashy one that hangs. / Being a piece up and fretting about a scratch on your pawns misses what matters. -> MISSING. It is a phrasing device; only the fixed rotation tables exist.

## Source 20
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[3482..3925]: 444 notes from 19 videos. By phase: 160 opening, 194 middlegame, 90 endgame. The student is White in 166 notes and Black in 278. Method: I read every note against its board, checked 9 positions with chess.js, and compared the slice with the two coarse readers who covered it (docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/raw-teach.json readers 4 and 5, with 19 and 26 acts). Every computer mapping was grepped in src/services with tests excluded.

Result: 73 acts. 59 of them are missing from the coarse pass; the other 14 sharpen or correct a coarse act. Each is tagged [NEW], [SHARPENS] or [CORRECTS] in its `move` field. The F0c role it fills is in its `verb` field.

THE BIGGEST GAPS IN THIS SLICE, ranked by notes times teaching value:
1. MOVE ORDER FOR POSITIONAL REASONS: cover the square a pawn push gives up, bring out the guard before the piece whose move would drop a pawn, castle before opening the centre, develop before chasing. moveOrder.moveOrder (src/services/moveOrder.ts:65) speaks only when the wrong order loses material or mates (guards at :10-17, ORDER_COST_CP at :29), so none of these ever qualify.
2. A GOAL HELD ACROSS MOVES:
   - Keep the prize: kingSafety.castleRoute (src/services/kingSafety.ts:202) counts only the student's own pieces in the way (:207-213). It cannot see an enemy bishop covering f8; chess.js confirms the b4 bishop does exactly that at note 3832.
   - Revise the plan when their resource appears.
   - Change the route, not the plan.
   - The keystone move.
   planArc.stepArc (src/services/planArc.ts:236) records that a plan was given up (:329), never why.
3. OPENING TEACHING (F02), mostly MISSING:
   - why the opponent plays a move (a habit carried over from another opening) and the one-pawn antidote;
   - look-alike openings separated by one difference;
   - why a sideline exists and what neutralises it;
   - a method for when the opponent leaves book;
   - two practical rules for meeting a gambit;
   - a transposition you can decline.
   Partial support: openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (src/services/openingIdentity.ts:85), openingBranches.branchesAt (src/services/openingBranches.ts:56), positionReadingService.structureTransfer (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:1047), which covers 3 structures only.
4. CALCULATION CRAFT:
   - why the check matters;
   - the reflex defence that drops a piece on the far side. refutedAlternativeCore.droppedJob (src/services/refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63) proves it, but it is never fed the opponent's defence;
   - a bait inside a capture;
   - checking whether a threat is real;
   - a sacrifice that isn't really one;
   - the guaranteed minimum of a sacrifice;
   - the opening's key motif re-checked at the end of every line;
   - settling the simplest question first.
5. STRUCTURE JUDGEMENTS: fix the target before attacking it, fix their pawns on your bishop's colour, blockade a pawn majority, doubled pawns as an asset, choosing between two pawn breaks.
6. THREADS ACROSS MOVES: voicing the objection to a counter-intuitive move before answering it, and naming the earlier quiet move whose point only shows now.

CORRECTIONS TO THE COARSE PASS:
(a) A live trapped-piece computer does exist: tacticsDetector.findTrappedPieces (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:451, run inside detectTactics at :833) and reviewTeachingPoints.findTrappedPiece (src/services/reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789).
(b) The cheapest-defender half exists: moveInsight.pawnCanGuard (src/services/moveInsight.ts:889), spoken by positionAsk at :220.
(c) The queen standoff also maps to moveFundamentals 'queen-off-file' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:68), not only keepTension.
(d) A pin aimed at a defender is moveFundamentals 'attack-defender' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:53).

SIDE FINDINGS (flagged, not acted on):
- onlyMoveSequence.walkForcedSequence (src/services/onlyMoveSequence.ts:57) is the only computer that can prove a forced perpetual (terminus at :96-99), and it has zero production callers: built but unwired (G8.5).
- positionalRead.ts:394 trims the spoken list of weak-colour holes to two squares with cc.squares.slice(0, 2). That is a cap on a spoken computed fact (V14).
- reviewSacrifice.sacrificeCompensation (src/services/reviewSacrifice.ts:44) is called only from Review (reviewFullData.ts:915, coachFeatureService.ts:2750). Learn cannot say what a sacrifice bought (F2/S1).
- Source data:
  - 45 of the 444 notes speak in first person, and note 3634 names a content creator. danyaTeachingService.teachingBeatText (src/services/danyaTeachingService.ts:1605) joins the note fields verbatim, and I found no first-person filter on that path (V1/F0d).
  - Notes 3577, 3578 and 3659 carry a percentage, rating bands and a claim about players at a level (V8/F10).
  - Notes 3741-3742 sit one ply early: 3742's prose about a pawn going to the f-file is anchored on 18...dxe2.
  - Note 3687 calls the student's own knight on c6 'Black's' (V16).
- 35...axb1=N, an underpromotion at note 3515, goes untaught in the source: a rare fact the coach would need its own computer for.
RHYTHM: Measured over all 444 notes, counting the words of explains + teaches + plans. One whole game is bare narration, so it is the floor, not the bar.

OVERALL: median 19 words, mean 25. 104 notes (23%) have 8 words or fewer; 25 (6%) have 60 or more.

THE OPPONENT'S MOVES GET LESS: median 15 words, against 21 on the student's own moves. 34% of notes on the opponent's moves are 8 words or fewer, against 16% on the student's own.

BY PLY:
- plies 1-10: median 16
- plies 11-20: median 23. This is the peak: mean 31, and 10 of the 25 long notes fall here
- plies 21-30: median 24
- plies 31-40: median 19
- plies 41 and later: median 15

BY PHASE: opening 20, middlegame 21, endgame 15.

COVERAGE: 232 of the 676 plies inside the videos' spans (34%) have no note. In seven games (videos Qkv7D, QxHsw, RSZf, Rehhb, SDIQ, TNaK, TPTu) nearly every ply has a note: 1-6 plies without one, over spans of 26-52 plies. The other videos have gaps of 5-46 plies, which fits annotating only the key moments (several are lectures). The distiller may also have dropped plies, so a missing note is not proof he was silent.

WHERE THE LONG NOTES FALL:
- the first real decision after book (one game has 9 long notes in a row, 3583-3591);
- the moment the plan is set (3648-3668);
- the justification of a gambit (3578);
- the conversion recipe (3689, 3743);
- the post-mortem.

ORDER INSIDE A LONG NOTE:
1. name the moment;
2. the obvious candidate and what it grabs;
3. the drawback that sets it aside;
4. the pattern the piece configuration suggests;
5. that move against their best reply;
6. a check of what they can do back;
7. the verdict;
8. a return to the shelved candidate if their move changes things.

AFTER A DECISION: the next 3-10 plies drop to one clause or a bare move, the sense of 'the rest is easy'.

QUESTIONS: 14 of 444 notes (3%). Five of them are the obstacle question: what is in the way, and how do you remove it.

THE FLOOR: one whole game (3529-3570, 42 notes) is only the move plus a two-to-four-word function, e.g. 'hitting the queen'.
- [NEW] Explains WHY the opponent chose their move (a habit carried over from a different opening) and gives the one-pawn antidote that blunts it (The opponent's first misapplied system move in the opening (a club-level habit the student will keep meeting)) e.g. Their bishop came to c4 because that's where it goes against the e-pawn reply, a reflex rather than a plan. Against this setup one pawn to e6 shuts its diagonal, and your d5 then hits it with tempo. -> MISSING. amateurPlayLookup.lookupAmateurPlay (src/services/amateurPlayLookup.ts:76) gives how often players at the level play the move, but nothing computes the habit-carried-over reason. The antidote half is missing too: theirMoveCost (src/services/theirMoveCost.ts:60) only reads THEIR pawn shutting in THEIR bishop; no fact names YOUR pawn cutting THEIR bishop's diagonal (grep 'blunt' in src/services hits prompt text only, coachPrompts.ts:105).
- [NEW] Separates two look-alike openings by the one structural difference, and says what that difference flips (The defining move of an opening that resembles a better-known one) e.g. This isn't the King's Gambit: both knights are already out, so if you grab the f-pawn, e5 kicks your knight straight back home. That's why the central counter-strike is the move. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.structureTransfer (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:1047) carries plans over for three named structures only (table at :1041-1045; called at CoachTeachPage.tsx:9590 and groundedAnswer.ts:6575). Reasoning about the DIFFERENCE between two openings and what it changes is MISSING.
- [NEW] Says why a sideline exists (the main line is dry) and how sound it really is: dangerous at club level, but a prepared opponent has an antidote; names which reply is the critical one (The defining move of an offbeat line, and again when the opponent leaves the critical path) e.g. The main line tends to fizzle into a level, symmetrical game, so this pawn move is played to unbalance it. It seems to break every development rule, and that's its sting at club level, but a well-prepared opponent can neutralise it, and the dangerous reply isn't the obvious bishop move. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (src/services/openingIdentity.ts:85) renders provokes / aims / gambit / sharp / famous from offline facts. 'Why this instead of the main line' and the antidote or critical reply are MISSING live. V8: the source states a draw percentage and rating bands (3577, 3578), which must become words.
- [NEW] Gives a move's surface idea, then the deeper one most players miss (A provocative opening move whose payoff is an in-between move a few plies later) e.g. The obvious point of f3 is to support e4. The real sting comes if they take on e4: instead of recapturing, you push d5 first, chase their knight, and only then take back, with a big pawn centre. -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.moveIntent (src/services/moveIntent.ts:124) reads one level of prepares/prevents; lookaheadPlan detects an in-between quiet move inside a forcing line (src/services/lookaheadPlan.ts:1267). Presenting the hidden second layer after the first is MISSING.
- [NEW] Announces the branch map before it happens: this plan needs their main reply; if they choose the other, here is your second idea. Surveys their tries at a branch, each with a one-word character (The first branch point of a line the student is about to play) e.g. Whether this line works depends on their knight going to f6; if it goes to c6 instead, you have a different, equally sharp idea. Against your early c5 they have four tries: taking at once is rare and poor, d5 is ambitious, c3 is modest, e3 is the modern choice. -> PARTIAL. openingBranches.branchesAt (src/services/openingBranches.ts:56) lists the roads from the opening DB with their names; linePickerPopularity.rankByPopularity (src/services/linePickerPopularity.ts:78) ranks them at the student's level. The one-word character (rare / ambitious / modest / topical) and 'your plan against each' are MISSING.
- [NEW] Out-of-book method: an unfamiliar move is probably not the best; reason it out and narrow to the one sensible reply by ruling out moves that hand them something (The ply the opponent leaves known theory) e.g. You haven't seen this e5 before, which usually means it isn't the critical try. Work it out: taking on d5 lets them grab d4 and plant a knight in the centre, so the only reasonable answer is to take on e5. -> MISSING as a method beat. bookDeparture.bookDeparture (src/services/bookDeparture.ts:49) and theoryDeparture.findTheoryDeparture (src/services/theoryDeparture.ts:73) detect the departure; methodBeat.liveMethodBeat (src/services/methodBeat.ts:296) has no off-book habit.
- [SHARPENS coarse r5#14] Two practical rules for facing a gambit, and the condition that picks one: against an obscure gambit, take the material and develop; against a gambit the opponent knows better than you, hand the material back and cash in development (The moment a gambit is offered, or when the opponent starts cashing in its initiative) e.g. This pawn offer isn't a known line, so don't agonise over its idea: take it and get your pieces out, guarding the extra pawn as you develop. But where they clearly know the critical line, give the piece back with your knight retreat and simply develop; gambit players hate a position with nothing left to attack. -> MISSING. Coarse reader 5 logged only the give-back half. The deciding condition (how well-trodden the line is) could come from explorer game counts (amateurPlayLookup.lookupAmateurPlay, src/services/amateurPlayLookup.ts:76), but no computer chooses between the two rules.
- [SHARPENS coarse r4#6] Move order for POSITIONAL reasons: cover the square a pawn push will give up before pushing; bring out the guard before the piece that would drop the pawn; castle before you open the centre; develop before chasing an annoying piece (Opening development and the run-up to a pawn break) e.g. Pushing a5 right now hands their bishop the b5 square, so put your bishop on d7 first; then a5 and a4 roll smoothly. Their bishop on b3 is aimed at d5, and only your queen guards it, so the knight to f6 comes out before the other bishop, whose move to d6 would cut the queen off and drop d5. -> MISSING for positional reasons. moveOrder.moveOrder (src/services/moveOrder.ts:65) speaks only when the wrong order loses material or mates (guards at moveOrder.ts:10-17, ORDER_COST_CP = 100 at :29), so a conceded square, a central pawn left hanging, or a king left in the centre never qualifies. groundedAnswer.explainMoveOrder (src/services/groundedAnswer.ts:3332) names check / pin / tempo / material mechanisms, chat only.
- [NEW act, computer already wired] Says what a pin is really FOR: it attacks the defender of a central point, not the pinned piece for its own sake (Opening pins where a bishop pins a knight that guards a central pawn or square) e.g. Your bishop to g4 develops and pins the knight that holds up their d4 pawn. That knight can no longer do its job, so d4 gets weaker: you restrain and develop in one move. -> WIRED, but the coarse readers didn't credit it: moveFundamentals 'attack-defender' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:53, computed by computeMoveFundamentals at :308; its own doc cites the bishop hitting the knight that guards e5). The tactical version is tacticsDetector.findRemovableGuards (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:630).
- [NEW] Explains the opponent's correct move by its hidden defensive resource, and corrects the common wrong reason for it (The opponent plays the accurate move against an idea the student knows) e.g. Their bishop to f5 is right, but not because of the queen check you might expect, since c3 meets that. It works because of the rook-to-c8 resource, which is why your knight jump to b5 achieves nothing here. -> PARTIAL. opponentMovePurpose.threatStoppedBy (src/services/opponentMovePurpose.ts:58) proves from the board that their move stopped your threat. Naming WHICH resource does it, and correcting the wrong reason, are MISSING.
- [NEW] Golden nugget: a pawn kick that sends a piece to the square it wanted anyway is a wasted move (The opponent kicks a developed piece early) e.g. Their b5 chases your bishop to b3, exactly where it wanted to go, while their own pieces are still at home. That pawn move cost them time and loosened their queenside. -> PARTIAL. moveFundamentals 'keep-working' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:56) says the kicked piece still works; tempoCount.tempoCount (src/services/tempoCount.ts:32) counts only repeated piece moves, not pawn kicks; theirMoveCost (src/services/theirMoveCost.ts:60) has no tempo reading. The verdict 'their kick helped you' is MISSING.
- [NEW] A transposition you don't have to enter, and the sly move order that keeps one open (Early move-order moments where the opening's identity is still open) e.g. Their e6 offers a French, but as a queen's-pawn player you don't have to play e4 into it. Their knight to c3 can still turn into an Open Sicilian next move, so choose your reply to suit the Sicilian you play. -> PARTIAL. openingDetectionService.detectOpeningTranspositional (src/services/openingDetectionService.ts:246) recognises the transposition. 'You may decline it' and 'your answer depends on your repertoire' are MISSING.
- [NEW] Says WHY a move has to come with check: the forced reply is what lets the follow-up land (Forcing sequences where a capture works only because it checks. Also a check used to move a rook onto the open file for free, and a queen check that also hits a loose piece) e.g. Take on c3 with the bishop, and it matters that it's check: they must take back, and your queen lands on c3 hitting the king and the rook on a1 together. Without the check they'd have a free move to save the rook. -> PARTIAL. groundedAnswer.explainMoveOrder (src/services/groundedAnswer.ts:3332) names 'comes with check, forcing the reply', chat only; lineReasons.lineWithReasons (src/services/lineReasons.ts:20) marks forcing steps in a spoken line. No Learn or Review clause says the check is the reason the line works.
- [NEW] Names the reflex defence and the piece on the other wing that it abandons (whole-board awareness) (A check or attack whose most natural defence loosens a piece somewhere else) e.g. The natural block is the queen to d2, but the queen on d1 is the only guard of the rook on a1. Block there and their queen takes a1 with check. -> PARTIAL. refutedAlternativeCore.droppedJob (src/services/refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63) proves exactly this from an alternative plus its punishment; I checked this board with chess.js: a1's only defender is d1, and Qd2 allows ...Qxa1+. It is fed the popular alternative for the side being taught (refutedAlternative.ts:127); the OPPONENT's reflex defence is never fed in.
- [NEW] Picks the capture that also baits a trap: it hits a piece, and if they grab your loose queen, you recapture with a fork (A winning position where two captures are available) e.g. Instead of the obvious capture on d5, take on a2: it hits their rook too, and if they take your queen on c3, your knight takes back with check and forks their king and queen. -> PARTIAL. forkTrick.forkTrickFor (src/services/forkTrick.ts:81) and trickSidestepped (:126) read the give-a-piece, take-back-with-a-fork shape, but only when the giving move is a capture. A piece left en prise whose capture walks into a fork is not covered.
- [NEW] Checks whether a threat is real before reacting, both ways: their one-move threat is weak because it can be met in many ways; your own 'threat' isn't real because the grab walks into their counter-check (Right after a threat appears, or before the student relies on a threat of their own) e.g. Their bishop to g4 hits your queen, but that's a one-move threat you can meet in several ways. And your bishop to e2 doesn't really threaten their knight: if you take it, their queen checks on h4 and forks your king and bishop. -> PARTIAL. bluffDetector.detectBluff (src/services/bluffDetector.ts:37) and falseAlarm (src/services/falseAlarm.ts:37) cover the opponent's side; groundedAnswer.captureHasCounterTactic (src/services/groundedAnswer.ts:2611) finds the counter-fork, chat only; moveInsight.emptyThreat (src/services/moveInsight.ts:909) covers 'the piece just steps away'. Counting how many ways a threat is met is MISSING.
- [NEW] Separates a real sacrifice from one that isn't: the material comes back by force (The student or opponent offers material that is regained at once) e.g. The knight to d5 isn't really a sacrifice: if they take it, your pawn recaptures, the e-file opens, and their bishop, pinned on e6, falls. -> MISSING as a named distinction (no logic in src/services decides 'only looks like a sacrifice'). brilliancy.detectBrilliancy (src/services/brilliancy.ts:61) decides real sacrifices; forkTrick covers only the fork-regain shape.
- [NEW] States a sacrifice's guaranteed minimum before its upside: at worst a perpetual check (Before or on a speculative sacrifice) e.g. Take on g3. If they take your bishop instead, the queen mates on f2, so they must capture, and then your queen takes back with at least a perpetual check, probably more. -> MISSING in practice. onlyMoveSequence.walkForcedSequence (src/services/onlyMoveSequence.ts:57) can prove a 'perpetual' end to a forced line (:96-99), but it has zero production callers: grep finds no importer outside its tests, so it is built but unwired (G8.5).
- [NEW] Habit: in the middle of an attack, check for a plain material win before continuing the plan (An attacking position after a reply that doesn't test you) e.g. They retreated the knight instead of testing you, and now their rook on e1 simply hangs to your bishop. When you're sacrificing, don't forget you can just take things. And before pushing the planned h-pawn, look again: the queen to g4 wins a rook outright. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.findHangingBySee (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:361) supplies the fact; safetyHabits.keepPressing (src/services/safetyHabits.ts:54) speaks only after a slow move already cost while winning. The habit said before the move is MISSING.
- [NEW] Calculation habit: at the end of every line you calculate, check whether the opening's key motif has come back (Sharp opening complications that loop back to the opening's signature tactic) e.g. They have a complicating capture on e5, and after it both your pieces look loose. But at the end of that line, remember the key idea: with their knight gone from c6, your bishop checks on b5 and the king has to walk. -> MISSING.
- [NEW] Calculation method: settle the simplest question first (the forced trade), then weigh the harder choices (Positions with several captures pending at once) e.g. The centre has burst open. Trade on g2 first: that removes their bishop, and if they grab your knight instead you take their rook and stay ahead. Only then think about how to recapture on f6. -> MISSING. thinkingExchangeChain orders captures by the cheapest capturer (src/services/thinkingExchangeChain.ts:191), not decisions by simplicity.
- [NEW] Golden nugget: a piece defended only by a piece that is itself attacked is as good as loose; and pieces planted next to the enemy king are in reach of the defender's pieces too (A piece goes deep into the enemy camp, or its defence is stretched) e.g. Their bishop on f2 looks defended, but its only guard is under attack itself, so it's as good as loose. Pieces that close to your king can be hit by your pieces too, which is why taking on g4 is suddenly a real threat. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.findRemovableGuards (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:630) and findOverloadedPieces (:690) find the tactic; loosePieces.findLoosePieces (src/services/loosePieces.ts:35) counts only pieces with no defender. The recognition category 'defended, but by a guard under fire' is MISSING.
- [NEW] A piece frozen by its duty: it can't move without dropping what it guards, so it can't stop your next move (Middlegame attacks against a defended king) e.g. After g4, their knight on f3 can't move without losing their other knight on f2, which leaves h2 with no defender. Their bishop is stuck guarding too, so it does nothing against your bishop to g4. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.queenGlue (src/services/speedRunReads.ts:567) and moveInsight.heavyTiedDown (src/services/moveInsight.ts:1022) read YOUR pieces; tacticsDetector.findOverloadedPieces (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:690) reads theirs, but only with two duties. An enemy piece frozen by a single duty is MISSING.
- [SHARPENS coarse r5#10] Nugget plus pattern: the king is a poor defender because every check must be answered; a pawn check that cuts the king off its pawn crushes once a pawn has reached g5 and e6 is weak (Kingside attacks with an advanced pawn near the enemy king) e.g. Push g6 with check: it splits their king from its pawn, and a king doing guard duty is easy to harass because you can always check it. If it tries to stay next to the pawn, look for a tactic at once. -> PARTIAL. kingAttack.kingAttack (src/services/kingAttack.ts:71) reads shelter pawns taken and files opened; latentDanger.detectLatentDanger (src/services/latentDanger.ts:87) gives the king/queen alignment alarm. The conditions for the thematic pawn check, and the king-as-defender nugget, are MISSING.
- [NEW] Removes their defensive resource before striking: take the square they would block on, then the check drives the king out (Converting an attack where one block is all they have) e.g. They want to meet a check by blocking on g5, so push your h-pawn to cover g5 first. Now nothing can block, and the rook lift to g5 forces their king out. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.escapeSquareFirst (src/services/moveInsight.ts:701) is the sibling for FLIGHT squares: cover the escape square, then the check mates. The blocking-square version is MISSING.
- [SHARPENS + CORRECTS coarse r5 missing#8] The rule of piece value, both ways: defend with the cheapest piece that does the job, and attack with the least valuable piece, so the attack WINS instead of offering a trade (Choosing which piece carries out a task (hit a square, guard a pawn)) e.g. To get a piece to e8, use the knight, not the queen: with the knight on c7 you win their queen outright, whereas your queen on e3 would only offer a trade. To guard that pawn, drop the rook back; a modest job for a rook, but that's what it's there for. -> PARTIAL. Corrects coarse reader 5, which called the defender half missing: moveInsight.pawnCanGuard (src/services/moveInsight.ts:889) is spoken by positionAsk (:220) as the cheapest defender, and thinkingExchangeChain.ts:191 covers capture order. The attacking-side rule (use the cheaper piece so the attack wins rather than trades) is MISSING.
- [CORRECTS coarse r5#20] Traps a piece by first taking away its retreat square (A piece is short of squares after a trade) e.g. Trade on d7 first: their knight on f6 loses its only way back, and e4 is covered twice and attacked once, so the knight has nowhere to go. -> WIRED, contrary to coarse reader 5 ('no live board computer'): tacticsDetector.findTrappedPieces (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:451, run inside detectTactics at :833) and reviewTeachingPoints.findTrappedPiece (src/services/reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789, used by Review and by moveInsight.moveMissed at moveInsight.ts:384). The causal half, 'the trade removed its retreat square', is MISSING (coarse reader 4 #8 noted this).
- [SHARPENS coarse r4#3] The critical-moment monologue, in order: name the moment; the obvious candidate and what it grabs; the drawback that sets it aside; the pattern the piece configuration suggests; that move against their best reply; return to the set-aside candidate when their move changes things; verdict (The first real decision after book, especially in sharp gambit positions) e.g. This is a critical moment. Taking on d5 wins a pawn, but you're behind in development and their bishop to c5 would stop you castling, so set that aside. Their two knights in the centre suggest the standard plan: f4 to chase one, then e5 to chase the other. Now that their knight has gone back to c6, taking on d5 comes with tempo, so it's worth another look. -> PARTIAL. thinkAloud.depthClauses (src/services/thinkAloud.ts:226, reached via positionFacts) chains what changed, what you owe, the line and 'not yet' (thinkAloud.notYet :145); deliberation.buildDeliberation (src/services/deliberation.ts:144) weighs candidates; criticalMoment.readCriticalMoment (src/services/criticalMoment.ts:164) flags the moment. The steps 'the pattern the configuration suggests' and 'set aside, then revisit' are MISSING.
- [NEW] Pattern plus nugget: two centralised enemy knights invite a pawn chase (one pawn kicks the first, the next kicks the second and builds a chain); kick with a pawn, not a piece, because a piece can be hit back (Enemy minor pieces centralised early, with pawns free to advance) e.g. Both their knights sit in the centre, which should make you think of chasing them with pawns: f4 hits one, then e5 hits the other and builds your centre. Don't do it with the bishop: if the knight drops back to g6, it's your bishop on f4 that's attacked. -> PARTIAL. moveFundamentals 'tempo' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:391; comment at :178 that a pawn kick gains a tempo) names a single kick. The configuration trigger and the pawn-not-piece reason are MISSING.
- [NEW] Chooses between two pawn breaks by what each does to the files and to your other break (Middlegame planning once development is complete) e.g. The break is a5, not f5: once f5 reaches f4 they can keep that side locked, while a5-a4 opens the b-file for your rooks and makes a passed pawn. With their pawn on e5 cramping you, f6 is the other break worth considering; prepare it with the knight to d7, which keeps c5 in reserve. -> PARTIAL. positionReadingService.findPawnBreaks (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:400) lists the breaks; moveTiming.readTiming (src/services/moveTiming.ts:47) says when one is right. - [NEW] Closes the position on purpose: to win an outpost and reopen later, or to buy time to castle (Middlegame transitions where a closed centre serves a concrete purpose) e.g. Normally you don't close the centre against a king that's out in the open, but d5 here has one job: it gives your knight e6, and then f4 reopens the position on better terms. Likewise g5 isn't attacking; it locks the kingside so you have time to castle long. -> MISSING. ruleException (src/services/ruleException.ts:70) covers three broken rules (the same minor piece moved twice, an f- or g-pawn in front of your castled king, an early queen), none about closing the centre.
- [NEW] Names the keystone move: the one move that solves your only problem and prepares the attack (A position with one standing problem and one attacking plan) e.g. Everything hinges on the rook to e6: it guards e8, so your knight on e4 is safe, and from e6 the rook can swing to h6 once their kingside is loosened. -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.moveIntent (src/services/moveIntent.ts:124) gives prevents + prepares ('one move, two jobs'); speedRunReads.takeTheSting (src/services/speedRunReads.ts:400) reads 'it stops their capture working'.
