- [NEW] Separates the plan from the route: when the first route fails tactically, keep the plan and change the route; a short-term blemish is fine for a lasting goal (When the natural execution of a sound plan is refuted) e.g. The obvious knight jump fails to a trade that leaves a pawn hanging to a fork. - [NEW] Revises the plan out loud when the opponent's resource appears (A reasonable plan meets a counter-resource the student hadn't seen) e.g. Taking the pawn on d5 looked fine until you notice their queen can swing to b6 and hit f2 while your queen is stuck in the centre. - [NEW] Holds one goal over several moves and lets it steer each decision (castling as the prize) (Consolidating a material lead, or any multi-move objective) e.g. Your goal is to castle short; that solves everything. - [NEW] Prepares a future escape square so a piece won't be forced into a trade (Quiet middlegame moves in balanced positions) e.g. c6 protects d5 and also frees c7 for your queen, so if their knight lands on g5 you don't have to take it; the queen can just step aside. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.noRetreat (src/services/moveInsight.ts:957) finds a retreat square before a PAWN can chase the piece; a version for a piece giving chase is MISSING.
- [NEW] Piece choreography: move one piece out so another can reach its best square (Slow manoeuvring phases) e.g. Your knight's best square is c6, where it hits d4 even harder, and d5 is a dead end. - [NEW] Notices when an obligation lifts, and what that frees you to do (After the opponent's retreat or defensive move changes the threats) e.g. With their bishop back on b3, your e5 pawn is no longer hanging, so d6 isn't forced. - [NEW] Points out when the opponent's move helped you: it solved your problem or gave you a new option (Right after an opponent move that changes your problems) e.g. Their bishop to h5 actually helps: your bishop was stranded on f7, and now you can take it with gain of time. Their c4 also gives you the option of c5 later. -> MISSING. moveInsight.theirMoveChanged (src/services/moveInsight.ts:573) reads their new targets and your new worries, not 'your problem solved' or 'an option gained'.
- [NEW] Welcomes the opponent's natural break, and predicts when their slow move will cost them (Early opening, with the student ahead in development) e.g. If they open the centre with d5 now, good: you're ahead in development, and that's exactly what you want. 'Their move would help you, because…' and the time until it costs them are MISSING.
- [NEW] Grades the opponent's move as 'right target, wrong piece', or as the least bad of several poor choices (Judging the opponent's moves in the opening) e.g. Their queen to e7 goes after your pawn, which is the right idea, but the queen is the wrong piece for it with nothing else out, and it blocks their own bishop. Splitting their goal from their means, and rating a move among bad options, are MISSING.
- [NEW] Shows that the opponent's principled, natural move is the decisive mistake here (A move that follows a principle fails to the concrete position) e.g. Developing the knight to f6 is normally right, but here it's the losing move: your pawn takes the pinned bishop on e6, and their position collapses. -> PARTIAL. - [NEW] Weighs a capture's drawback against its gains in one breath (Captures that change the pawn structure) e.g. Taking on c4 does open their bishop, but it leaves them a backward pawn on d2 on an open file you can pile up on, and it gives you the open centre your opening wants. -> PARTIAL. tradeQuality.readTrade (src/services/tradeQuality.ts:124), concessionBeat.findStudentDrawback (src/services/concessionBeat.ts:360) and theirMoveCost (src/services/theirMoveCost.ts:60) each supply one side; weighing the two together is MISSING.
- [NEW] Doubled pawns as an asset (Recapture choices in sharp structures) e.g. Take back toward the centre even though it doubles your pawns: the front pawn becomes a battering ram you can push, the one behind still guards, your king gets more cover, and a file opens toward their king. -> MISSING. positionReadingService.findWeakPawns (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:1176) treats doubled pawns only as a weakness.

- [NEW] A weakness made permanent by the defender that can't get there, and the mirror warning: don't trade off the bishop of the colour your weak squares are on (Gambit compensation, and minor-piece trades) e.g. The light squares around their king are full of holes, and their light bishop can't get to g2 to cover them, so that weakness lasts. - [NEW] Pawn arithmetic: a wing pawn for a centre pawn is a good bargain, and a flank pawn push can chase off one of a centre pawn's two guards (Middlegame plans against a defended centre pawn) e.g. a4 chases away one of the two pieces guarding e4. If the trades go your way, you win their centre pawn for your rook pawn, which is a good deal. -> MISSING as a fact (I found no centre-versus-wing pawn valuation in src/services). Removing a single guard is partly covered by tacticsDetector.findRemovableGuards (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:630).

- [NEW] Fixes the opponent's pawns on your bishop's colour so your bishop can attack them (Bishop endgames) e.g. e3 invites b5, and that has an upside: their pawns end up fixed on light squares, where your bishop can go after them. -> MISSING. reviewTeachingPoints.badEnemyBishop (src/services/reviewTeachingPoints.ts:184) and the other bad-bishop reads count pawns on a bishop's OWN colour as a bad-bishop fact, not as targets for your bishop.

## Source 21
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[3926..4369]: 444 notes, 37 videos, 247 opening / 149 middlegame / 48 endgame, student Black 264 / White 180. `concepts` is empty on every note and `teaches` is filled on 72, so the teaching sits in `explains`. All code paths below are under /home/user/wt-work and were grep-verified. Any count given as a share is a regex count over this slice, so allow about ±15%.

The coarse reader of this range (Reader 6, notes 3750–4499, 26 acts) missed about 30 distinct acts. The highest-value ones:
1. **A standing opening alarm, heard in 3 different openings:** "your f-pawn has gone, so the queen check on h4 is always in play." No computer reads it. detectKingExposure needs a castled king. detectCentralKingDanger only looks down the king's file.
2. **Reading the board by what is missing:** an absent bishop makes a weakness harmless, or changes what kind of opening it is.
3. **Pin geometry the pin computers don't know:**
   - the would-be pinner is itself pinned;
   - your own quiet pawn move creates a pin on your knight (verified with chess.js);
   - why an offered piece can't be taken (also verified).
   All three are in the family of questions.md item 7.
4. **Piece jobs that change over time:** a job finishes, a job passes to another piece, or a piece is kept because of its job. dutiesOf computes the duty but only feeds chat.
5. **Smaller acts:**
   - castling still allowed by the rules but impossible now, because your piece covers the square;
   - doubled pawns that are not a weakness (tradeQuality.ts:181 scores them as a gain, so today's code teaches the opposite);
   - the "glue" move that re-protects several loose pieces at once;
   - a piece that can't move because every square is forked;
   - the gambit decision menu;
   - analogy to another opening, and where the analogy breaks;
   - in a recap, naming a quiet prophylactic move as the most important move of the game (Review's moment-pickers rank slips only).

**Pattern for F4/F5:** several computers exist for one side only:
- heavyTiedDown and noRetreat run only for the side to move (moveInsight.ts:156);
- speedRunReads runs only on the student's turn (thinkAloud.ts:257);
- theirMoveCost's "bishop shut in" reads only their move;
- blunderCheck reads only the student's blunder.

So the opponent half of each (chase their heavy-piece guard, their piece one pawn push from trapped, their self-block, naming the tunnel vision behind their blunder) is unwired.

**Corrections to the coarse read:**
- A live trapped-piece detector does exist: tacticsDetector.ts:451, run through detectTactics at :833. Only the one-move-ahead version for the opponent is missing.
- mutualPins (speedRunReads.ts:194) exists but uses isPinnedPiece (nextPlans.ts:118), which sees pins against the king only. The slice's case, both knights pinned to queens, never fires.
- The quiet-move-purpose computer is moveIntent.ts:124.

**Do not copy:**
- 35 notes (7.9%) use first person or voice uncertainty.
- One whole 52-note game (#4137–4188) is bare play-by-play.

The name of the reference coach appears nowhere in this output.
RHYTHM: Measured over the 444 notes:
- **Length:**
  - Average words: opening 25.2, middlegame 27.6, endgame 15.2.
  - 136 notes (31%) are under 12 words and 45 are 5 words or fewer.
  - 8 notes run over 80 words: #3944 170, #3978 570, #4012 180, #4209 85, #4213 152, #4288 154, #4340 87, #4344 86.
- **When he talks at length:** density follows how much the decision weighs, not the move number. The long lectures land where the opponent leaves book, where a tactic appears, or at the one strategic crossroads of the game. Quiet conversion drops to "you can simplify" or a bare capture.
- **Bare play-by-play:** one game, #4137–4188, is 50 of 52 notes under 12 words. That is description, not a rhythm to copy.
- **A thought often spans several moves.** 19 notes end mid-sentence and the idea finishes on the next one or two plies (#3936-37, #3962-65, #3969-71, #4006-09, #4213-17, #4278-83, #4342-43). Commentary runs continuously while the moves are played: a plan is stated across the plies that carry it out, and a setup move's purpose is paid off later (c6 at #3997 explained at #4001). Design note: the unit of teaching is the thought, not the ply. The composer must be able to open a thought on ply N and close it on N+1 or N+2.
- **Order inside a dense note:**
  1. the tempting or natural move;
  2. why it fails, concretely;
  3. the move;
  4. its reason;
  5. a one-line portable takeaway (72 notes carry one in `teaches`).

  The 570-word note #3978 runs the full F18 chain in order: risk assessed and dismissed with a resource, tension accepted, the glue move with its three jobs, what hangs and what doesn't, prophylaxis asked and answered, the piece kept for its duty, their aggressive-looking move reframed by its drawback, the line, the overload, the recap, then the king hunt as a method.
- **Questions:** 10 of the 11 question marks are rhetorical and answered at once. Thinking out loud in question form is not the F05 quiz.

## Source 22
Read every note in voiced-teachings.json notes[4370..4813]: 444 notes from 28 videos. Mapped 102 distinct teaching acts against src/services: 30 exist, 50 are partial (one of them is blocked by a gate), 22 are missing. The earlier census and the insight catalogue already cover the broad categories. This slice adds fine-grained acts that no computer produces.

WHAT THE COARSE READERS MISSED:
1. The 'a pinned piece is no guard' nugget, spoken in Learn or Review. Legal SEE counts it silently (positionReadingService.ts:212); only How-to-Think says it aloud (thinkingExchangeChain.ts:131).
2. What a pin is really aimed at: the job of the pinned piece.
3. 'Your move is good AND sets a trap for their natural reply', outside the gem library. trapAheadAt (gemCrushLines.ts:564) only covers curated gems for the side to move.
4. Trapped-piece detail: which piece covers each flight square, the threat to trap one move early, keeping the cage shut, and walking the king over to collect. findTrappedPiece (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789) is present-tense only and generic (coachFeatureService.ts:3226).
5. Refuting THEIR in-between move, and praising the student's positional in-between move.
6. The wrong-recapture assumption.
7. Choosing mate over material, and the reverse.
8. The empty-check verdict (bluffDetector skips checks, bluffDetector.ts:33), and dismissing a back-rank alarm when they have no heavy piece.
9. Re-scanning the board after a flurry of exchanges.
10. King to b1 after castling long; pawn pushes that commit your castling side.
11. Preparing a recapture in advance.
12. A shiny one-move tactic versus the plan.
13. Move-order tempo arithmetic (keep the pawn home so the break costs one move), and opening trigger ideas.
14. Opening analogies, including reversed openings with an extra tempo.
15. Small edges accumulating.
16. Right idea, wrong piece.
17. The defender's accounting when the opponent's sacrifice overpays. sacrificeCompensation is Review-only and returns nothing on a losing sac (reviewSacrifice.ts:38/44).
18. Two minors against a rook. materialPlan covers only the rook side (moveInsight.ts:993).
19. Ranking the reasons for a move, raising the student's objection and answering it, and keeping brainstorm separate from forced lines.

DATA DEFECTS in this slice of shipped notes (spoken on S7 surfaces):
- 43/444 notes are in the first person (V1).
- 3 contain percentages (V8: #4501, #4509, #4741).
- 22 are cut mid-sentence at transcript boundaries.
- 1 credits a named person in the first person (F0d/V1: #4693).
- 2 promise an explanation later that never comes (#4526, #4724).
- 1 claim is verified false on its board (D10): vc-YzI6qI-33_U-16 (#4376) names an f4-pawn and a d4-bishop, but chess.js shows f4 empty and the bishop on e3. The note is anchored about five plies early.
RHYTHM: Measured on all 444 notes: mean 28 words, median 23, p90 51, max 175.
- By phase: opening mean 26 (median 24). Middlegame mean 35 (p90 71); the long notes are decision points (which capture, whether to sacrifice, which side to castle), weighing 2-3 candidates with the opponent's replies in 60-175 words. Endgame mean 17.5; these are technique verdicts (only square, up a whole knight, rook behind the pawn).
- Opponent's moves get as many words as the student's (28.1 vs 28.0). What their move does, costs or threatens is narrated just as fully.
- Bare description: 48/444 (11%) are one clause with no reason (9 words or fewer, no connective). 20 of them come from one distilled game (yt:Zko_JUK06vM: 51 notes averaging 6 words), so this is distillation variance, not his teaching. Elsewhere even routine moves carry a purpose clause (preparing b4, tucking the king away).
- Ply coverage: notes exist on 64% of plies inside each game's span (444 of 692). The distillation drops plies, so a gap here is not evidence that he was silent.
- Shape of a long note: what the move does, then the tempting alternative and its concrete refutation, then the line with their replies in words, then the count or verdict, then the principle or habit.
- Openings front-load identity in moves 1-6: name, philosophy, main line vs sideline, the slip typical at the level. Middlegames lead with the threat or plan and weigh candidates. Endgames lead with the technique and stop.
- About 11 rhetorical question-then-answer pairs model the student's own thinking.
- Name the opening as it appears and say what the whole opening is trying to do (moves 1-6, the move that defines or changes the opening) e.g. After the knight to f6 and the pawn to d6, this is the give-them-the-centre defence for real: you let them build a big centre now and plan to hit it from the side later; the whole game becomes whether you crack it before they use it. -> PARTIAL: naming via openingDetectionService.detectOpening (openingDetectionService.ts:166) and openingAnnouncement (openingAnnouncement.ts:54); philosophy via openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (openingIdentity.ts:85: provokes/aims/gambit/sharp/famous). The game's strategic question (who wins the race for the centre) is not computed.
- Grade the opponent's opening choice against theory and name the main move it is not (opponent's move that leaves the main line) e.g. Their queen to d2 is a lesser sideline; the usual move is the bishop to c4. Their bishop to d3 shows they've left book, and it doesn't do the job the c4-square would. -> PARTIAL: bookDeparture (bookDeparture.ts:49), theoryDeparture.findTheoryDeparture (theoryDeparture.ts:73), strongChoice (strongChoice.ts:16), refutedAlternative (refutedAlternative.ts:81). Missing: what the main move does that theirs does not; moveContrast.contrastMoves (moveContrast.ts:64) only compares which pieces each move leaves undefended.
- NEW: move-order tempo arithmetic: keep a pawn at home so its break costs one move, and avoid the order that lets them transpose (opening, choosing which move comes first) e.g. Castle but leave the d-pawn at home: from d7 it reaches d5 in one move later, while d6 now would let them switch to the sharper f3 set-up and cost you a tempo when you break. -> PARTIAL: speedRunReads.flexibleFirst (speedRunReads.ts:549) says piece first, pawn later. MISSING: the double-step tempo count for a delayed break, and the transposition-avoidance reason (the only double-step read is endgamePawnReads.ts:157, for pawn endings).
- Name the transposition as the point of the move (opening, the move that changes which opening it is) e.g. Hitting their centre pawn with the knight instead of taking the gambit pawn forces a calm c3-Sicilian structure, with far less theory than the accepted gambit. -> PARTIAL: detectOpening (openingDetectionService.ts:166) can see the new name; no service turns 'this transposes into X, and that is why' into teaching.
- Opening analogy: this is opening X with one difference, and the difference changes the plan (opening, the structure matches a sibling opening) e.g. It's the fianchetto set-up without their c-pawn on c4, so the game turns tactical. In the plain London you'd answer ...c5 with c3, but your knight is on c3, so take on c5 instead. Against 1.e3 you are playing a French with an extra move. -> MISSING: positionReadingService.namedPawnStructure (positionReadingService.ts:1060) names a structure but never compares it with a sibling opening; no service detects a reversed opening with an extra tempo.
- Practical gambit handling: decline cleanly, and say why (facing a gambit offer) e.g. Decline the pawn: taking it is playable but you must know a lot to survive, which is the fight they want. The best decline develops and hits their centre at the same time. -> PARTIAL: openingIdentity's gambit fact (how long the material imbalance lasts, openingIdentity.ts:124). The accept/decline advice is repertoire guidance with no computer.
- Mark the slip that players at your level typically make here (known slip positions, usually the opponent's natural move) e.g. The bishop check on f2 is the standard error at this level; taking on f6 here is a frequent blunder because people expect the bishop to take back. -> PARTIAL: gems mined at rating bands, gemCrushLines.trapAheadAt / gemMoveSignal (gemCrushLines.ts:564/582); safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42) uses the popular move at the student's level. Outside the gem library, nothing says 'this is the usual mistake here'.

But when the win is near and there is no forced mate, take the material and keep it simple. -> MISSING: matePatterns.classifyMatePattern (matePatterns.ts:341) names a mate after it lands; nothing weighs mate against material.
- Name the mating pattern and the order of the finish (a mating attack forms) e.g. First open the centre so their king has no way out; then the queen arrives on a3 for the mate against the queenside king. With their king boxed in the corner, the queen to h4 is mate in two. -> PARTIAL: matePatterns.classifyMatePattern / explainMate (matePatterns.ts:341/379); moveInsight.escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701).
- Refute the tempting alternative with its concrete reply (a natural move that fails) e.g. The bishop to f5 looks natural, but the knight to h4 hits it and the set-up falls apart, so push the f-pawn to f5 instead. -> EXISTS: refutedAlternative (refutedAlternative.ts:81), refutedAlternativeCore.droppedJob (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63), playCommentary.buildRejectedTempting (playCommentary.ts:497), deliberation.buildDeliberation (deliberation.ts:144), whyItFailed (whyItFailed.ts:170).
- NEW nuance: don't chase a piece to the square it wants (an attacking move whose forced retreat improves their piece) e.g. The knight to f5 hits their queen, but only sends it back to where it wanted to go; develop the bishop instead. -> PARTIAL: moveInsight.emptyThreat (moveInsight.ts:909) catches 'the piece steps away and you gained nothing', but not the retreat IMPROVING their piece.
- NEW nuance: don't trade into their plan or away from your own (a capture whose recapture activates their piece, or removes your key supporter) e.g. Don't take the bishop on g4: their recapture brings the queen out to hit g7, so chase it with the f-pawn, which also lengthens your chain. And don't take the knight on g5; that would undo the whole point of your e4-knight. -> PARTIAL: tradeJudgement 'gave-best' (tradeJudgement.ts:25/40), positionTransformation 'unfavorable-trade' (positionTransformation.ts:83). MISSING: 'their recapture develops a piece with tempo'.
- A quiet move that quietly drops something (a routine move with a side effect) e.g. Castling here leaves the e4-pawn hanging; their queen move to c2 stops guarding d4, and the c5 break hits exactly that. -> EXISTS: moveInsight.theirMoveChanged / weakenedBy (moveInsight.ts:573/523), boardDelta.computeBoardDelta (boardDelta.ts:65), theirMoveCost (theirMoveCost.ts:60), concessionBeat.whatItAllowed (concessionBeat.ts:427).
- Their defence has a price (naming the opponent's defensive try) e.g. If they prop the pawn up with the f-pawn, that's a big concession: it weakens their diagonal and invites a central strike. If their knight retreats to d2, it just gets more passive. -> PARTIAL: speedRunReads.forceConcession (speedRunReads.ts:512) covers only lost castling or a new weak pawn; theirMoveCost (theirMoveCost.ts:60). A weakened diagonal or growing passivity is not covered.
- Recapture choice, with the reason (every recapture choice) e.g. Take back with the knight, not the queen, so you keep the dark-squared bishop that guards your weak squares. Take with the bishop so their rook can't grab the open file with tempo. Take with the pawn that hits their bishop. -> EXISTS: recaptureChoice.recaptureChoice / readRecapture (recaptureChoice.ts:103/56).
- NEW: prepare the recapture in advance (before a likely exchange on one of your pieces) e.g. Put the king's knight on e2 first, so that if they take on c3 a knight recaptures: no doubled pawns, and e4 stays guarded. -> MISSING: recaptureChoice works after the fact; moveIntent's 'prepares' half (moveIntent.ts:124) asks what you'd play with a free move, not who recaptures if they take.
- Choose the developing square, and say why the natural one fails (development choices) e.g. The bishop to d6 rather than b4: d6 supports the centre and points at their king. The knight to e7 rather than f6: on f6 it would block your bishop's grip on d4. -> PARTIAL: deliberation (deliberation.ts:144), moveContrast.contrastMoves (moveContrast.ts:64), boardDelta BLOCKS (boardDelta.ts:154). Blocking your own piece is named only after the move is played.
- NEW: don't be distracted by the one-move tactic; serve the plan (a shiny tactical move against a plan-consistent move) e.g. The pin with the bishop is tempting, but it's a one-move idea. - Hooks and overextension: lever the advanced pawn, punish with a central strike (overextension half missing) (the opponent advances pawns near their king) e.g. Their kingside pawn push gives you a hook to pry against; the further they push, the more they overextend, so answer with a strike in the centre. With your h-pawn already on h4 you'll go long nearly every time. In a mess, ask first: can I castle? -> PARTIAL: speedRunReads.castleSide (speedRunReads.ts:108) compares pawn cover only; moveInsight.castleByHand (moveInsight.ts:840). MISSING: the link from pawn advances to castling side, and the 'can you castle?' habit.

- Opposite-side castling: race the attacks, but the centre may still decide (opposite castling) e.g. Kings on opposite wings means two separate battles; your attack looks faster, but keep an eye on the centre and on their short-term threats every move. -> EXISTS: splitPosition (splitPosition.ts:14), planRace.planRaceClause (planRace.ts:246).
- Reroute a piece toward a named destination (quiet middlegame) e.g. Reroute the knight from c3 toward the kingside, to f4, where it's defended and eyes e6, g6 and the support of d5. -> EXISTS: forwardTeaching.computePieceRoute / computeSliderRoute (forwardTeaching.ts:186/236), nextPlans.findWorstPlacedPiece (nextPlans.ts:81).

- The missed punishment (the win handed back) (a side misses a winning reply) e.g. The b4 push was the kill, because the knight on c5 has nowhere to go; they played the rook move instead and the win evaporated. -> EXISTS: missedTacticService.detectMissedTactics (missedTacticService.ts:964), opponentGap.detectOpponentGap (opponentGap.ts:38).
- NEW nuance: conversion discipline: simple beats spectacular, and win material rather than trading on autopilot (clearly winning positions) e.g. No need for anything spectacular: the calm capture wins a pawn and the rest follows, while a flashy queen check that lets their king out could throw it all away. Don't trade by reflex; if you can win a minor piece, that's better. -> PARTIAL: conversionMethod.readConversion (conversionMethod.ts:44) gives the method step; safetyHabits.keepPressing (safetyHabits.ts:54) pushes the other way (forcing moves when winning). 'Simple over spectacular' and 'material before trades' are not computed.

- King activity in the ending (endgames) e.g. Walking the king backward in an ending is a small error; it belongs up the board. - Announce the switch from tactics to technique (after the decisive gain) e.g. The sharp part is over; it's technique now. Remove their last passed pawn, then bring the knight back. -> EXISTS: positionCharacter.stepCharacter (positionCharacter.ts:130), conversionMethod (conversionMethod.ts:44).
- The defender's only move (forced defence) e.g. Against this attack the knight to a5 is the only move, giving a pawn back for the bishop pair; the king's only good square is e7. -> EXISTS: criticalityScan.scanCriticality (criticalityScan.ts:103), criticalMoment.readCriticalMoment (criticalMoment.ts:164).
- Their best try (damage control) (after a decisive blow) e.g. Their best is to take on e5 and not recapture, still a piece down; their best try to hang on is the bishop to e4 guarding f3. -> EXISTS: opponentIntent.buildOpponentIntent (opponentIntent.ts:55).

How do you get rid of the pin without a passive retreat? With h3 and g4. -> PARTIAL: thinkAloud.depthClauses (thinkAloud.ts:226) chains reasons but has no question-then-answer device. F05 gates questions that wait for an answer, not ones the coach answers itself.
- NEW: raise the student's objection and answer it (a move that looks anti-principled) e.g. You may feel that taking on c5 gives up the centre. A little, yes, but now their d5-pawn is under real fire. -> MISSING.
- Safe versus ambitious: name both, then choose with the reason (two good options with different risk) e.g. Castling is simplest; the bishop to g5 is more ambitious and awkward for them. The quiet queen move was easier, but your development lead is huge, so the principled line is justified. -> PARTIAL: deliberation.meaningfulAlternatives (deliberation.ts:306); conversionMethod's 'attack-king' vs 'trade-pieces' steps (conversionMethod.ts:44).
- NEW: the move with no downside, played without long calculation (messy positions where one move improves every branch) e.g. The bishop check can only help: at worst it lets you castle and gives you a guaranteed way out, so play it. -> PARTIAL: speedRunReads.goodInEveryBranch (speedRunReads.ts:383) checks only that no reply wins material; 'it enables castling' is not computed.
- NEW: keep brainstorming separate from forced lines (complex positions with many ideas) e.g. In the worst case you could give up the knight and swing a rook in with tempo, but that's an idea to keep in mind, not something you have calculated as forced. -> MISSING: spoken lines carry no forced/speculative tag; thinkAloud.lineAchieves (thinkAloud.ts:71) only reports a line's outcome.
- Intuition versus calculation (do not port the first-person form) (known attacking structures) e.g. In this structure the g- and h-pawn storm simply works; a strong player plays it from pattern without calculating every branch. -> MISSING as a structure-pattern library. The source's 'it feels right' form must not be copied, because RULEBOOK F18 says the coach never guesses.
- Credit the opponent's good move and flag that calculation is needed (after a strong opponent move) e.g. Good defence: they found the knight to c5, hitting c6 and preparing a capture on e6 that attacks your rook. Now you have to calculate. -> PARTIAL: coachFeatureService.ts:1175 credits a found only-move; methodBeat's slow-down habit (methodBeat.ts:60).
- Forkable squares, and the second route (queen and rook on knight-forkable squares) e.g. Their queen on d5 can be forked from c7 by a knight coming via b5; once ...a6 shuts that route, b6 becomes the fork square, so the knight goes to c4. -> EXISTS: latentFork.detectLatentFork (latentFork.ts:161).
- NEW: squares your unmoved units leave uncovered (early middlegame) e.g. Their knight can land on f5 precisely because your central pawn hasn't moved yet, so nothing covers that square. Check which squares your undeveloped units leave open. -> MISSING.
- NEW: the interposing move on a line where two pieces face each other (rooks or queens facing each other on a file) e.g. The rook to d4 steps in between on the same file where the rooks stare at each other, a useful resource whenever pieces face off along a line. -> MISSING: collinearity appears only in geometry helpers (kingSafety.ts:257, pinGeometry.ts:106), never as a taught concept.
- The greedy queen that can't get home (after a pawn-grabbing queen raid) e.g. Their queen took b7 and a7 and is now stuck on a7, unable to come back and defend; you can even try to trap it with a quiet a5. -> PARTIAL: moveInsight.moveMissed greedy-pawn-grab (moveInsight.ts:386), for the student's own grab only.
- Habit: look for free material every move (the opponent's routine move hangs something) e.g. They castled on autopilot and dropped a pawn. Never play on autopilot against an unusual opening; check every move for something free. -> EXISTS: methodBeat's forcing-scan habit (methodBeat.ts:60), looseTrigger (looseTrigger.ts:14), safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42).
- Habit: don't move instantly when it matters (after a recapture, where moving straight away is tempting) e.g. Don't play this one instantly; take a couple of seconds to make sure you aren't missing something. -> PARTIAL: methodBeat's slow-down habit (methodBeat.ts:60) is the board-side form; moving in advance (pre-moving) cannot be observed.
- The student's own record with this opening (move 2-3 of the student's repertoire) e.g. This is your opening: out of the opening it has given you a good position in nearly every game at your level. -> EXISTS: openingRecordBeat.openingRecordClause (openingRecordBeat.ts:29), homeOpening.chooseHomeOpening (homeOpening.ts:153).
- Repertoire and practical advice off the board (after the opponent plays a dubious sideline) e.g. Don't make dubious sidelines your main weapon until you are very strong, and keep a ready set-up against them. Some set-ups look gimmicky yet set real practical problems. -> MISSING by design: the census classes repertoire advice as an off-board lane.

## Source 23
I read all 444 notes in voiced-teachings notes[4814..5257] (28 videos) and catalogued 76 distinct teaching acts. Every code claim below was checked by grep with file:line; nothing is from memory. 20 acts are tagged [census missed]: the coarse codes of the 2026-09-27 teaching census do not name them.

Most acts in this slice already have a computer:
- the 26 speed-run reads in speedRunReads.ts, live via thinkAloud.ts:257, called from positionFacts.ts:1009;
- the insight reads in moveInsight.ts, live via positionAsk (:130) and moveMissed (:368);
- the census lanes: moveIntent, moveOrder, recaptureChoice, ruleException, falseAlarm, theirMoveCost, kingAttack, tempoCount, bluffDetector, forkTrick, pinPressure, latentFork, methodBeat.

Three structural gaps dominate.

1. Surface parity (F2, S1).
- computePositionFacts has no Review caller. Its only call sites are CoachTeachPage.tsx:9692, useLiveCoach.ts:264, usePhaseNarration.ts:635, positionReadComposer.ts:130 and whyBestMove.ts:118. So no think-aloud or speed-run read reaches Review.
- Learn-only, all in CoachTeachPage.tsx: moveOrder (:10799), moveIntent (:10837 and :10928), planChoice, trapAhead, openingPlan, rejectedTempting (:9862), opponentIntent (:9558) and opponentGap (:9559).
- moveContrast is Review-only (reviewFullData.ts:938). computePieceOptions is chat-only (coachService.ts:1507).
- The studentMoveTeaching lanes do reach Learn, Review and chat: recapture, ruleException, falseAlarm, kingAttack, trade, kneeJerk, blunderCheck, autopilot, strongChoice. Proof: learnBoardTeaching.ts:138-330, called at coachFeatureService.ts:1970, and through learnBoardTeaching.ts:759 into chat.

2. Dual-use seat gaps (F4).
- latentDanger is only ever called for the student's own seat (positionFacts.ts:488, moveInsight.ts:138). So 'your rook x-rays their king, move the blocker' is never said.
- noRetreat runs only for the student's pieces (moveInsight.ts:287). So 'one pawn move traps their piece' is never said.
- forkTrickFor is voiced only when a quiet move sidesteps it (forkTrick.ts:126-136). It is never voiced as 'available to you but premature' or 'this candidate walks into theirs', even though V19 names this exact trick.

3. Missing computers (new under B6, for David to decide):
- reputation vs reality;
- recapture-names-the-variation and branch-point theory survey (openingBranches.branchesAt exists, no lane speaks it);
- calibrated expectations;
- worst-case firepower test;
- which piece carries out the idea;
- an opponent dilemma where every reply loses something;
- respecting the opponent's resource (today only an LLM instruction at coachPrompts.ts:1225-1231, a G0 smell);
- battery order;
- reassigning a piece whose job is done;
- choosing a rook by the other rook's future job;
- don't kick a piece toward a better square;
- a positional weakness keeps, so there is no rush to punish it;
- opening the position favours the better-developed side (computed today only in Review, not live);
- opposite-coloured bishops as an attacking aim;
- 'bad bishops defend good pawns' and the pawn-colour rule;
- a fortress detector;
- rule exceptions beyond ruleException's three rules;
- the self-question-then-answer device;
- an imagery bank keyed on fact kinds.

Register: 72 of 444 notes are first person and about 4 self-correct. V1 and F18 forbid both, so they must be converted to reasons, not copied.

Side find (G4.5 cap): openingIdentity.ts:144 truncates the computed famous-game list with .slice(0, 2).

Process note: the scratchpad directory is shared across swarm agents. A sibling overwrote my first dump at the generic name slice.txt with other notes (#5258 onward). I discarded it and re-dumped under a unique name, verified to start at #4814 and end at #5257. Swarm agents should use unique scratch filenames.
RHYTHM: Measured on the 444 notes:
- Length: median 25 words a ply, mean 29, p90 57, max 143. Opening: median 26, mean 29. Middlegame: median 27, mean 31. Endgame: median 20, mean 24. Endgame talk is short and rule-like (active king, pawn colour, fortress, push the majority).
- Coverage: in the full-game streams he speaks on 90-100% of plies. Overall coverage within each video's span is 68%, because distilled lesson videos keep only key moments. A played game is effectively never silent.
- Their move vs yours: he says MORE on the OPPONENT's move (mean 31, p90 67) than on the student's (mean 28, p90 47). The thinking happens when they move: what it changed, what it wants, what to do about it. The student's own move often gets a short confirmation.
- Bare dictations: 8% of notes are 6 words or fewer. They come in runs through book or forced sequences (a gambit's moves dictated one by one), followed by a burst.
- Thoughts span plies: 22% of notes start mid-sentence and 15% end open. One thought regularly runs across two or three plies, so the narration is a stream, not one card per move.
- Where the bursts land: the longest notes (90-143 words) come at the first out-of-book decision (a survey of options with a reason each), at a gambit's compensation summary, and at a tactical crux with branching lines.
- Order inside a burst: what their move does or wants → what you would like and what is in the way → the tempting or natural option and why it fails → the chosen move with its line and their reply → the rule or habit, usually last. This matches F18.
- Language mix: 43% carry an explicit because/so/but link, 9% an if-then branch, 10% a question, 86% name a square, 61% address 'you', and 16% are first person (to be converted). Almost none use numbers; one 'ninety-five percent' frequency claim was the lone hit.
- [OPENING] Names the opening and says in one line what it is trying to do, often by contrast with its sibling line (the move that defines the system, and again when it turns into a named branch) e.g. This setup keeps their light bishop shut in, which the plain pawn advance would let out; the slow version fianchettoes, this one aims straight at f7. -> openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (openingIdentity.ts:85; provokes/aims/gambit/sharp/famous facts :8-14) via learnBoardTeaching.openingIdentityTeaching (learnBoardTeaching.ts:642, Learn CoachTeachPage.tsx:8470; also openingGenerator.ts:2485, reviewOpeningTheory.ts:638); naming timing openingAnnouncement (openingAnnouncement.ts:54). The sibling-contrast sentence is MISSING.
- [OPENING] Structure analogy: carries a known plan over from another opening (handle it like a standard queen's-gambit structure; French-style queen pressure on d4; King's-Indian-style f-pawn break; the knight reroute familiar from the Ruy; a Benoni-type structure minus their lost tempi; the same loose-bishop motif seen in another opening) (once the pawn structure settles, just after development) e.g. This is really a French structure where your bad bishop got out first, so play it like a French: queen to b6 hitting d4. -> PARTIAL: structure facts exist (boardStructure.describeStructure boardStructure.ts:269, isolani :296, minority/Carlsbad :305; positionReadingService.namedPawnStructure :1060; structureSignature.computeStructureSignature structureSignature.ts:65 / signatureMatchScore :165). Today the only transfer runs through corpus notes, which may not speak in Learn free play or Review (S7). A computed lane saying 'this is structure X, so X's plan applies' is MISSING.
- [census missed][OPENING] The recapture names the variation, and the other recapture is named too (a recapture fork inside book) e.g. Taking back with the e-pawn is one named line; the g-pawn recapture is a different, more weakening line, and taking with the queen would be another opening altogether. -> PARTIAL: openingBranches.branchesAt (openingBranches.ts:56) already names each database road from a fork, and refutedAlternativeCore.renderRefutedAlternative (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98) costs the sibling. No lane says 'this recapture is line X, the other is line Y'. MISSING as narration.
- [OPENING] Theory survey at a branch point: the main replies, which is the main line and which the old main line, then which one this game plays (first branch point after the book exchanges) e.g. Three sound replies exist here: the bishop out, the queen's knight to d7, or the king's knight to f6; you are choosing the third. -> PARTIAL: openingBranches.branchesAt (openingBranches.ts:56) and refutedAlternative.candidatesForPosition (refutedAlternative.ts:137) supply the options. The survey lane is MISSING.
- [census missed][OPENING] Reputation vs reality: a line with a bad name that is fine, or a famous one that is overrated; 'it looks ugly, but don't assume it loses' (an offbeat move by either side) e.g. That pawn move leaves a big hole and looks wrong, but it is a legitimate sideline with some venom if they follow up well. -> MISSING. No reputation read in src/services. It is computable as masters share and score vs engine eval vs amateur share (explorer data plus the engine).
- [OPENING] The popular wrong move at the student's level, named with why it fails (positions where club players commonly go wrong (either seat)) e.g. Players who don't know this line usually push the d-pawn one square here, and you simply get a better centre with a free square for your knight. -> refutedAlternativeCore.renderRefutedAlternative (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98; amateur source = 'players at your level' :110; candidatesFromAmateur :159), with band data from amateurPlayCache.getCachedAmateurPlay (amateurPlayCache.ts:37); safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42) after the student plays the reflex.
- [OPENING] Verdict on their departure from book: a slip, premature, or just bad, with the reason it costs them (the ply the opponent leaves book) e.g. Pushing the f-pawn this early is premature: it loosens their own king long before they have a plan for it. -> openingAnnouncement.theirOpeningVerdict (openingAnnouncement.ts:166), in Learn (CoachTeachPage.tsx:10985) and Review (coachFeatureService.ts:2037). The reason half comes from theirMoveCost (theirMoveCost.ts:60).
- [OPENING] The formula against an offbeat or troll setup: develop, take the centre they hand you, open it, then attack; don't lunge with early checks that let them block while developing; never let them close the centre (first moves against a non-theoretical system) e.g. Against this setup, don't give an early queen check — they block with a move they wanted anyway. Develop the most flexible piece first, then open the centre. -> PARTIAL: theirOpeningVerdict names the dubious move (openingAnnouncement.ts:166); ruleException covers only the early-queen rule (ruleException.ts:70). The formula as a plan, and 'a premature check helps them develop' (no match in src/services), are MISSING.
- [OPENING] What to avoid: warns, before the move, that a natural move ruins the student's structure (student to move, with a natural move whose cost is a lasting structural one) e.g. Don't reach for the e-pawn move here: they take the knight, push their pawn forward, and you are left with dark-square holes on three squares. -> PARTIAL: refutedAlternative.refutedAlternative (refutedAlternative.ts:81) costs the popular alternative. Pre-move naming is limited to deciding moments or the student's own record (nextMoveAdvice.ts:74, S3/F05). Showing the holes a forced sequence leaves, before it happens, is MISSING.
- [OPENING][TRAP] Sets a trap with bait: a quiet move that invites a natural grab, then reveals (or asks the student to decode) why the grab loses (opening positions where the greedy natural reply loses material by force) e.g. This little rook-pawn move looks like nothing, but it takes away the queen's escape square — if they grab the centre pawn now, a bishop move traps the queen. -> PARTIAL: gemFinder.findGemsForLine (gemFinder.ts:286) and openingTrapDetector.detectTrapInPosition (openingTrapDetector.ts:79) find positions where a popular move loses. - [OPENING][TRAP] Warns of the opponent's hidden trap or poisoned capture (the opponent has just made a quiet move that sets up a counter-tactic against the obvious capture) e.g. Their queen move sets a trap: if you take the centre pawn now, the line-up of their bishop and rook springs a discovered attack that wins it back. Stay a pawn up. -> Trap-ahead lane learnBoardTeaching.trapAheadTeaching (learnBoardTeaching.ts:538, Learn CoachTeachPage.tsx:9442), gated by trapLearning.trapSpeaks (trapLearning.ts:105); positionTrapScan.scanPositionForTrap (positionTrapScan.ts:126); moveInsight.moveMissed pawn-grab trap check (moveInsight.ts:382-386). A poisoned middlegame capture is caught only after the fact.
- The tempting move and why it fails (the F0c TEMPTING CHOICE role): attacking their queen walks into a pin; a knight jump exposes the king to a check; a pawn grab opens a file at your king; a natural square allows a pawn fork (a natural-looking candidate has a concrete refutation) e.g. You would love the knight jump to b4 to hit c2, but it lets their bishop check you from b5, so keep the knight home and put the queen on b6 instead. -> playCommentary.buildRejectedTempting (playCommentary.ts:497; lane 'rejectedTempting' learnTurnDoor.ts:165; Learn only, CoachTeachPage.tsx:9862); tacticalRead TemptingMove (tacticalRead.ts:51); deliberation Shortfall 'drops-material' (deliberation.ts:66); whyItFailed (whyItFailed.ts:170) for the move already played. - [OPENING] Development discipline with a board reason: not enough pieces out to threaten anything; finish development before chasing their queen; don't relax after winning material; when they lag, every developing move should threaten something (early middlegame, especially after the student wins material) e.g. You can't attack yet — only two pieces are out. - Provokes a commitment, or undermines the over-advanced pawn (the opponent has an advanced pawn chain or loose flank pawns) e.g. Push your a-pawn: if their pawn comes forward to meet it, it becomes a lasting target; if it stays, a hole opens on b5 for your bishop. -> speedRunReads.provokes (speedRunReads.ts:125); moveInsight.pawnHook (moveInsight.ts:782); a minority-attack facet exists only in Review (reviewFullData.ts:872-874). A live 'undermine the base of the chain' lane is MISSING.
- Restricts an enemy piece by taking its best square (the opening, against the opponent's best development square) e.g. A quiet h3 keeps their bishop off g4 for good — every other square it has is passive. -> moveFundamentals deny-the-square clause (moveFundamentals.ts:757-758); moveIntent 'prevents' (moveIntent.ts:124; Learn only). Census M#4.
- Prophylaxis: make the break they wanted first, take their pawn advance off the table, or guard a pawn so their next attacking move comes without tempo (the opponent has a clear next idea) e.g. Step the king to h7 now, so that when their bishop comes to e3 it no longer hits your pawn with tempo. -> moveFundamentals 'prophylaxis' (moveFundamentals.ts:45); moveIntent 'prevents' (moveIntent.ts:124). Learn only.
- Recapture choice, with its reasons (every recapture choice) e.g. Take back toward the centre — and as a bonus the c-file opens for your rook; and take with the bishop, not the queen, which their knight would chase. -> recaptureChoice (recaptureChoice.ts:103; readRecapture :56), inside studentMoveTeaching (learnBoardTeaching.ts:156), so it reaches Learn, Review (coachFeatureService.ts:1970) and chat (learnBoardTeaching.ts:759). Census M#8.
- Trades: who benefits, and why (any exchange decision) e.g. Trade their best piece for yours — you have more good pieces left; and swap off that attacking bishop before it settles on c4 aimed at f7. -> tradeJudgement (tradeJudgement.ts:40; reasons 'their-best', 'gave-best', 'attacker-gone', 'bad-bishop' at :25); tradeQuality.readTrade (tradeQuality.ts:124) and findTradeTarget (:273); pieceValueRead strongestByDelta / weakestByDelta (pieceValueRead.ts:148/:166). Note census §A group 7: the two trade verdicts disagree between Learn and Review.
- Good vs bad bishop nuances: a bishop biting on its own pawns; bad bishops that defend good pawns; pawns off your bishop's colour; a bishop outside its pawn chain (the structure is set and a bishop's scope is in question) e.g. That bishop looks buried behind its pawns, but it is holding the whole chain together — a bad bishop guarding good pawns is doing its job. -> positionReadingService.findPieceQuality (positionReadingService.ts:512; bad-bishop test :466 and :539-543); tradeJudgement reason 'bad-bishop'. 'Bad bishops defend good pawns' and the pawn-colour prescription are MISSING.
- [census missed] Names the key piece and its job, and reassigns a piece whose job is done (a piece is load-bearing, or its task is finished) e.g. Keep this bishop — it is the piece that pressures their pawn. Your other bishop has finished its job of supporting e5, so send it to a3, where it stops them castling. -> PARTIAL: pieceOptions.dutiesOf (pieceOptions.ts:63; chat path only); perturbation.computeLeansOn (perturbation.ts:42); pieceValueRead.strongestByDelta (pieceValueRead.ts:148); speedRunReads.queenGlue (speedRunReads.ts:567, queen only); moveInsight.heavyTiedDown (moveInsight.ts:1022). 'Job done, reassign the piece' is MISSING.
- [census missed] Which rook: decided by the other rook's current or future job (putting a rook on a file) e.g. Use the a-rook, because the f-rook is guarding your back rank; later, put this rook on d1 so the other can swing to c1 and pin again. -> PARTIAL: moveContrast.contrastMoves (moveContrast.ts:64; what each move leaves undefended; Review only, reviewFullData.ts:938); principleVoice.ts:76 is a static stem. The future-job reason is MISSING.
- Keeps the tension and trades on its own terms (captures available for both sides) e.g. You could take on d4, but the better move is to develop and let them take first; and you don't need to take their rook — let them make the trade that improves your bishop. -> speedRunReads.keepTension (speedRunReads.ts:49), via depthClauses.
- [census missed] Leaves what will still be there: the capture keeps, and the weakness keeps (a capture or a punishment is available but not urgent) e.g. Don't take that bishop yet — it isn't going anywhere, and taking now would open the f-file for them and remove your knight that pressures d4. Their weakening f-pawn move also keeps; finish developing first. -> PARTIAL: thinkAloud.notYet (thinkAloud.ts:145/164) covers captures only, and only when a forcing move comes first; holeAccess (moveInsight.ts:1102) times how fast a hole can be used. 'The positional weakness keeps' is MISSING.
- [census missed] Don't kick a piece toward a better square (a reflex pawn kick at a harmless enemy piece) e.g. Don't chase their knight with a6 — on b5 it attacks nothing, and kicking it only sends it back to c3, where it clamps d5. Save that pawn move for later. -> MISSING: nothing reads where a chased piece goes and whether it is better there.
- Castling decisions for either side: which wing, opposite-side logic, keeping their king in the centre, deterring castling into an attack (castling decisions) e.g. Castle queenside: you are going to attack on the kingside, so tuck your king away from the storm. Meanwhile your bishop on b5 keeps their king stuck in the centre. -> speedRunReads.castleSide (speedRunReads.ts:108); splitPosition (splitPosition.ts:14); moveInsight.castleByHand (moveInsight.ts:840); reviewConcepts king stuck in the centre (reviewConcepts.ts:166). 'Deny their castling' as a plan is MISSING; moveIntent 'prevents' may catch it.
- Pawn-break timing: the pressure has peaked; strike the overextended centre; develop before the break; don't let them close the centre; push a flank pawn only with a follow-up; push a pawn to carve out a square for a piece (middlegame break decisions) e.g. Your pressure on d4 has peaked — now open a second front with the f-pawn break. And the g-pawn advance isn't an attack: it carves out g6 for your knight. -> mastersPlanRead (mastersPlanRead.ts:83; live via learnBoardTeaching.openingPlanTeaching :627, Learn only CoachTeachPage.tsx:8638); speedRunReads.finishStarted (:370), retreatKeepsBreak (:421), positionOpened (:224); moveFundamentals 'prepare-break' (moveFundamentals.ts:59). The timing call ('now is the moment') is MISSING.
- [census missed, live] Opening the position favours the better-developed side (a choice between closing and opening the position) e.g. You actually want them to capture: it opens lines, and the side with more active pieces gains from open lines. With your lead in development, go after them. -> Review only: reviewPositionalAssessment development lead (reviewPositionalAssessment.ts:248) and reviewSacrifice (reviewSacrifice.ts:90). The live lane is MISSING.
- Plan stated as an itinerary or a known formula (once development is complete) e.g. Rook to e8, knight round to f8 and then g6, with a second route via b6 to d5 — the same reroute you use in many closed openings. -> forwardTeaching.computePieceRoute / computeSliderRoute (forwardTeaching.ts:186/:236); planArc.stepArc (planArc.ts:236); nextPlans.deriveNextPlans (nextPlans.ts:161); boardPlan.structurePlan (boardPlan.ts:84); reviewPieceItinerary (reviewPieceItinerary.ts:47; Review, played routes only).
- [census missed] Aims for the right imbalance (trade choices that shape the ending) e.g. Go for opposite-coloured bishops: in the middlegame they help the attacker, and here they make their dark-square weakness permanent. Two extra pawns win even with opposite bishops. -> PARTIAL: conceptEngine's opposite-bishops entry says 'drawish' only (conceptEngine.ts:155); pushOrHold (pushOrHold.ts:42); endgameMatchup.classifyMatchup (endgameMatchup.ts:153). Using opposite bishops as an attacking aim is MISSING.
- Ties back across moves, and re-evaluates when circumstances change (an earlier move's purpose pays off, or the situation flips) e.g. This is why the rook-pawn went to a3: now b4 cements the extra pawn. And the bishop you were keeping — the deal has changed; taking it now wrecks their structure. -> GamePromise (learnBoardTeaching.ts:883), carried on speedRunReads reads (promise field, speedRunReads.ts:36); planArc.stepArc (planArc.ts:236); motifLedger.transferClause (motifLedger.ts:31). 'Circumstances changed, the old rule no longer holds' is MISSING.
- Endgame rules stated on the board (entering an ending) e.g. With the queens gone your king is a fighting piece — march it to the centre; keep your pawns on the opposite colour to your bishop; and your extra kingside pawns aren't just running to queen, they're closing a mating net. -> moveFundamentals king-activity (moveFundamentals.ts:670-682); reviewConcepts centralise the king (reviewConcepts.ts:420); endgameTechnique (opposition :100, key squares :138, rule of the square :180, Lucena :261, Philidor :300); endgamePawnReads passerKinds (:52) and kingCourse (:166); stalemateWatch (stalemateWatch.ts:24). The pawn-colour prescription, a fortress detector and knight-dominates-bishop are MISSING.
- Conversion technique (clearly winning) e.g. If you offer the queen trade, do it so your recapturing rook lands on an active square; don't be stubborn — step the rook back, knowing they are about to win the piece back. -> conversionMethod.readConversion (conversionMethod.ts:44; steps :28); moveInsight.materialPlan (moveInsight.ts:993); tradeQuality ahead/behind (tradeQuality.ts:213/252); safetyHabits.keepPressing (safetyHabits.ts:54). 'Offer the trade actively' is MISSING.
- Habit beats: their threat first, the forcing scan, candidates before calculating, spot the loose trigger (deciding moments) e.g. Before you move, ask what their last move is doing; then list your checks and captures; then pick two or three candidates and compare them. -> methodBeat.liveMethodBeat (methodBeat.ts:296; opponent-threat stems :309-313; loose-trigger :338-345; candidates :353). Wired.
- Thinks aloud with a question, then answers it in the same breath (before the key move of a sequence) e.g. What's the thematic move here? Take on f3 — the pawn chain is already crippled. -> MISSING as a phrasing device. F05 limits real questions (that wait for an answer) to record-proven weaknesses; a self-question answered in the same breath is a different act. The one existing stem is methodBeat's 'what is their last move doing?' (methodBeat.ts:309).
- Anticipates the student's objection and answers it: a rule and its exception, voiced aloud (the move breaks a general rule) e.g. You might ask: isn't this giving up the bishop pair and moving one piece twice? True — but the centre is closed, your king is safe, and owning d4 matters more. Combining e6 with g6 is only a sin when the centre is open. -> ruleException (ruleException.ts:70) knows three rules (same minor piece twice, a shield pawn, an early queen; header :10-17) and reaches Learn, Review and chat via studentMoveTeaching (learnBoardTeaching.ts:272). The exceptions in this slice are MISSING: the bishop pair in a closed centre, colour-complex holes only when the centre is open, the same pawn twice in a closed centre, a king recapture against an undeveloped opponent, an early knight sortie with a concrete aim.
- Credits a real game or strong players' choice (F0d allows credit for a game, never for teaching) (naming an opening or a critical position) e.g. Strong players have taken this recapture up; in one top game from this very position the side with the better game even went on to lose. -> openingIdentity famous games (openingIdentity.ts:26; rendered :143-144); proGameReferenceService.getGameReferencesForOpening (proGameReferenceService.ts:23); strongChoice (strongChoice.ts:16, depersonalised). Note: openingIdentity.ts:144 caps the computed list with .slice(0, 2), which G4.5 bans.
- Practical and emotional coaching calibrated to the student's level (after a result-shaping choice or a long defence) e.g. This kind of direct play works well at your level, so don't be afraid of it; keep up the pressure, stay calm, and something will come. -> PARTIAL: refutedAlternativeCore 'players at your level' (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:110) and amateurPlayCache band data (amateurPlayCache.ts:37) could ground 'this works at your level'; safetyHabits.keepPressing (safetyHabits.ts:54). The attitude lines have no board fact behind them (census #3), so they are MISSING by design.
- Imagery tied to a board fact (naming a structural fact) e.g. A bishop walled in by its own pawns gets a stone-wall image; an over-advanced pawn gets a sticking-out image; a sole guard is the glue; a dominant knight is a monster; a blockading pawn is a speed bump. -> MISSING as a phrase bank keyed on fact kind. The rotation machinery exists (speedRunReads.ts:27 rot(), keyed on the move number), so this would follow the PHRASING tier (F6/V12).
- DO NOT COPY: the first-person register and self-correction (wherever the reference coach states a preference or corrects himself) e.g. Instead of 'I like the bishop to d3' or 'I overlooked that knight move', our coach says: the bishop to d3 is cleaner, because it keeps both wings supported. -> Not a computer. V1 forbids the coach talking about itself, and F18 says it always knows the answer. The register is governed by perspectiveRule (perspectiveRule.ts:86).

## Source 24
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[5258..5701]: 444 notes from 31 videos (240 opening, 178 middlegame, 26 endgame; 360 with the student as White). I read every note, then checked each act against all 642 acts in docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/teach.md. Reader 6 covered this slice coarsely, inside a 1,500-note pass. Every code citation below was opened and checked at the cited line.

WHAT THE COARSE READERS MISSED. 21 acts in this slice have no counterpart in the coarse digest; they are listed first and marked NEW. Most are conditions and geometry, not whole new topics:
- Not every check is good.
- A committed pawn can no longer block a check.
- Make their KING do the recapturing.
- A hole guarded only by a piece is still a hole.
- Don't capture with the piece that holds your net.
- Short-run asset, long-run liability.
- The price of opening a line, and whether the king can just leave.
- Lure their piece onto a square you can kick with tempo.
- Trade off their only developed piece.
- A bishop behind your own pawn is loaded.
- Keep their piece where it clogs their own system.
- Don't park a piece on your own open file.
- Don't cage your own piece with a pawn move.
- Keep the pawn that can still kick their piece.
- Keep a standing watch on their one break.
- Allow their break when they can't support it.
- Name the defender's method.
- Mate threat plus material threat in one move.
- Deny castling through the transit square.
- Know the pawn that stalls a storm.
- Trust the attacker count (only when the engine agrees).

Five refinements follow. They sharpen acts the coarse readers had, including the self-answered question, which is NOT an F05 question.

The canonical example for questions.md item 7 sits in this slice, at #5408-5414. I checked it with chess.js: after the knight takes on e5 with check, the pinning bishop on g4 is attacked by the knight and the queen and defended once. By material count that sequence nets pawns, not a piece. So under F04 it is a pattern taught with its conditions, not a trap, and David's first gem may need the engine to clear F04's piece bar.

CODE FINDINGS on the way (verified):
1. V14 caps:
   - CoachTeachPage.tsx:220 caps the tempting-move beat at 2 per game.
   - positionalRead.ts:225 caps the open files it names at two (`.slice(0, 2)`).
   - positionalRead.ts:396 and :399 cap the colour-complex squares it names at two (`.slice(0, 2)`).
2. playCommentary.ts:533 silences the tempting-check refutation whenever the student stays 2 pawns up, which is exactly when the reference coach says "no reason to give material back".
3. theirMoveCost.ts:120-121 gates lost castling on queens being on, so the forced king recapture after an early queen trade is silent by design.
4. reviewSacrifice.ts:113-134 calls a king "stuck" with no castling check. The legal test already exists at positionalRead.ts:147.
5. droppedJob (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63) is reached only from the explorer path. Deliberation's shortfalls (deliberation.ts:66) can't voice "that piece was guarding X".
6. learnMemory.ts:270-277 clears the record of taught terms every game, while V18 wants it kept per student.
7. Reader 6's gemCrushLines.ts citations are stale: :554, :572 and :305 should be :564 trapAheadAt, :582 gemMoveSignal and :311 computeGemCrush.

CORPUS HAZARDS THAT SHIP (S7: "teach me X" serves voiced walkthroughs first, voicedWalkthroughs.ts:1-10, :140):
- One ~820-word note (#5327) is a single node idea at src/data/voiced-walkthroughs.json:77472. It narrates about 14 later moves as if played, in the first person.
- Two videos are pure play-by-play (#5630-5676, #5472-5511). They ship board restatements such as voiced-walkthroughs.json:38982.
- Thirteen cross-ply fragments ship split across nodes. The walkthrough builder has no whole-sentence guard; noteIsWholeSentence runs only in danyaTeachingService.ts:113.
- These all ship in voiced walkthroughs and matchups: engine talk (#5308, #5311, #5312), ratings and numbers (#5279, #5313, #5339, #5567), a named coach credited with analysis (#5555, F0d), and self-critique (#5572, #5628, #5686).
- voicedDepersonalized.test.ts:12-25 bans none of these.
RHYTHM: These figures are measured over all 444 notes:
- Words per note: median 18, mean 23.7, p10 6, p90 40.
- By length: 31% are 9 words or fewer, 63% are 10-49, 4.7% are 50-99 and 1.1% are 100+.

Two videos skew the low end:
- jwFOi039eeg: 47 of 47 notes are 9 words or fewer.
- ihv2TK04WPg: 34 of 40 are.
- They are play-by-play with no teaching.
- Without them: 357 notes, median 23, bare move-calls 14% (29% with them). Opening median 23, middlegame 22.

He speaks on nearly every ply (V11):
- 340 of 413 consecutive same-video pairs skip no ply.
- 51 skip one, 22 skip two or more.
- Own move median 20 words vs 15 on the opponent's move. He says more as his own move is played, and thinks while their move is on the board.
- 44% of notes over 9 words carry an explicit link (because, so, but, instead, the point, rather than, if).
- 13 notes (3%) end mid-thought and finish on the next ply.

Long monologues: only 5 notes reach 90+ words (#5322, #5327 at about 820, #5332, #5467, #5545). All sit at plies 6-20. They lay out a whole plan or a whole lesson at one decision point.

Order inside a long note (#5286, #5322, #5408, #5420, #5545):
1. What their move did or threatens.
2. What the student is probably thinking (a worry or a tempting move).
3. Why that falls short, with a short line.
4. The move and its one deciding reason.
5. The line played out with their reply.
6. A habit or tip to close.

The opening is explained move by move with the theory status. Middlegame decision points get the deliberation. Forced replies get 3-8 words. Only 3% of notes contain a question mark, and every one is answered in the same breath.
- NEW - Judges a check by the opponent's best answer: a check is good only if the block or king move doesn't hand something back; chooses between two checks by what each wins (Converting a won position; any check that 'develops with tempo'; choosing between checks) e.g. When you're already a piece up, the bishop check on b5 looks like free development. But their c-pawn blocks it while hitting the bishop, and the tactic that follows only swaps two of your minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so you'd hand material back for nothing. Elsewhere: of two queen checks, pick the one that collects a pawn on the way. -> PARTIAL. playCommentary.ts:497 buildRejectedTempting refutes a tempting capture or check from the multipv lines (at least 1.5 pawns worse). Two problems: playCommentary.ts:533 skips it whenever the student still stands 2+ pawns up after the check, which is #5286's exact case; and CoachTeachPage.tsx:220 caps the beat at 2 per game (applied at CoachTeachPage.tsx:9852), a count cap that V14 forbids. Choosing between two checks: MISSING.
- NEW - Notices that a pawn already committed can no longer block a future check, so that check becomes the target of your next moves (When the opponent pushes the pawn that used to be their interposing pawn) e.g. Their c-pawn has already gone to c5, so a later bishop check on b5 can't be met by c6. With their queen and king lined up on the e-file, your quiet moves are building toward exactly that check. -> MISSING. checkMethod.ts:32 reads only the student's own answers when they are already in check (answer kinds at checkMethod.ts:46). latentDanger.ts:87 reads alignments against the student's own king and queen. Nothing counts the opponent's future interpositions.
- NEW - Makes THEIR king do the recapturing: a queen trade that strips castling and leaves the king badly placed even with queens off (Early opening exchanges where the queens can come off on the king's file) e.g. Take on e4. After the pawn trade you swap queens with a capture on d1, their king has to take back, and it sits on d1 for the rest of the game: no castling, and in its own pieces' way. -> PARTIAL, blocked by a gate. theirMoveCost.ts:117-130 names 'castling given up', but only while queens are on (theirMoveCost.ts:120-121, reasoned at :118-119), so this exact case is silenced by design. recaptureChoice.ts:91 flags 'would give up castling' only for the student's own king. The gate should key on phase (an early queenless middlegame with every minor piece on is not an ending), not on whether queens are on.
- NEW - Answers the objection 'but they cover that square': a hole guarded only by a PIECE is still a hole; occupying it forces the guard to trade itself, and trades help the side that is ahead (When the student hesitates over an outpost an enemy piece watches; trades near a hole) e.g. Yes, their dark bishop watches d6. That doesn't fix the hole. Put the knight there anyway, and if the bishop takes it that's one more trade, which is what you want when you're a queen up. That's also why you give up the bishop and keep the knight. -> PARTIAL. outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge and outpost.ts:39 isOutpost already count only PAWN guards, so the square is computed as a hole. speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole prefers the knight. tradeJudgement.ts:74 says trades favour the side ahead. MISSING: the joined sentence (a piece guard can be traded off, a pawn guard can't).
- NEW - Before grabbing, checks whether the capturing unit is part of your net: taking with it lets the trapped piece escape (After trapping a piece, when they throw in a counter-attack or desperado) e.g. Their knight jumps to g5 and hits your queen. Taking it with the f-pawn feels natural, but that pawn is what covers e5, the trapped queen's only exit. Step your queen back to e2 instead, and their queen stays caged. -> PARTIAL. refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63 droppedJob yields exactly this reason (the pawn on f4 was guarding e5). It is fed only from the explorer-popularity path (refutedAlternative.ts:127, refutedAlternativeCore.ts:243). The middlegame deliberation (deliberation.ts:144) has shortfall kinds drops-material, trades-queens, clearly-worse and less-precise (deliberation.ts:66), and filters out alternatives with no material proof (deliberation.ts:278). So the reason never speaks there. Wire droppedJob into deliberation.
- NEW - Separates the short run from the long run: a pawn that helps now becomes a weakness once the position changes (Structural pawn moves justified only by a temporary job) e.g. Their f-pawn on f4 looks good right now because it props up the knight on e5. Once their king castles on that side, that advanced pawn turns into a liability, so file it away as a later target. -> MISSING. moveInsight.ts:523 weakenedBy and theirMoveCost.ts:60 read only the board right after the move. Nothing projects a pawn's worth past the opponent's coming castling. Inputs exist: kingSafety.ts:202 castleRoute (which castling is coming) and positionReadingService.ts:400 findPawnBreaks.
- NEW - Sets the price of opening lines: a pawn or two is fine; a whole piece only if mate is forced, because the king can simply castle away from the open file (Before a sacrifice whose point is an open line; using a large material lead) e.g. A queen up, shed a pawn to open the centre, since in a closed position the queen has nothing to do. But giving a knight to rip open the e-file buys nothing: their king castles to the other wing, and the open file has no one left to attack. -> PARTIAL. reviewSacrifice.ts:113 enemyKingStuckInCenter returns 'stuck' from fullmove, a central king and an open centre file only (reviewSacrifice.ts:134). There is no castling check, so it can call a king stuck when the king can just castle. The legal test already exists in positionalRead.ts:147 castleIsOneMoveAway (legality read at :156-168) and kingSafety.ts:202 castleRoute. reviewSacrifice.ts:44 sacrificeCompensation is Review-only. MISSING: the price rule.
- NEW - Chooses the capture that leaves THEIR recapturing piece on a square you can kick with tempo (Opening captures where one recapture is forced) e.g. Capture on e5 with the pawn instead of developing. Their knight has to take back on e5, and from there your f-pawn and then your e-pawn chase it, each kick a free developing move for you. A piece in the centre with no pawn behind it gets kicked. -> MISSING as a reason for a choice. Inputs: outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge (here the inverse: a pawn CAN kick it) and tempoCount.ts:32 (counts their repeat moves afterwards). moveInsight.ts:411-421 is the mirror for the student's own piece ('don't hand them a tempo').
- NEW - Trades off the opponent's only developed piece, which resets their development (Opening gambits; when the opponent has one active piece) e.g. Developing the bishop looks like it drops a pawn, and it does. But it's going to trade off their knight, the only piece they've brought out, and after that you're far ahead in development. -> MISSING. tradeJudgement.ts:25 TradeReason has no development reason. development.ts:67 developedMinorCount supplies the before and after counts.
- NEW - A bishop aimed behind your own advanced pawn is loaded: when the pawn moves, the line opens all at once (Middlegame plans with a central pawn wedge) e.g. Keep the central pawn as an anchor and put your bishop behind it. For now the pawn shields the diagonal, but the bishop is loaded: the moment the pawn advances, the line onto their king opens. -> MISSING. latentDanger.ts:87 detectLatentDanger reads only the student's own king or queen behind a shield (the defensive side). tacticsDetector.ts:571 findDiscoveredAttacks reads only discoveries available now.
- NEW - Keeps the opponent's piece committed to a square where it blocks their own system's pawn plan (Against fixed systems in the opening) e.g. Against the London, push your d-pawn one square so their knight is content to stay on c3. That's exactly the square their c-pawn needs for the usual pawn triangle, so the whole setup jams. -> MISSING. speedRunReads.ts:125 provokes covers only provoking a PAWN advance. theirMoveCost.ts:94-115 covers their pawn shutting in their own bishop, not their piece blocking their own pawn. A system's standard pawn squares could come from mastersPlanRead.ts:83.
- NEW - Doesn't park a piece on your own open file (Attacks along a half-open file) e.g. The bishop to f4 looks active, but it plugs the f-file your rook is using. - NEW - Checks that your own pawn move doesn't cage your own piece (Pawn moves next to your own bishop or knight) e.g. Not g3: after their pawn comes to g5, your bishop on h4 has nowhere to go. Drop the bishop back to g3 yourself instead. -> PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:957 noRetreat finds a piece that one enemy pawn push would hit with no safe square, which would catch this if run on the CANDIDATE's resulting position.
