## Source 25
I re-read every note in voiced-teachings notes 5702-6145 (444 notes, 27 videos). Before keeping any act I searched the full 12-reader digest (docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/teach.md) for it by keyword. The two coarse readers whose ranges cover this slice already caught most of what it does: outposts and routes, recapture choice, trading on your own terms, keeping the queens on against a stuck king, kicking the central knight, checks from a distance, in-between moves, ignoring the slower wing, not h4 before they castle.

I am returning 24 entries: 20 acts that are not in the digest, and 4 sharpenings of acts it already has, each with a new code finding (structural threat, the in-between move's record half, the development bind, a break that isn't a threat).

Highest value for the opening (F02):
- a piece in front of its own pawn turns a neighbouring pawn into an isolated pawn in all but name (5748);
- a resource that bites only after their commitment, such as the check on b4 saved until their knight is on c3 (5905);
- a capture that is sound only with one specific follow-up (6035);
- a pawn grab refuted because the queen trade costs your king castling (6039);
- preparing a recapture with a piece so a pin can't damage your pawns (6023);
- the king hiding behind the attacker's own bishop in the Bxf7 attack, and the forcing move that clears it (6045-6046).

CODE FINDINGS (read-only). Line numbers are against HEAD f00cf6a. Another session has uncommitted edits in the worktree: positionReadingService.ts (+18 lines after line 258) and CoachTeachPage.tsx.

1. F4/F5, a computer that teaches but never records.
- The in-between move is taught (thinkAloud.ts:145, called at :273; moveInsight.ts:642, called only from PuzzleBoard.tsx:652).
- It is never posed: positionPosed's comment says it covers the autopilot recapture (moveInsight.ts:731-732), but its body does not (:743-761).
- It is never classified: 'zwischenzug', 'deflection' and 'interference' are TacticType members (types/index.ts:1714, 1709, 1713) with no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64). A miss in a real game is filed under another motif or 'tactical_sequence' (missedTacticService.ts:770-808).
- Result: from games, the heat map can never turn these red or green.

2. V14, a cap that changes other computers' answers.
- findPieceQuality sorts good notes first and keeps four (positionReadingService.ts:604-605).
- tradeQuality.readTrade (tradeQuality.ts:151-153) and pieceValueRead.ratedPoor (pieceValueRead.ts:504-507) look up the traded or questioned piece in that capped list. With four good pieces on the board, a bad bishop or rim knight is silently missing.
- findWeakSquares caps its hole list the same way (:650-651), and findColorComplexWeakness filters that already-capped list (:679, :688-689).

3. Two detectors skip what the reference coach counts.
- The overload detector skips duties to anything worth under 3, including pawns (tacticsDetector.ts:699).
- The skewer detector deliberately ignores a pawn behind and requires the front piece to outrank the attacker (tacticsDetector.ts:284-293). So the rook skewer of an undefended bishop with a pawn behind (5827) is never named.

CORPUS DEFECTS, if spoken (D10 / V1 / V8):
- Two notes are anchored a ply early and say the student's next move as if already played: 5978 (on White's Be2 it says you develop the bishop to g7) and 5980 (on White's castling it tells a Black student 'you castle').
- 5753 is anchored after h3 but treats h3 as hypothetical.
- noteSeatMatches checks only the declared seat (noteAnchorIntegrity.ts:435-443), so none of these is caught there. I did not trace whether the anchor checks catch them.
- 5869 has a corrupted join ('setup.against') plus a first-person anecdote that names a player.
- 18 notes are in the first person; 5 mention ratings (5704, 5742, 5830, 5971, 5983).
- The 53 'teaches' labels are terse tags, some with move symbols, and usePhaseNarration joins them straight after the note (usePhaseNarration.ts:488-491). The same labels would make a ready concept vocabulary (R5, V18).

FOR F04 (Bishop's Opening): the corpus holds one video on 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 (39 notes, from Black's side, steering into an Italian). There is little to borrow for the hand-built Bishop's Opening gems, and this slice's 2.Bc4-against-the-Sicilian game is pure move narration.
RHYTHM: Measured on this slice (444 notes, 27 videos; 223 opening / 190 middlegame / 31 endgame; 249 notes on the student's move, 195 on the opponent's). Words per note: median 17 (p10 6, p90 42, mean 21); opening 16 (p90 39), middlegame 20 (p90 46), endgame 12 (p90 29). Bands: 1-9 words 30%, 10-24 37%, 25-49 28%, 50-99 5%, plus one 198-word lecture (5911). Own move median 18 words, opponent's move 14.

Two whole videos are bare move narration with no reason anywhere: a Rossolimo (7 notes) and a 2.Bc4-against-the-Sicilian game (55 notes, in which the student loses the queen and a rook with no word on why). They hold 56 of the 134 bare notes. Without them the median is 20 words and 21% of notes are bare, the same share the 1,500-note reader found. Do not copy those videos (V11).

Ply coverage: of 417 consecutive same-video pairs, 74% skip no ply, 19% skip one, 8% skip two or more.

TWO DELIVERY MODES, inversely related, measured per video. Live play-by-play videos comment on 87-100% of plies at a median of 6-24 words. Lecture-style videos comment on 28-45% of plies at a median of 40-48 words: in one quiet Carlsbad game, 13 notes cover 46 plies and 12 of them run 41-69 words. In quiet structural play he does not shorten; he skips the routine ply and spends the words on the next decision. For our coach (V11, never silent) that means a short clause on the routine ply and the full thought at the decision.

Where he goes long (11 notes of 60+ words, none in the endgame):
- the opponent's opening inaccuracy (5748, 84 words: verdict, what it costs them, the structural reason, the sounder set-up, the principle);
- a level position where he has to manufacture chances (5819);
- the conversion recipe after winning material (5863);
- quiet structural decisions (5947-5955);
- one lecture (5911) that folds into a single move a plan, the answer to their tactical try, a recapture rule, a calculation habit, a sacrifice with its conditions, and a mating net.
5 of the 11 sit on the OPPONENT's move: he lays out the student's coming choice while their move is on the board.

Links: 47% of notes over 9 words carry an explicit because / so / but / instead / the point / since / otherwise / rather than / unless / if. 13 notes ask a question and 12 answer it in the same breath; one class-style question is left hanging across two notes (5753-5754). One sentence runs across four plies (5851-5854). The endgame is terse: technique or a result, often one clause.
- A piece standing in front of its own pawn takes that pawn's jobs away, most sharply when the blocked pawn was the only one that could ever support a neighbour: the neighbour becomes an isolated pawn in all but name (A developing move (theirs or the student's) lands directly in front of an own pawn in the opening: c3 in front of c2, f3 in front of f2, a bishop in front of the g-pawn) e.g. After the early pawn swaps on d5, their knight comes to c3, right in front of the c2-pawn. No pawn can now ever come to c3 to back up d4, so while the knight stands there d4 is as weak as an isolated pawn. The sturdier set-up was the bishop to d3 and then c3, a pawn guarding a pawn. -> MISSING. boardStructure.ts:127-134 calls a pawn isolated only when no own pawn stands on an adjacent file, so d4 with c2 behind the knight never counts; describeConcessions reports only a true new isolani (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:745-746); theirMoveCost's kinds are hole / bishop-shut / castling / structure and its hole and bishop checks run only for pawn moves (theirMoveCost.ts:23, :73, :95); concessionBeat's DrawbackKind has no blocked-pawn kind (concessionBeat.ts:31-36). Buildable on findWeakPawns (positionReadingService.ts:1176): an adjacent-file pawn whose advance square holds its own piece gives no support.
- Hold a resource in reserve until the opponent's commitment makes it bite, and say the condition: a pin, a queen sortie, a lever or a pawn freeze is often worth a move only after one specific enemy move (Opening moves where a known motif's target has not committed yet; quiet middlegames where the opponent's break is still a move or two away) e.g. Don't give the check on b4 yet. That bishop earns its move once their knight stands on c3, because then taking it doubles their pawns; with only e3 played they simply block on d2 and you have spent a move for nothing. In the same spirit, the a4 freeze against their b-pawn can wait until that advance is really coming; bring a rook over first. -> MISSING as a general read. speedRunReads.threatStronger keeps only a CAPTURE hanging (speedRunReads.ts:144); moveIntent says what a played move prevents or prepares, never 'this works once they play X' (moveIntent.ts:124); pinGeometry.pinBites prices a pin only in material (pinGeometry.ts:178-187), so the structural payoff that makes Bb4 worth a move (the capture that doubles their pawns) is never computed, although tradeQuality.recaptureDamage already classifies doubled / isolated / king-cover for a recapture (tradeQuality.ts:71).
- A conditional verdict on the move itself: this capture or commitment is sound only if one specific follow-up comes next, said before the follow-up is played (Opening captures and commitments whose soundness hinges on the very next move) e.g. Their capture on e4 is not a mistake, but it binds them to one answer: the ...e5 strike against your two centre pawns. The coach says so on the capture, then credits them when the strike arrives. -> PARTIAL. criticalMoment.readCriticalMoment counts how many moves hold on the CURRENT board (criticalMoment.ts:164); run on the board after their capture it would show that only one reply keeps the balance, but no lane speaks the forward 'fine only if' verdict on the capture itself.
- Refute a pawn grab by what it does to your king, not by material: the capture lets them trade queens on the d-file and your king has to take back, losing castling (Early central captures that open the d-file while both queens face each other on it) e.g. Taking on e5 is still wrong here. There is no check to fear any more, but the capture lets them swap queens on d1, your king must recapture, and it is stuck in the centre for the rest of the game. Develop instead. -> PARTIAL. recaptureChoice says 'would give up castling' only when the recapturing piece is itself the king (recaptureChoice.ts:91); speedRunReads.forceConcession names lost castling only for the OPPONENT after the student's forcing move (speedRunReads.ts:524); refutedAlternativeCore.renderRefutedAlternative refutes by a tactic concept, a proven material line, a dropped job or a cost in words (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98-148), with no castling-loss reason.
- Prepare the recapture before the capture comes: put a piece where it can take back, so their capture cannot damage your pawn structure (The opponent threatens a capture whose pawn recapture would double or isolate your pawns) e.g. Their bishop pins your knight on c6 and wants to double your c-pawns. The queen to b6 answers that in advance: if the bishop takes on c6, the queen takes back and your pawns stay whole. -> MISSING. recaptureChoice runs only after a capture has happened (recaptureChoice.ts:103); moveIntent.whatItDoes describes what a move prepares only as castling, hitting a target or taking a file (moveIntent.ts:429-460); tradeQuality.recaptureDamage knows a pawn recapture would double or isolate (tradeQuality.ts:71) but nothing asks it before the capture.
- Recapture reasons the coach gives that the recapture computer cannot say: take back with the piece that keeps your options open; trade with check first and let them show how they take back; recapture with the pawn so a square opens for your other piece (Every exchange with more than one recapture, and exchanges where giving check first forces their choice) e.g. Take back on d4 with the pawn: the knight would commit too early, while after the pawn you can still choose between grabbing on e4 and a quiet rook move. Later, swap rooks on e1 with check first and see which piece they take back with. And if your knight is ever exchanged on e4, recapture with the d-pawn so d5 is free for the other knight. -> PARTIAL. readRecapture's reasons are: opens a file for the rook, toward the centre, doubles, isolates, frees the bishop, the knight lands centrally, loses the piece, the queen gets hit with tempo, gives up castling (recaptureChoice.ts:60-92). - A threat to wreck the structure counts as a threat: a move that unmasks a capture which would double the pawns in front of their king (Moves that unmask a bishop or rook onto a knight guarded by a pawn next to the enemy king) e.g. Pushing the c-pawn opens your b7-bishop's diagonal, and now it threatens to take on f3; if the g-pawn takes back, the pawns in front of their castled king are wrecked. -> PARTIAL. - Whose key pawn advance lands first decides the opening: when one side never finds time for its thematic push, the other side plays it instead and takes the space (Mirror or reversed structures where both sides aim at the same central advance) e.g. This reversed King's Indian is dangerous for them precisely because they never get time for ...e5, so you are the one who plants a pawn on e5, and the space and the kingside attack are yours. -> MISSING. planRace races only two passed pawns or one shared open file (planRace.ts:26-40, detectPlanRace :180); tempoCount counts their repeated moves (tempoCount.ts:32); moveIntent's PREVENTS can say a move stops their push (moveIntent.ts:124) but not whose key advance arrives first.
- Name the shelter on a line: a king can hide behind a piece standing on the attacking line, even the attacker's OWN piece; the cure is to move that shield off the line with a threat so the line opens with tempo (Right after a sacrifice or check when the defending king steps behind the attacker's piece; also when your queen recaptures behind your own pawn so the pawn shields it) e.g. After the bishop takes on f7 with check, the king steps to f8 and hides behind your own bishop. Your rook on f1 looks up a file blocked by your knight on f3 and your bishop on f7, so moving the knight uncovers nothing yet. First take the bishop off the f-file with a move that demands an answer (it steps to e6 and offers itself again); then the knight's move uncovers the rook against the king. -> MISSING. findDiscoveredAttacks reads only the first two pieces on a ray and drops it when the second is your own (tacticsDetector.ts:571, :583-585), so a rook behind two of its own pieces in front of the king is invisible; latentDanger.detectLatentDanger is the student-side mirror, with at most one own shield in front of a king or queen (latentDanger.ts:87, :113-119). Nothing names the king sheltering behind the attacker's piece or proposes moving that shield with a threat; the tempo test at tacticsDetector.ts:607-610 is the reusable part.
- The in-between move instead of the automatic recapture (caught by earlier readers), listed here because the record half is missing (Inside exchanges, whenever the recapture looks automatic) e.g. Their bishop takes on e4, correctly, and you don't take back on reflex: push the d-pawn to d6 first, forking queen and minor piece while their bishop still hangs. In another game, after their bishop takes on c3, the pawn takes on c6 instead and they must lose the queen or the bishop. -> TEACH half computed: thinkAloud.notYet (thinkAloud.ts:145, called :273) and moveInsight.autopilotRecapture (moveInsight.ts:642, whose only production caller is the puzzle wrong-try line, PuzzleBoard.tsx:652). RECORD half MISSING (F4/F5): positionPosed's comment lists the autopilot recapture (moveInsight.ts:731-732) but its body never poses it (moveInsight.ts:743-761); 'zwischenzug' is a TacticType (types/index.ts:1714) with no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64), so detectTacticType files a missed in-between move from a real game under another motif or 'tactical_sequence' (missedTacticService.ts:770-808). The same holds for 'deflection' and 'interference' (types/index.ts:1709, :1713).
- Maintenance trade: not every exchange wins something; when your pawn is attacked and cannot be held, trading it off is just keeping the balance, and the coach says that (Central tension where your pawn is attacked more often than it can be defended) e.g. Your e5-pawn is attacked and can't be kept, so take on d4. The trade wins nothing; it simply stops you losing a pawn, and now you get on with development. -> MISSING. tradeJudgement returns null on any pawn capture (tradeJudgement.ts:47) and its reasons are their-best / gave-best / ahead / behind / bad-bishop / attacker-gone (tradeJudgement.ts:25); speedRunReads.keepTension goes silent when the capture IS the engine's move (speedRunReads.ts:57), so nothing explains why releasing the tension is right here. The fact is one exchange count away (legalSeeGainFor, positionReadingService.ts:212).
- A trade whose real point is the recapture: the piece that takes back abandons a defensive duty (Exchange offers where the recapturing piece is the only guard of something (the back rank, a piece)) e.g. Offer the queen trade on d4 even though trading feels passive: when their rook takes back, it leaves the back rank, and from then on their knight on e5 cannot move without allowing mate on the back rank. The next moves pile on that frozen knight. -> MISSING. tradeJudgement and tradeQuality.readTrade judge the pieces traded (tradeJudgement.ts:25; tradeQuality.ts:124), not what the recapturing piece leaves; findRemovableGuards is capture-the-guard (tacticsDetector.ts:630); weakenedBy tracks pieces losing guards, not an empty back rank (moveInsight.ts:523); 'deflection' has no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64).
- Diagnose why their position is stuck: one weak pawn ties down the piece that must develop, so every developing move costs material except one; take that one away and they have nothing (The opponent's undeveloped minor is the only guard of an attacked pawn) e.g. Their dark bishop can only come out with tempo on g5; anywhere else and their b2-pawn drops. Step your queen off that bishop's line in advance and they are left without a useful move: the whole position hangs on b2. -> PARTIAL. pieceOptions.dutiesOf finds the duty, pawns included (pieceOptions.ts:63), and computePieceOptions refutes each square (pieceOptions.ts:126), but its only caller is the chat question path (coach/coachService.ts:1507). findOverloadedPieces skips any target worth under 3 (tacticsDetector.ts:699), so 'their bishop alone guards b2' never reads as a tie; speedRunReads.takeTheSting defuses a threat to YOUR piece (speedRunReads.ts:400), not their only tempo move.
- Duty parity: before treating a tied defender as a cost, look at what the attacker is tied to; if their attacking piece is just as bound to the attack, it is a fair trade of duties (An enemy heavy piece probes a pawn and the cheapest adequate guard is a rook) e.g. If their queen comes after your b-pawn, guard it with a rook. Yes, the rook is now stuck on defence, but their queen is just as stuck on the attack, and neither piece does anything else. -> MISSING. moveInsight.heavyTiedDown flags only your own heavy piece as a sole guard, as a cost (moveInsight.ts:1022); pieceOptions.dutiesOf lists a defender's duties (pieceOptions.ts:63); nothing reads what the attacking piece is tied to.
- Before kicking a piece with a pawn, check where it lands: a careless kick hands it a better square. Cover its landing square first, then chase it toward the rim (An enemy knight sits well placed in front of your pawns and you want to drive it back) e.g. Pushing a pawn at their knight right away would only send it to a fine new square in your camp. Close that square with another pawn first, then chase the knight into the corner with the rook-pawn, and only then advance the f-pawn: one pawn shuts the door, the other does the pushing. -> MISSING. moveInsight.noRetreat is about your own piece facing a pawn push (moveInsight.ts:957); findTrappedPieces needs the piece already attacked (tacticsDetector.ts:468-472); no read scores a pawn kick by the kicked piece's best landing square (outpost.isOutpost on the board after the kick would answer it, outpost.ts:39).
- The semi-outpost: a central square an enemy pawn could challenge only one day and at some cost; worth routing a knight to instead of opening the centre (Closed or semi-closed centres with no true outpost available) e.g. Rather than breaking in the centre, which would only open lines for them, send the knight to d5. It is not a true outpost, since their e-pawn could one day come to e4, but for now it is a fine central post. -> MISSING. outpost.isOutpost is binary: any enemy pawn that can ever reach an attacking square disqualifies the square (outpost.ts:22-39); findPieceQuality praises only a pawn-supported knight on a true outpost (positionReadingService.ts:526-535).
- A pawn break whose purpose is to get rid of YOUR weak pawn: trading off the backward pawn removes the target the game was revolving around (You carry a backward or isolated pawn and an advance can trade it off safely) e.g. Once their knight drops back, push d5: it is the direct way to get rid of your weak d6-pawn, and the open centre then favours your better bishop. -> MISSING as a reason. findPawnBreaks admits a break by pawn contact and a safe landing (positionReadingService.ts:400, :425-435) and never says what the break fixes; findWeakPawns lists backward pawns (positionReadingService.ts:1176) but no read compares them before and after the break.
- Name the square that will become weak once the pawn guarding it is traded away, before the exchange happens (Pawn exchanges near the enemy king or in the centre that will remove a pawn guard) e.g. Take on g6 with the h-pawn: besides opening the h-file, it is aimed at e6, which loses its pawn guard once their f7-pawn is drawn away to recapture. -> MISSING as a forward read. theirMoveCost's hole and moveInsight.holeAccess read only the hole a move just made (theirMoveCost.ts:72-91; moveInsight.ts:1102); weakenedBy tracks pieces, not squares (moveInsight.ts:523). Running outpost.noPawnCanChallenge on the end of the engine's exchange line would give it (outpost.ts:22).
- Restriction as an asset: a piece that takes away the enemy rooks' entry squares is worth keeping and defending, and the coach names that as the bonus of the move (A minor piece lands deep in the enemy camp on squares their rooks need) e.g. Taking on c2 wins a pawn, and the bishop there also keeps their rooks off b1 and d1. A piece that good is worth protecting rather than trading. -> PARTIAL. moveIntent's square-denial branch names ONE of their engine-preferred moves that the played move now covers (moveIntent.ts:464-487); moveFundamentals' prophylaxis covers only a pawn push denying an enemy minor a square (moveFundamentals.ts:732-737). Nothing names 'their rooks can no longer use these squares' as a lasting asset of the piece.
- A self-block you control: a pawn put on your bishop's colour restricts it for now, but it holds squares the bishop cannot reach and a capture can reopen the diagonal whenever you choose, so it is no real concession (Committal central pawn moves onto your own bishop's colour) e.g. Pushing to d5 seems to bury your b7-bishop, and for the moment it does. But the pawn controls e4, the bishop will protect a pawn that later recaptures on e4, and you can reopen the diagonal any time by taking on c4. No hurry: finish developing first. -> MISSING. bishopBlockingPawns names the pawn in the bishop's way (positionReadingService.ts:484); the bad-bishop note ignores a bishop still at home (positionReadingService.ts:546-547); theirMoveCost's bishop-shut kind reports only the cost (theirMoveCost.ts:94-115). Nothing reads that a capture is available to reopen the line, or that the blocking pawn is guarded by that bishop.
- Judge the opponent's pawn break by its answer: if the pawn it hits can simply advance past it, the break is not a threat yet (The opponent prepares a pawn break against your centre) e.g. Their ...c5 break doesn't worry you: if it comes, d5 runs past it and gains space. -> PARTIAL. falseAlarm needs a concrete threat from detectNewThreat (falseAlarm.ts:37, :52-53; kinds mate / fork / capture at groundedAnswer.ts:6865), so a quiet pawn break never reaches it; moveIntent reads only a move already played (moveIntent.ts:124).
- Count the enemy king's flight squares: a king with none means the next check may be mate, so bring the heavy pieces in (Kingside attacks after the shelter has been broken) e.g. After the h-file trades their king steps to f7 and has no square left at all; that is the signal to bring your queen in. -> MISSING as a standing read. kingSafetyRead counts shield pawns and open files, not flight squares (positionReadingService.ts:1760); kingAttack's kinds are strips-shelter / removes-defender / adds-attacker / heads-for-king / opens-lines / opens-file (kingAttack.ts:26); moveInsight.escapeSquareFirst counts the king's squares only for one check the engine is about to give (moveInsight.ts:701, :716); the king-safety concept text tells the student to count flight squares (conceptEngine.ts:782) but no computer does.
- Post-mortem on a piece: name the piece that did nothing all game and why its planned road was a dead end (When the game is decided, looking back over the opponent's plan) e.g. Looking back, their knight on a6 never did anything: its only road ran through c5, and their own pawn ended up standing there. -> MISSING. thinkAloud.opponentHabits counts only minors still at home and repeated moves (thinkAloud.ts:180); pieceScope and strongestWeakestPiece read one position (positionReadingService.ts:787, :1140). A per-game history of each piece's scope would answer 'idle all game'.
- Name the small pawn formation a set-up builds and what it is for (Set-up building moves in the opening) e.g. a6 together with b5 and c6 makes a small pawn triangle that backs the queenside expansion; the same triangle in other set-ups gives the dark bishop a safe home on d6. -> MISSING. namedPawnStructure knows the French chain, the closed centre, the isolated queen's pawn and hanging pawns only (positionReadingService.ts:1060-1134).

## Source 26
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[6146..6589]: 444 notes from 30 videos, every note read (dumped by index and replayed with chess.js). 61 teaching acts catalogued below, each mapped to a computer in src/services with file:line, or marked MISSING / PARTIAL.

HEADLINE. Many of the reference coach's habits already have a computer, built since the speed-run study:
- speedRunReads.ts: 27 reads
- thinkAloud.ts: lineAchieves, sayLine, notYet, obviousStopFlaw
- deliberation, moveIntent, opponentIntent, bluffDetector, falseAlarm, refutedAlternativeCore, conversionMethod, stalemateWatch, tempoCount, ruleException, theirMoveCost, openingIdentity, theirOpeningVerdict

What this slice adds is the finer layer the coarse readers missed. Eight clusters:
1. POSITIONAL reasons for rejecting a candidate. Deliberation only rules a move out for dropping material, being clearly worse or less precise, or trading queens (deliberation.ts:66). It never rejects for cutting a defensive contact, giving up the bishop pair, blocking a future rook file, or conceding a square.
2. Pin nuances. A pin can ban a capture while still allowing a push. The pinned piece stops counting as a defender. Pins can be compared, kept through a recapture, or made permanent once the bishop that could challenge the pinner is gone.
3. The IMMUNE piece: it can be taken, but taking it walks into a fork.
4. Restricting an ENEMY piece with your own pawn.
5. Trade geometry: which side's file the trade opens, keep pieces on when you have more space, trade to defuse an attack, and trade only when the trade comes free.
6. The goal → obstacle → remove-it chain (F0c, not built).
7. About eight missing habits, for example: start calculating with the simplest move; when a file opens toward the kings, look for checks on the second or seventh rank; before grabbing with the queen, list her escapes; look for an in-between move before moving an attacked queen.
8. Line familiarity in Learn ('you've met this many times', 'you haven't faced the main line'). This exists only as a Review intro, which still speaks numbers.

FOUND IN PASSING, verified by running the real detectors from the scratchpad (read-only):

(a) D10 RISK, at the note-6543 board.
- Board: r4rk1/pp3pb1/2npp2p/2q1n1p1/4P2P/1B2NbB1/P1PQNPP1/1R3RK1 w
- The reference coach teaches that Black's bishop on f3 is immune: gxf3 Nxf3+ forks king and queen.
- findHangingBySee (positionReadingService.ts:361) returns that bishop as hanging, gain 2.
- findRemovableGuards (tacticsDetector.ts:629) offers White 'the knight on e5 is the only defender of the bishop on f3 — and it can be taken'. But Bxe5 is answered by Nxe5, which restores the guard.
- heldByTactic (speedRunReads.ts:162) cannot catch it. It requires more attackers than defenders (:169) and gives up whenever SEE says the capture wins (:170).

(b) PIN-PRESSURE BLIND SPOT, at the note-6318 board.
- Board: r1bqr1k1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/8/3BP3/PP1B1N2/2PN1PPP/R2QK2R b KQ
- findPinPressure (pinPressure.ts:85) returns nothing for Black before …d5. canLeaveLine (pinGeometry.ts:80) only counts a pawn's capture when there is already something on the capture square.
- So the pawn strike that creates the bite is exactly the move it can never suggest. After …d5, detectTactics does report the pin.

(c) V8 (numbers in speech).
- openingRecordBeat.ts:33-35 speaks ordinal game counts and a percentage in the Review intro.
- openingIdentity.ts:124 and :139 speak move counts as digits.

(d) tempoCount.ts:58-59 deliberately returns null on a capture. So 'their bishop moved twice just to take a knight that moved once' can never be said.

The reference coach's name is not used anywhere in this report.
RHYTHM: Measured on the 444 distilled notes (word count of the note text):
- Overall median: 22 words.
- Opening: the student's own moves median 25, the opponent's 18.
- Middlegame: own 24, theirs 21.
- Endgame: own 19, theirs 11.

17% of notes are a bare move statement of 8 words or fewer. That rises to 28% on the opponent's middlegame moves and 36% on the opponent's endgame moves. Recaptures, king shuffles and forced replies get one clause, never a lecture.

Long notes (60+ words, 15 in all) come at decisions and lean early:
- 9 are tagged opening, and all 15 fall by ply 34. This matches F02 (opening first).
- Examples: a three-candidate recapture decision (#6309, 317 words); the plan for a whole gambit main line (#6241, 411 words); a gambit's idea (#6306, 115); a strategic defence plus a habit (#6279); a calculated rejection of a candidate (#6526, 95); the queen-escape check (#6525); a calculation habit (#6442); a game's whole-board lessons (#6313, 177).

Order inside a long note is stable:
1. Frame the moment as a decision.
2. List the candidates.
3. Give each one's consequence.
4. The geometric check that settles it (escape squares, who guards what).
5. The line with their best reply.
6. Their likely mistake and why.
7. A safety check before cashing in.
8. The simplest win.
9. A closing maxim or habit.

Other patterns:
- In two book runs (#6226-6237, #6242-6252), one thought spans several plies while the moves go quickly: the narration is about the line, not the ply.
- 127 of 414 consecutive-note transitions skip at least one ply, so the distilled corpus does not carry a note on every ply.
- Opponent moves are framed by INTENT ('they are steering into X', 'that is a mediocre choice') rather than described.
- About 12 notes pose a rhetorical question and answer it at once.
- About 20 notes speak in the first person ('I like', 'I got greedy'). The act inside them, usually a better alternative, is kept; the self-reference must go (V1).
- Names the opening system the moment it appears, together with what that system is built to do and what the student's job is against it (The opponent's defining move, or the student's first system move (plies 2-7)) e.g. This is the quiet anti-Sicilian with c3 — its whole point is d4 next, so your task is to stop that big centre before it forms. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity.ts:85 openingIdentityLine (provokes, aims, gambit, sharp, famous) and openingAnnouncement.ts (first-identification rule; transposition sentence at :82). MISSING: the goal-for-you clause ('your job is to stop d4') and the system's character ('the fighting, unbalanced reply').
- Gives a soundness verdict on the opponent's opening choice, together with how common it is at the student's level (The defining move of an offbeat system, or the move that leaves main theory) e.g. This bishop sortie turns up all the time at club level, but it simply isn't a good answer to your setup. -> PARTIAL. openingAnnouncement.ts:166 theirOpeningVerdict (dubious vs the main move, with engine cost). refutedAlternativeCore.ts:117 (level frequency in words). MISSING: a verdict on the whole system ('this defence hands over the centre'); IdentityFacts has no soundness field (openingIdentity.ts:18-26).
- Explains why their mediocre move is mediocre as a balanced ledger: credit what it does, then list each cost (An opponent's opening inaccuracy) e.g. Their c3 does support the knight and dulls your bishop a little — but it develops nothing, takes c3 away from their own knight, and leaves them passive. -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 (new outpost for you, their own bishop shut in, castling lost, lasting concessions). moveIntent.ts:362-366 (what their move prepares). MISSING facets: 'takes the natural square from its own piece', 'develops nothing', and the credit half.
- Punishes a premature or passive opening move by naming the exact follow-up that exploits it (The move after an opponent slip in the first ten moves) e.g. Because they pushed d6 before taking on d4, d5 now grabs space and kicks the knight — and every retreat spoils their pawns. -> PARTIAL. positionalRead.ts:273 and reviewOpponentCommentary.ts:185/:222 (open the position against an undeveloped setup). refutedAlternativeCore.ts (line + concept). The gem/punish library (gemFinder.ts:286). The punishment is rarely tied back to the slip's specific defect.
- Springs an opening trap and explains it: hold the tension first, then the threat, why there is no good answer, and why players fall for it. Also warns 'a trap is lurking here' (The ply the trap becomes live, or one ply before as a warning) e.g. Don't take on c5 — keep the tension. Now the knight jumps to b5 aiming at a fork on c7, and the only defence is an ugly king move. -> PARTIAL. trapLearning.ts:105 trapSpeaks, openingTrapDetector.ts:79 detectTrapInPosition, gemFinder.ts:286 (F04: still about 8 separate trap systems). The 'hold the tension so the trap stays live' step is not linked to the trap.
- Holds tension and says the concrete reason releasing it helps them (A pawn-tension standoff in the opening) e.g. Taking on d4 now would only open c3 for their knight — let them be the one to release it. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:49 keepTension gives only the generic reason ('that helps them'). MISSING: the concrete payoff of releasing (which square or file it hands them).
- Develops a piece specifically to take away the square the opponent's planned break needs (Before the opponent's thematic break) e.g. Put the bishop on c4 straight away — the whole point is that they never get d5 in. -> moveIntent.ts:124, the PREVENTS read ('h3 — so the bishop can't come to g4'), phrased at :351-358.
- One move, several jobs: lists every job a move does (Developing or regrouping moves that serve several purposes) e.g. The queen to d2 gets ready to castle long, hits a piece, and prepares to swing over to the king later — three jobs at once. -> PARTIAL. moveIntent.ts:351 ('does two jobs: it stops X and prepares Y'). Defending, hitting a piece and centralising are separate producers (moveFundamentals.ts:507 'with tempo'), never joined into one count.
- Develops with tempo: the best developing move carries a threat, including castling with check (Any developing move that also attacks) e.g. Castle long with check — the king tucks away and you gain a free move at the same time. -> PARTIAL. moveFundamentals.ts:507 (with tempo, hitting X). MISSING: castling with check as a free move.
- Tempo arithmetic: counts the moves spent, including inside a trade (An opponent trade or a repeated piece move in the opening) e.g. Their bishop has used two moves just to take a knight that moved once — you are a move up out of that trade. -> PARTIAL. tempoCount.ts:32 (a piece's third move). It returns null on any capture by design (tempoCount.ts:58-59), so the trade count is MISSING.
- Shows the payoff of a deferred move: holding a pawn back lets it be played in one step later, or turns out not to be needed (After the opponent commits, or when a held-back pawn is finally played) e.g. Because you never spent a move on a6, the trade on c6 cost them time, not you — and you never committed d6, so d5 now comes in one go. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:549 flexibleFirst (forward version only); moveOrder.ts:65 (the student's own move order). - Gambit compensation: what you get for the pawn, and the clock on it (Gambit decisions in the opening) e.g. Don't bother defending d4 — give it up for development, space and a grip on e5. Checked on the #6200 board (r1bk4/1pp2p1p/p4nr1/2p1p3/2BnP2Q/2NP4/PPP2PPP/R4RK1 w): detectTactics reports only White's own pin. The sacrificial knight check that rips open the g-file under a rook already on g6 is not a static threat anywhere; threatOut.ts:13-16 says its played-out extension is not built.
- Phantom threat: it looks scary, but names the guard already in place (An opponent move that hits near the student's king or pieces) e.g. That knight jump looks like it sets up mate on h2, but your knight on f3 already covers h2 — don't spend a move on it. -> bluffDetector.ts:37 detectBluff; falseAlarm.ts:37.
- Conditional threat: names the single condition that would make their idea work (An apparent tactic for either side that fails on one detail) e.g. Their knight to c7 would only bite if your rook were already on e8 — it isn't, so the rook steps to b8 and nothing happens. -> MISSING.
- Loose but safe: an undefended piece is fine when nothing can fork it and everything else is covered (A centralised loose piece after a pawn grab) e.g. Your knight on e4 has no defender, but nothing of theirs can fork it and the rest of your pieces are covered, so it stays. -> MISSING as a verdict. Building blocks: loosePieces.ts:35 findLoosePieces, latentFork.ts:161 detectLatentFork, forkTrick.ts:81 forkTrickFor.
- Queen-grab safety check: before snatching with the queen, list her escape squares and ask whether one move takes them all (Pawn grabs with the queen ('poisoned pawn' situations)) e.g. Before taking on b2, count where the queen can run — a3, a5, c5 — far too many for one move to cover, so the pawn is safe to take. -> MISSING as a predictive check. tacticsDetector.ts:451 findTrappedPieces only reads the present board.
- Before moving an attacked queen, look for an in-between move, and make sure they have no checking desperado (The student's queen is attacked) e.g. Before you move the queen, see whether a capture in between comes first — and check they can't hit back with a queen check that takes something. -> MISSING. MethodHabit has 4 kinds (methodBeat.ts:60) and LiveHabit has 4 (methodBeat.ts:291); zwischenzug has no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:60-64).
- The immune piece, and the piece that survives only on a tactic (A piece placed deep in enemy territory) e.g. They can take your bishop on f3, but then your knight forks king and queen — so it is untouchable. Keep checking it, though: if their queen leaves d2, the protection is gone. -> PARTIAL / D10 RISK. speedRunReads.ts:162 heldByTactic cannot fire here: it needs more attackers than defenders (:169) and skips whenever SEE says the capture wins (:170). Verified on the #6543 board: positionReadingService.ts:361 findHangingBySee calls this bishop hanging, and tacticsDetector.ts:629 findRemovableGuards offers White a removal of the guard that fails (Bxe5 Nxe5 restores the guard; gxf3 walks into Nxf3+).
- A tied guard: a piece's tactic or protection depends on another piece staying put (After a regrouping that ties a piece to a duty) e.g. Their knight can't give that check now — it is the only thing guarding their queen, so the moment it moves, the queen falls. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:567 queenGlue (the queen as sole guard of two pieces); tacticsDetector.ts:690 findOverloadedPieces (needs two targets). MISSING: a single 'it is tied, it cannot leave' reason in the threat and answer lanes.
- A pin that bans a capture: a pawn pinned along a file can still push but cannot take, so strike it with a pawn (An enemy king on a file opened by your rook) e.g. Their e4 pawn sits on the file between your rook and their king — it can't capture, so d5 attacks it and wins it; and if they castle out of it, your pawn forks two pieces. -> PARTIAL / VERIFIED GAP. pinPressure.ts:85 findPinPressure returns nothing for Black before d5, because pinGeometry.ts:80 canLeaveLine only counts a pawn's capture when something is already on the capture square. After d5 the pin appears.
- A pinned piece no longer defends — attack whatever it was guarding (A pin lands on a defender) e.g. Their f2 pawn is now pinned to the king, so it stopped protecting the knight on g3 — bring the rook to the g-file. -> PARTIAL. Legal SEE accounts for it silently (positionReadingService.ts:212 legalSeeGainFor). It is voiced only in the How-to-Think lesson (thinkingExchangeChain.ts:131). MISSING as a live or Review reason.
- Pin management: whose pin is stronger; hold the pin; keep it through a recapture; a pin becomes permanent once the bishop that could challenge it is gone; a pin is not automatically useful (Long-standing pins in the middlegame) e.g. Recapture with the knight, not the bishop — that keeps your pin. They've already traded their light-squared bishop, so nothing can ever challenge your pinning bishop. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:194 mutualPins ('whoever breaks free first wins; kicking costs pawn cover'). MISSING: pin durability (no same-coloured bishop left to challenge the pinner), recapture-to-keep-the-pin (recaptureChoice.ts:56-99 has no pin facet), and 'a vague pin vs a piece doing specific work'.
- Chooses how to break a pin: a quiet unpin, an unpin with tempo, or castling (two problems solved with one move) (The student is pinned in the opening) e.g. Castle — it breaks the pin and finishes development in one go; the pawn poke at the bishop is the reflex, not the answer. -> PARTIAL. reviewMoveTeaching.ts:205 unpinPoint (says that a move unpinned); threatAnswer.ts:58 (answers to a threat). MISSING: a comparison of the ways to unpin.
- Pins the king to the queen on the open file and forces the trade on your terms, with the habit of looking for second- and seventh-rank checks when a file opens toward the kings (A central file opens with kings and queens still on it) e.g. The e-file just opened toward both kings — look for the check along it: the queen to e2 pins their queen to their king and they must trade on your terms. -> PARTIAL. tacticsDetector.ts:193 findPins. MISSING: the habit.
- A pawn push's drawback: the square behind it, or the diagonal it opens next to the king (Any pawn move, by either side, especially in the opening) e.g. e5 is playable, but it leaves d5 soft for good — strike with d5 instead. And when their pawn moves beside their king, look straight down the diagonal it just opened. -> PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60 (their moves); concessionBeat.ts:31-36 'outpost-conceded' and 'pawn-weakened' (played moves); reviewTeachingPoints.ts:557 describeNotableMove (wing pushes); speedRunReads.ts:224 positionOpened (only when a slider of yours already stands on the opened line). MISSING: scoring a REJECTED pawn push in the weighing, and the 'look at the diagonal it opened' habit.
- Restricts their piece with your pawn: blunts a bishop, or shuts it out of the game (Answering an active enemy bishop) e.g. e6 takes the life out of their c4 bishop and prepares d5; later g5 cuts their other bishop off from the game. -> MISSING. boardDelta.ts:65 BLOCKS only covers your own sliders; theirMoveCost.ts:60 only covers their own pawn shutting in their own bishop.
- A wedge pawn that cramps their setup, and that pays off later (Anti-Alapin and other centre fights) e.g. Jam a pawn on d4 before they get there; a few moves later that same pawn covers c3, so their knight can't block your check. -> MISSING. reviewConcepts.ts:478 only says 'space/cramping' in general. The later payoff could ride the GamePromise thread (speedRunReads.ts:36).
- Outpost technique: remove the defender of the square, then plant the knight (Fixed holes in the enemy structure) e.g. To get a knight to d5 you first remove the knight on f6 that guards it — the bishop takes it, and d5 is yours. -> PARTIAL. outpost.ts:39 isOutpost; speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole; moveInsight.ts:1102 holeAccess. MISSING: 'trade off the guard of the square first' (speedRunReads.ts:463 preparationOf handles capture targets only).
- A centralised piece is only as strong as it is hard to chase: anchored vs unanchored pieces (An enemy piece lands in the centre without pawn cover) e.g. Their knight on e5 looks impressive, but f4 will kick it — so take it, and keep the f-pawn push for later, with tempo. -> PARTIAL. outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge (the underlying check); moveFundamentals.ts:395 ('kick it with a pawn and gain the time'). MISSING: 'that is not an outpost — plan the chase'.
- Judges imbalances: the bishop pair vs knights on an open board, and doubled pawns accepted in return for the bishops (After minor-piece trades) e.g. One doubled pawn is nothing next to keeping both bishops on an open board. -> reviewConcepts.ts:272; nextPlans.ts:335; tradeQuality.ts:124 readTrade (bishop pair given up).
- Provokes the trade you want, and knows when NOT to put the question to a bishop (An enemy bishop pins or eyes your minor) e.g. a3 makes them take on c3 and hands you the two bishops — worth the move. But that other bishop isn't doing anything and will probably take anyway, so don't waste a move chasing it. -> MISSING. speedRunReads.ts:125 provokes covers pawn commitments only; threatAnswer.ts asks the question only against a pin threat.
- Keeps the fianchetto bishop, because it guards the holes your own pawn moves made (Exchange offers against a fianchetto, and trading off the opponent's dark-squared defender) e.g. Don't give that long-diagonal bishop away cheaply — it is what covers the squares your g6 left behind. -> MISSING. tradeQuality.ts:48 kingGuardCount counts it only while the king is under fire.
- Trade decisions tied to the position, not to material alone (Every exchange offer) e.g. You have the extra space, so don't trade — it would let them breathe. Taking on b6 would open the f-file for them; drop back so that if they take, the a-file opens for you. Swap the queens and their attack is gone, even if the pawn goes back. -> PARTIAL. tradeQuality.ts:124 (piece quality, king defence, bishop pair, ahead/behind); deliberation.ts:232 (don't trade queens with space or an attack); conversionMethod.ts:123 (trade when ahead). MISSING: space → keep the non-queen pieces on; which side's file the trade opens; trading to defuse their attack; 'only when the trade comes free'.
- Identifies the single most important feature of the position and makes it the plan (Quiet middlegames after an opening transformation) e.g. The worst thing in your position is their pawn on e5 choking your pieces — challenge it with f6 and get rid of it, whatever it costs. -> PARTIAL. positionCharacter.ts:59 characterOf (what the position is about); boardPlan.ts:84 structurePlan. MISSING: a ranking of the one feature that matters most.
- Sorts problems into temporary and permanent (Choosing between fixing a piece and fixing the king or structure) e.g. That awkward bishop sorts itself out in a move or two; get the king safe and the rooks working first. -> PARTIAL. conceptEngine.ts:787-788 (pawn weakness = permanent; development lead = temporary). MISSING: a general sorter.
- Multi-move plans and patience: attacks take time, bring the reserves, make useful waiting moves, and admit when a plan has failed (Middlegames without immediate tactics) e.g. Prepare b4 with a3 first — plans now take two or three moves. And when their reply refutes your knight jump, bring the knight back rather than insisting. -> PARTIAL. lookaheadPlan.ts:1103 buildLookaheadPlan; planArc.ts:236 stepArc; kingAttack.ts:71; speedRunReads.ts:307 usefulWaiting. MISSING: noticing that the student's OWN plan has been refuted, and 'decide the queen's square relative to the rook first'.
- The practical choice: the move that sets the opponent the most problems (Several sound options of different sharpness) e.g. The quiet d6 is fine, but the knight leap to g4 asks far harder questions of them. -> MISSING as a fact. Building block: criticalityScan.ts:103 scanCriticality (could measure how many only-moves the opponent faces).
- Places the king by the structure: into a closed centre, onto the side whose pawns are intact, long when queens are off so the rook joins at once (Castling decisions, and middlegame king walks) e.g. With the queens gone, castle long — your king is in no danger, and the rook lands on the open file in the same move. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:108 castleSide (pawn cover only); ruleException.ts:70 (closed centre, for f- and g-pawn pushes). MISSING: 'the king is safer in the closed centre' and 'castle long to activate the rook'.
- Runs a winning checklist when ahead (After winning material) e.g. An extra queen up: hold the centre, keep developing, stop their threats, and don't overpress — trade when trades come naturally, then make a passed pawn, and watch for stalemate at the end. -> conversionMethod.ts:44 readConversion (step texts at :108-132); stalemateWatch.ts:24; safetyHabits.ts:54 keepPressing.
- Passed-pawn technique: choose the passer your pieces can escort; bishops escort, knights block badly; patience over a hasty push (Endgames with an extra pawn) e.g. You have two passers, but push the c-pawn — your bishops already control the squares in front of it. Don't run it yet either: bring the last rook in first, so they can't simply give a rook for it. -> PARTIAL. reviewTeachingPoints.ts:252 (knights are poor blockers); endgamePawnReads.ts:52 passerKinds. MISSING: choosing a passer by who controls its path, and 'don't push yet — they'd give a rook for it'.
- In the endgame the king is a fighter; don't hurry; an attack can live on without the queens (Queens off) e.g. Walk the king toward the centre — no need to castle — and improve one step at a time rather than rushing. -> PARTIAL. moveFundamentals.ts:680-682 (king to the centre); kingAttack.ts:71. MISSING: the 'do not hurry' maxim as a live fact (it exists only as lesson text).
- With no forced mate, cash in the material, and don't get drunk on combinations (Winning tactical positions) e.g. There's no mate here — they can always block with the bishop — so just take the rook with check and win cleanly. -> MISSING. groundedAnswer.ts:1343 ('take the simplest road home') is chat-only. thinkAloud.ts:71 lineAchieves tells mate apart from material but never states the preference.
- Several moves win — picks the cleanest and says the others also worked (Decided positions) e.g. The rook lift also wins, but the knight check finishes it fastest. -> MISSING. speedRunReads.ts:68 anyMoveFine covers only quiet, equal choices.
- Named habits of thought, each attached to the trigger that calls for it (At the moment the trigger appears) e.g. Start calculating with the simplest move. When their bishop sits on e3, keep an eye out for a knight hit followed by a queen double attack. The closer the action is to your king, the more careful you must be. Survey every option before playing the obvious check. -> PARTIAL. methodBeat.ts:296 liveMethodBeat (opponent-threat, forcing-scan, loose-trigger, candidates); countMethod.ts:17; checkMethod.ts:32; safetyHabits.ts:25,:42,:54; kneeJerk.ts:15. - Asks a rhetorical question, then answers it (think-aloud framing) (The start of an explanation at a key move) e.g. Why is that a mistake? Because it lets you gain space with tempo. Castle short or long? Long. -> PARTIAL. threatAnswer.ts:58 (question first, answer second, rotated). MISSING in the general composer (F18).
- Appearance vs reality: it looks awkward, ugly or like a blunder, and here is why it is right; the general rule gives way to the concrete point (Moves that break a beginner rule) e.g. The queen on e3 looks clumsy, but it watches everything. Normally you'd keep the bishop, but taking with the knight lets them recapture with tempo — the rule bends here. -> PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:82 uglyButRight (doubled pawns, or a piece walked home); ruleException.ts:70 (three rules); speedRunReads.ts:267 playAnyway. MISSING: the awkward-square case, 'blocks its own bishop for a reason', and the preserve-the-bishop rule.
- Says routine moves in one plain clause and saves the words for decisions (Recaptures, forced replies, king shuffles, endgame moves) e.g. They take back with the knight. The king steps to e7. -> spokenMove.ts:68 sayMoveClause; continuationMoveNarration.ts:75 narrateContinuationMove.

GamePromise (speedRunReads.ts:36); causalChain.ts:639 buildCausalChain; planArc.ts:236. MISSING: promises for prophylactic rook moves and wedge pawns.
- Credits a real game for an idea (game credit only, never a person's teaching) (Opening structures with a classic model) e.g. This exact pawn advance comes from a famous game — it fixes the dark-square holes for good. -> PARTIAL. openingIdentity.ts:143-145 'famous' (real master games). No live structure-matched game lookup (swarm question 2).

## Source 27
I read all 444 notes in the slice (6590–7033): 19 videos, split 176 opening, 169 middlegame and 99 endgame. They contain 63 distinct teaching acts. I checked each one against the teaching census (2026-09-27) and the insight catalogue in docs/. 35 are new or only partly covered. Of those 35, 20 have no computer at all and 15 are partial: a computer reaches the fact but cannot say the mechanism, or it is wired for one seat only.

One finding about the brief comes first. Its FIRST GEM does not work as written. The line is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Bg4 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Ng5+. After 5.Ng5+, chess.js lists 5...Qxg5 among Black's legal replies: the d8 queen sees g5 through the empty e7 and f6 squares. After 5...Qxg5 the g4 bishop is guarded by the queen, so White is simply down a piece. Even the line as written (5...Ke8 6.Qxg4) only nets one pawn: material comes out 36 to 35.

Note 6601 is the real-game version where the pattern does work. It is an Alapin position after 7...Qxd6 8.O-O, and the coach calls ...Bg4 there "an incredibly common blunder". On that board no Black piece attacks g5 and nothing guards g4 (the Black queen is on d6), so 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Ng5+ followed by 11.Qxg4 is legal. By count it still nets only a pawn plus Black's castling rights; I could not get an engine value (no binary at /usr/games/stockfish). Under F04 this is a pattern taught with its conditions, not a trap. Note 6601 is the right position to teach it on, and the brief's line is the right position to show it failing. None of the 344 gems in src/data/punish-gems.json contains Bxf7+ followed by Ng5+, and none holds the Fried Liver slip (recapturing with the knight on d5) that note 6801 warns against.

The most valuable missed acts, opening first per F02:
- A pattern taught by the condition that decides it.
- En passant as a structural weapon.
- Which move commits you to an opening, and which moves are only gateways.
- An opening rule of thumb stated with its reason.
- A purposeless opponent move treated as a free tempo whose cost arrives later.
- Choosing h3 over f3 by what each weakens.
- The Greek-gift conditions used defensively ("castle, it doesn't work here"). This is an F4 gap: moveInsight.greekGift (moveInsight.ts:668) only fires when the sacrifice is the best move.
- Their own piece blocking their own pawn or development.
- Don't kick a misplaced enemy piece; the attack only improves it.
- The principle of two weaknesses.
- Self-interference: the checking piece blocks your own line to the flight square.
- A mating net one guard away, with the trap that needs one natural pawn push.
- Trapping a piece, or fixing a king in place, by taking its last escape square first. escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701) covers only a check that becomes mate.
- The castling rule when it is the obstacle.
- Counting the pawn-storm race; planRace (planRace.ts:180) deliberately excludes it.
- Imbalance trading rules for two minors against a rook.
- Engine verdict versus practical difficulty. The census calls this "not a computer", but scanCriticality (criticalityScan.ts:103) run for both sides would compute it.

Defects in the shipped corpus (public/data/voiced-teachings.json; S7 speaks these in "teach me X opening"), all checked on the board:
- Note 6720 says a8=N is checkmate; the stored position is not even check.
- Note 6984 says the rook underpromotion avoids stalemate, but e8=Q+ also gives check with the same four king replies.
- Note 6984 says Re5 starts a mate in two; after either king reply (Kc3 or Kc4) White has no mate in one.
- Notes 6733–6737 are tagged studentSide black but tell the student White's moves ("you don't play a knight to f3"), a V16 seat inversion.
- In notes 6834–6835 the student is White, but White's own 2.Ba6 is narrated as the opponent's move and Black's recapture as the student's.
- "elephant", a transcription error for "Alapin", appears 8 times corpus-wide, 4 in this slice (6592, 6614, 6721, 6722).
- Note 6995 says "Panov" where the King's Indian line is the Panno, and attributes a recommendation to a named player (F0d).
- Garbled text at 6996 ("onethe") and 6999 ("Heretwo").
- 42 of 444 notes speak in the first person (V1), and 3 cite ratings (V8).

Two items in the catalogue need care:
- Its "Imbalances" bullet (line 408) says two minors against a rook usually favour the rook. This slice teaches the opposite (6637, 6887, 6892).
- Its type 12 copies "activity matters less in an endgame" (from 6927). That is unsound as a general rule; build only the defensible form: without queens, their active pieces cannot build a mating attack.
RHYTHM: Measured on this slice. The corpus is a compressed paraphrase; the thinkAloud.ts header measured the raw spoken narration at about 50 words a move (20–47 on routine moves, 90–133 at decisions), so these counts understate the spoken length.

- Opening: 176 notes, median 18 words, mean 22.5. 34 notes are 8 words or fewer and 25 are 40 or more (longest 143).
- Middlegame: 169 notes, median 19, mean 25.5. 29 are 8 words or fewer and 29 are 40 or more (longest 146).
- Endgame: 99 notes, median 12, mean 12.4. 35 are 8 words or fewer and none reach 40 (longest 35).
- 60 of 444 notes are bare restatements of the move ("Black recaptures on d5."), always on routine replies.
- 192 of 444 notes sit on the opponent's move: he narrates their moves too, usually as what it wants, what it cost them, or what they should have played.

Shape:
- In the opening, a lecture video (the Alapin, notes 6590–6618) gives every move several points: theory status, the move's job, what the opponent could have played and why that is scary, and the plan ahead. Speed-run games give routine book moves one clause and spend words where the opponent deviates (6629: their a3 is a wasted move).
- Long notes cluster at decision points (6604, 6617, 6618, 6802). Their internal order: the move's real point, then what it fixes or denies, then the tempting alternative and why it helps the opponent, then the line with their reply, then a list of things to watch, then one general lesson ("two weaknesses", "calculate on your turn").
- The middlegame alternates one-clause moves with a full weighing whenever there are real candidates (6611 changes its mind twice).
- The endgame is one technical clause per move ("king first", "push, don't grab") plus a safety check before the finish (stalemate, 6705–6719). The game closes on a one-sentence moral (6720, 6758).
- Foreshadowing ("there's a concrete point coming", "I'm anticipating b6") and rhetorical questions answered at once ("Where does the knight go?") carry the thread from move to move.
- [NEW] Teach a trap pattern by the condition that decides it, on a real position where the condition holds (Opening, before the opponent's most natural mistake) e.g. Note 6601 names ...Bg4 as a very common blunder after the queen recaptures on d6 in this Alapin, but gives no refutation. On the board the refutation is the rulebook's own pattern: the bishop takes f7 with check, the knight jumps out of the pin with check, and the queen takes g4. It works here because their queen on d6 cannot reach g5 and nothing guards g4 (chess.js: no Black attacker of either square). In the brief's own first-gem line it fails, because the queen on d8 simply takes the knight on g5. -> MISSING: there is no 'pin broken with check' computer (questions.md item 7). 0 of 344 gems in src/data/punish-gems.json contain 'Bxf7+ ... Ng5+', so the Learn gem lane (computerRoles.ts:47 → punishGems) has nothing to voice.
- [NEW] En passant as a structural weapon, and as a decision (Opening, when an en passant capture is available or a later push would allow one) e.g. 6597: the reply they didn't play was the scary ...c4, because once you push d4 they take en passant and break your chain, leaving e5 without its base. 6598: take en passant now, or they get their ideal setup with the bishop out to g4; taking also keeps your bishop's diagonal open. -> MISSING: no teaching computer mentions en passant (it appears only in edge-case handling in pinGeometry.ts, positionFacts.ts and groundedAnswer.ts).
- [NEW] Name the move that commits you to an opening, and the moves that only open doors (Opening, at a transposition crossroads) e.g. 6991: you haven't chosen the King's Indian yet; d6 commits you, while c6 and d5 could still head for a Grünfeld-style setup. 7008: their c3 has no value of its own, it's a doorway to the London, the Torre or a fianchetto, so wait for them to show their cards. -> MISSING: openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (openingIdentity.ts:85) renders only what the opening provokes, aims for, whether it is a gambit, how sharp it is and famous games. Computable from openings-lichess.json by comparing the set of named lines reachable before and after the move.
- [NEW] State an opening's rule of thumb together with the reason that makes it true (Opening, when the thematic break is one move premature) e.g. 6629-6630: the central break is almost playable, but before you castle their bishop check on b5 pins your c6 knight against your king. So in this opening the rule is: break in the centre only after castling. -> Partial: moveOrder (moveOrder.ts:65) proves a swap only when the reply wins material by count, and pinGeometry.isRealPin finds the pin itself. Nothing generalises the pin into the opening's rule.
- [NEW] Treat a purposeless opponent move as a free tempo, then show when its cost arrives (Opening, on the quiet pawn move, and again when its cost lands) e.g. 6629: their a3 stops nothing, because nothing of yours was heading for b4, so play as if you'd been handed a free move. 6636, moves later: they pay for that a3 now, because in the normal version their king would already be castled. 6806 notes the same kind of move in another game. -> Partial: tempoCount (tempoCount.ts:32) only counts a piece moved for the third time. moveIntent on their seat (moveIntent.ts:124) can prove a move prevents and prepares nothing, but no beat turns that into 'a free move'. causalChain (causalChain.ts:639) links only tactic chains, not a slow move to a later cost.
- [NEW] Choose between two stopping pawn moves by what each one weakens (Opening prophylaxis against a knight jump) e.g. 6743: to keep their knight off g4 you can push the rook pawn or the bishop pawn. Nearly always take the rook pawn, because the bishop pawn weakens far too much, and with your king going long the h-pawn also becomes the anchor for a later push at their king. -> Partial: moveIntent (moveIntent.ts:124, stopReason :383) proves either move stops the jump. thinkAloud.obviousStopFlaw (thinkAloud.ts:302) covers only h3 creating a hook against a pinning bishop. The cost comparison between the two moves is MISSING.
- [NEW] Leave a misplaced enemy piece alone: attacking it only sends it somewhere better (Middlegame, when a natural attacking move targets a badly placed piece) e.g. 6604: the rook to e1 hitting their queen on e6 is tempting, but that queen is good for you where it stands, because it blocks their own e-pawn and so their bishop. Chasing it would only help them develop. -> Partial: moveInsight.emptyThreat (moveInsight.ts:909) catches 'the target steps away and you are no better', not 'the target ends up better'. Needs piece quality (pieceValueRead) compared before and after the retreat.
- [NEW] Point out that their own piece is blocking their own pawn or development (Middlegame; it also feeds the pawn-storm race count) e.g. 6603: they'd love ...e6 to free their bishop, but their queen sits on e6 and has to move first, which costs time. 6844 and 6850: their bishop on g5 stands exactly where their g-pawn needs to go, so the storm they wanted in one move now takes several. -> MISSING for their seat: speedRunReads.retreatKeepsBreak (speedRunReads.ts:421) handles only your own piece standing in front of your own pawn, and only when the engine retreats it.
- [NEW] Answer the 'no bishop of that colour' objection: the queen can use the weak colour too (Middlegame, after the matching bishop has been traded) e.g. 6608: pushing to a6 leaves weak light squares in their camp. It seems you can't use them without your light-squared bishop, but the queen moves on diagonals as well and will be the piece that gets in. -> MISSING (the catalogue's colour-complex type is still unbuilt).
- [NEW] Show that their recapture sealed your own weakness (Middlegame, after an exchange changes the structure in front of your weak pawn) e.g. 6853: after they take back on d5, that pawn plugs the centre and walls your backward d6-pawn off from the d-file, which is the very weakness they were pressing. -> MISSING: theirMoveCost (theirMoveCost.ts:60) names what their move cost them, never what it handed you.
- [NEW] The principle of two weaknesses (Middlegame squeeze) e.g. 6617: their queenside is already weak, and the queen to g4 forces kingside weaknesses too. A defender stretched across both wings cannot hold both. -> MISSING: 'two weaknesses' exists only as concept-tag wording; no detector counts weaknesses per wing.
- [NEW] Use thinking time by turn: calculate on yours, think about plans on theirs (Any phase; a method line suited to the opponent's turn in Learn) e.g. 6617: work out concrete lines when it is your move; while they think, build your picture of the position, its weak squares and its plans. -> MISSING: methodBeat.liveMethodBeat (methodBeat.ts:296) only has habits for their threat, the forcing scan, loose pieces and candidates.
- [NEW] Say what a threat is really for: forcing a winning transition, not winning the piece it hits (Middlegame, when the cleanest win is an ending you can already see) e.g. 6618: the rook to d1 threatens c4, not to win their knight but to force trades into an endgame where your knight reaches b5 and their a7-pawn falls. In the same note, the greedy capture fails because your rooks aren't connected and your back rank is mated. -> MISSING: deliberation explains the line, not the purpose behind the threat.
- [NEW] Trap a piece by taking away its last escape square first (Middlegame or endgame, a piece short of squares) e.g. 6901-6902: their rook is nearly trapped. a4 would trap it except that it can escape to d5, so first your rook goes to d1 to cover d5, and then a4 has no answer. -> Partial: moveIntent's 'prepares' read (moveIntent.ts:124) can prove 'Rd1 so that a4' with the engine but never names the escape square. escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701) covers only a check turning into mate, and tacticsDetector.findTrappedPieces (tacticsDetector.ts:451) sees the piece only once it is already trapped.
- [NEW] Fix the enemy king in place before you attack it (Middlegame attack on a king that can still slip away) e.g. 7021-7022: the queen to a5 looks good, but their king could run to b1 and a1. - [NEW] Teach the castling rule when it is the obstacle: you can't castle through a square they control (Middlegame or endgame, when castling is blocked by an attacked square) e.g. 6674: you'd like to castle long, but their rook on the d-file controls a square your king must cross. - [NEW] Self-interference: the checking piece can block your own line to the escape square (Middlegame mating attack with two ways to check) e.g. 6749: the natural knight check is not mate, because that knight lands on the line your queen needs to cover the king's escape square. A piece that moves can cut a line you were relying on. -> MISSING: moveInsight.mechanismContrast (moveInsight.ts:459) compares only 'hits two things' against 'hits one'. - [NEW] Note a mating net that is one guard away, then set the trap that needs one natural pawn push (Middlegame, a boxed-in king with one guard on the key square) e.g. 6755: their king has no squares; remember that. 6757: after h6 and Bh4 you are hoping for ...g5, because then the knight to f6 is smothered mate; the only thing stopping it now is their g7-pawn covering f6. 6758: they push it, and it is mate. -> MISSING: matePatterns.classifyMatePattern (matePatterns.ts:341) names only a mate already delivered; latentDanger is about your own king; latentFork (latentFork.ts:161) covers forks only.

- [Known] Cover your weak square before they occupy it (Opening) e.g. 6843: develop the light bishop to e6 so it guards d5, and they can't just plant a knight there and blockade. -> Partial: moveIntent's 'prevents' read (moveIntent.ts:124)

- [Known] The hidden point of a quiet move (Opening and middlegame) e.g. 6768: c3 looks purely positional, but it opens the queen check on a4 while their king sits on e8. 6752: the bishop on c4 looks passive but is stored energy behind their e6-pawn. 6604: a4 looks like a one-move threat, but the point is pushing to a6 to fix a7 and the light squares. -> moveIntent.whatItDoes (moveIntent.ts:423) partial.
